en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases in the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Connected Discourses on the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatanasaṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Internal Impermanence (Ajjhattāniccasuttavaṇṇanā)

1. It is called *cakkhu* (eye) because it sees (*cakkhati*). The meaning is that it functions like one pointing out what is even or uneven by knowing the object according to its true nature; thus it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Likewise, there is the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*); for that too is called "eye" because it sees forms.

The "eye of the Buddhas" alone is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), because it is not shared [with others] regarding the views of eternalism and annihilationism within the continuums of sentient beings.

The knowledge that has clearly discerned, as they truly are, both the conformable knowledge and the knowledge of things-as-they-are, as well as the underlying tendencies such as the latent tendency to sensual lust, is the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*) and the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*).

The three lower paths, by way of their occurrence in accordance with the manner described for the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths, are the "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*); likewise, their respective fruits [are so called] in relation to their specific opposites.

Because it proceeds by way of abandonment through subsiding; because it accomplishes the function of the eye with respect to all phenomena on every side, it is the "all-around eye" (samantacakkhu), which is omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
Because it is to be obtained by relying upon the divine abode (dibbavihāra), it is like the divine eye of the devas;
thus it is the "divine eye" (dibbacakkhu), a specific supernormal power (abhiññā). It is called "by the pervading of light" because of seeing forms after having increased the light.
It is said: "Bhikkhus, regarding these things unheard of before, the eye arose in me that 'this is the noble truth of suffering,'" and so forth.
Because it has come down in this manner, the knowledge that defines the Four Truths is called the "eye of wisdom" (*paññā-cakkhu*).
Some call this "insight-knowledge" (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), while others say it is the "knowledges of reviewing the path and the fruit of insight."
They are called *sambhārā* because they are brought together (*abhisambharīyanti*) by these [elements] acting as conditions; they are the supporting material forms arising from the four causes.
"Together with the *sambhārā*" means *sasambhāraṃ*. It is called *pasāda* because it is clear (*pasīdati*) in dependence upon the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*).
"In the eye-sockets" means by both the eyelids (*akkhidalehi*). "Origin" (*sambhava*) refers specifically to the water element as that which has become the origin. Here...
It is stated, “thirteen requisites. However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it appears as “fourteen requisites,” including shape (*saṇṭhāna*).
Therein, “shape” refers simply to the sense-sphere of color (*vaṇṇāyatana*) existing in the form of circular and other such shapes.

The reason for mentioning it separately is that, within the aforementioned mass of flesh, there exist both those instances of the water-element and the sense-sphere of color that possess such shapes and those that do not.
Because of its existence. Regarding "arising" (*sambhava*), which is spoken of in dependence upon the four elements, one should apply the state of being dependent on the triad of elements.

In the phrase "in the circle of vision" (*diṭṭhimaṇḍale*): it refers to the circle that serves as the locus for the manifestation of the reflected image for those standing face-to-face, and which serves as the locus for the occurrence of vision—termed "eye"—consisting of the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*).
By the word "situated" (*sanniviṭṭha*), the fact that the eye-sensitivity consists of many groups of atoms (*kalāpa*) is indicated.
It is thus demonstrated; for it functions by pervading the seven layers of the eye-ball.

Because it remains by being supported—sustained and surrounded by the life-force (*āyu*), beauty (*vaṇṇa*), and other qualities that depend upon it and provide assistance through those [elements] situated by pervading the seven layers of the eye-ball—and because it persists while being propped up by the temperature (*utu*), consciousness (*citta*), and nutriment (*āhāra*) which originate the threefold continuity of material form, it is "capable of seeing visible forms."
Capable of seeing the visible base by means of consciousness that occurs dependent upon the self.
"Detailed exposition" refers to a detailed discussion of that eye and of the ear and so forth, both by way of causes, conditions, and so on, and by way of their characteristics and so on.
"The mind in the course of comprehension" is the mind that is to be seen with insight, serving as the locus for the occurrence of insight. Some...
They say it is "a functional consciousness associated with insight" (*vipassanupagata-kiriyamaya-citta*); that is merely their own opinion.
For the teaching proceeds by way of demonstrating the three characteristics, intensifying insight, and leading one to the state of Arahatship.
The commentary on the *Ajjhattānicca-sutta* is concluded.
2–3. Commentary on the *Ajjhattadukkhasutta* and others.
"Two characteristics" refers to the characteristics of suffering (*dukkha*) and non-self (*anatta*). "One characteristic" refers to the characteristic of non-self.
"The remaining ones" refers to the characteristics other than those already mentioned. "By them" means by those [suttas] by which the second and third discourses were taught. "Observed" means...
They have been correctly determined. "By this much" means by the statement of either two or one characteristic.
The commentary on the *Ajjhattadukkha-sutta* and others is finished.
4–6. Commentary on the *Bāhirānicca-sutta* and others.
4–6. *Vuttasadisova* means "exactly like what was stated" by way of the passage beginning with "two characteristics. *Naya* refers to the method of extended application (*atidesanaya*).
The commentary on the external impermanence suttas and so forth is concluded.
7–12. Commentary on the internal impermanence, past, future, and other suttas.
7–12. *Sallakkhetvā* (having observed): because the past and future do not exist, [the meditator] observes with a firm grasp;
because they do exist in the present, this is said with reference to those disciples who are weary of entering the path of insight due to a powerful grasping by way of craving and the like.
The commentary on the *Ajjhattāniccātītānāgatasutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Impermanence (*Aniccavagga*) is finished.
2. The Chapter on Pairs (*Yamakavagga*). 1–4.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Formerly Unawakened, etc. (*Paṭhamapubbesambodhasuttādivaṇṇanā*).
13–16. Since the teaching by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*) has the same flavor in both suttas, the single phrase "in the first and second" is extracted together as a compound.
That wherein the conceit "I am" (*ahaṃmāna*) is established is the self (*atta*); it is the personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Internal" (*ajjhatta*) means with reference to the self;
because they are included therein, those things existing therein are "internal" (*ajjhattika*). And what is called "internal" is that which is internal within the internal.
It is fourfold: the internal-internal (*niyakajjhatta*), the objective-internal (*gocarajjhatta*), and the object-internal (*visayajjhatta*).
Therein, because they exist within the internal and are thus internal, it says: “by way of the internal-internal, of the internal [bases] (*ajjhattikānan*)”.

Because these [bases], such as the eye and so forth, possess the state of being internal even among the internals due to being the objects of excessive affection, it says: “of desire and lust (*chandarāgassa*)...”
“Because of its extreme power. Now, demonstrating that meaning therein by means of an illustration together with its counterpart, he says, “Of human beings,” and so forth.
That is self-evident. “External” means those things existing outside of the internal.
The commentary on the first *Pubbesambodha Sutta* and others is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Non-Delight in the World, etc.
17–18. *Nikkhantā* means gone forth from the world. *Visaṃyuttā* means not bound, because of the abandoning of the defilements which are the causes of bondage.
*No adhimuttā* means not having set their hearts [on worldly things]. *Vimariyādī... pe... cetasā* means by a mind from which the boundary of the cycle of defilements has been removed.

With a mind that has not been made a basis for attachment. Only the Four Noble Truths have been explained here, because the gratification and so forth of the eye and the other [faculties] have already been explained.
The commentary on the first *Assāda-sutta* and others is concluded.
7–10. Commentary on the first *Abhinandana-sutta* and others.

19–22. Only the "wheels of becoming" (*vaṭṭa*) and "unfolding of the wheel" (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained, because the teaching proceeds by way of the arising and cessation of delight (*abhinandanā*). "Successive exposition" (*anupubbakathā*) refers to the commentary on the meaning of the words starting from the beginning. "Of these" (*nesam*) means of the discourses (*sutta*).
The commentary on the *Paṭhamābhinanda-sutta* and the others is finished.
The commentary on the *Yamakavagga* is finished.
3. The Chapter on All (Sabbavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on All (Sabbasuttavaṇṇanā). 23.
Since the word "all" (sabba) sometimes functions in a limited sense according to its specific context, [the following is stated] in order to exclude that [limited application].
The term "all-all" (*sabbasabba*) is stated by qualifying it with the word "all" (*sabba*) in its exhaustive sense;

the meaning is that which is "all" and yet "all. "All-basis" (*āyatanasabba*) refers to everything that has the nature of a sense base (*āyatana*); the same method applies to the remaining two [categories].
Because there is nothing outside its scope, it is said: "There is nothing whatsoever here that has not been seen. Here, *idha* is a mere particle, or it means "here in this world with its devas."
The meaning is that in the world, there is nothing whatsoever that has not been seen by knowledge which functions as vision.

If this is so, one might ask: "What then is the object of inference? To this he says: "And furthermore, the unknown. There is nothing for him that is unknown even though it is not directly perceived by others;
thus, there is nothing unseen or unknown. The knowable is comprised solely of the present and the past; the future—
He asked, "How so? and replied, "There is nothing to be known," connecting this by bringing in the phrase "for him there is nothing.
To show that for him there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be known or understood, he said, "He has directly known all," and so forth.

Because the entire phenomenon of personal existence (*sakkāya*) has been fully encompassed, it is called "all of personal existence" (*sakkāyasabba*). Regarding the phrase "in all phenomena": [this refers to] the five...
Regarding all phenomena that have become objects of the doors: since a "partial all" does not occur when even six types of objects are apprehended, it is therefore stated as "merely the five objects.

A partial all does not reach the extent of the "all of personality" (sakkāya-sabba), because the latter does not include one part of the phenomena belonging to the three planes. [The "all of personality"] reaches the "all of bases" (āyatana-sabba).
It does not reach [the ultimate] because it does not encompass supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). The "all" of the sense bases (*āyatana-sabba*) does not reach the "all-of-all" (*sabbasabba*).
This is because by the "all" of the sense bases, only the phenomena belonging to the four planes are included, and not the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) or designations (*paññatti*);
and because when showing the "all-of-all," the objective range of the Buddha's knowledge is shown. Therefore, it is said: "It does not reach the all-of-all."
Here too, the entire question and answer—“Why... [etc. ...because of non-existence”—is formulated solely with reference to a known object.

They say: “All bases (*āyatana*) should be understood here as only those phenomena that come within the range of insight (*vipassanā*), because even according to the exposition of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-niddesa*), it is precisely the course of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*) that is intended.”
"Having rejected" means having rejected thus: "All this is not so. "Of him" refers to one who says, "I shall designate another 'all'.

"Merely the matter to be expressed by the speech" means that his speech would consist only of the mere subject matter to be expressed—like the speech regarding the son of a barren woman or a flower in the sky—and would have no actual referent; it would be a mere utterance.
The meaning is as follows. "Having transcended" means not touching upon or not grasping. "For what reason? means by what cause does one encounter distress?
"Just as in that which is not one's domain" means just as anyone else who would strive in what is not their own sphere; such is the meaning.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the very reason stated in the *Pāḷi* as "for what reason? is presented by way of application.

The passage beginning with "yathā taṃ" was stated in order to demonstrate this. Furthermore, since the application of a reason is itself a reason, it should be understood that the phrase "yathā means a statement of the reason" was said for that purpose.
For this very reason, he said: "In the same way, here too, in this non-objective domain," and so forth.
The commentary on the entire sutta is concluded.
2. Commentary on the *Pahāna Sutta* 24.

“Of all” (*sabbassa*) means of that which proceeds through the sense doors together with their respective objects. “For the abandoning” (*pahānāya*) means for the relinquishing by way of abandoning the desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) bound up with that.
“Eye-contact” (*cakkhu-samphassa*) means contact dependent upon the eye. “Root condition” (*mūla-paccaya*) means the root-condition.
Having made [the preceding consciousness] a condition, there is simply nothing to be said regarding its status as a condition for the eye-contact that arises simultaneously with the feeling.
By the phrase "in this same manner," it is shown that one should say, "having made ear-contact the root-condition," and so forth.

"Mind" refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), because the mind-door is intended here. "Object" refers to the mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*). "Together with the impulsion that follows the adverting [consciousness]"—
The impulsion (javana) is that which causes the mind-door adverting.

Because it precedes mental consciousness, contact, and feeling, and because it serves as the root condition for all of them across the eye-door and so forth, it is described accordingly as "contact co-nascent with the life-continuum" (bhavaṅga-sahajāto samphasso).
The feeling of the impulsion is intended here as "that which is felt" (vedayita), whereas the feeling associated with the life-continuum...
Regarding the grasping of feeling, there is simply nothing to be said.

Without releasing from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), having taken up the adverting [consciousness] together with the life-continuum consciousness itself, the mind-door adverting consciousness should be regarded as the life-continuum.

As for "the teaching herein"—that teaching which occurs here by way of the phrase "for the abandoning," etc., is the Teacher’s instruction, his command. This is what is called its "designation" (*paṇṇatti*).
This is because it makes known that meaning in its various aspects. Here, by the inclusion of the word "all," all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) are included;

however, in order to demonstrate what designations (*paññatti*) are through an investigation into how they are formed, the passage beginning with "But those which are here... should be understood as having been stated.
The commentary on the *Pahāna-sutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Sutta on Higher Knowledge, Full Understanding, and Abandoning (Abhiññā-pariññā-pahāna-sutta).
25. "Abhiññā" means by way of higher knowledge (*abhiññāya*). This is an elided expression based on the dropping of the letter *ya*, as in "sayaṃ abhiññā" and so forth;

the same applies here to the term "pariññā. "Sabbam" refers to the totality of the sense bases (*āyatana-sabba*), for that is what is to be known through higher knowledge (*abhiññeyya*). "Having fully understood" (*abhijānitvā*)...

"Having known" means having understood through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). "Having fully understood" means having fully understood as impermanent and so forth by way of the full understanding of scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*).

"For the sake of abandoning" means for the sake of abandoning without remainder by way of the full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*). The commentary on the Sutta of Direct Knowledge, Full Understanding, and Abandoning is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Non-Comprehension (Paṭhama-aparijānana-sutta). 26.

By means of the passage beginning with “He directly knows,” the Blessed One first shows the dark side (the side of defilement) and then shows the bright side (the side of purification), according to the inclinations of those to be trained. Thus, herein, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its reversal (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
The commentary on the First Discourse on Non-Comprehension is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Non-Comprehension (Dutiya-aparijānana-sutta) 27.
Regarding the statement, "The phenomenon to be cognized by eye-consciousness is the sense-base of form alone," he says, "it is precisely the form grasped below.

This is because here, even that which has not come into the range [of the senses] is spoken of as "phenomena to be cognized by eye-consciousness. Below, however, it was [spoken of] even when it had come into the range.
Even that which has not come into the range [of the eye] is indeed included, because it is stated without exception in the phrase "and whatever forms.

For those aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations are to be cognized together with eye-consciousness. Indeed, eye-consciousness arises simultaneously with them, shares the same basis, ceases simultaneously, and has the same object.
Regarding the remaining phrases, this applies to the subsequent sections beginning with "and whatever ear, and whatever sounds," and so forth.

Regarding the five factors on the dark side and the six factors on the bright side that have been mentioned: "The same method applies" means that one should take up exactly the same form as was grasped below;
this is precisely the method for explaining the meaning there as well.
The commentary on the second *Aparijānana-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Ādittasutta 28.
Not far from the river named Gayā is a village called Gayā;
"he dwells at Gayā" is a locative expression used here in the sense of proximity. For near the village of Gayā, on a flat rock named Gayāsīsa—
The Blessed One was dwelling there at that time. Therefore it is said: "The Blessed One was dwelling there.

Regarding the word "there": as for the monks whom he addressed when saying "he addressed the monks," and how this teaching became suitable for them—this gradual discourse, concerning these two points to be clarified, begins from the point of its origin.
The discourse on the successive order. "Iti" means from this present kappa. "Kira" is a particle used in the sense of hearsay.

"When it had reached maturity through the cultivation of the perfections" (*pāramitā-paribhāvanāya paripākagate*). "In knowledge" (*ñāṇe*) means in the knowledge of enlightenment (*bodhi-ñāṇe*). The youngest son was the half-brother of the Blessed One.
Having surrounded [the dwelling] with bamboo-walled huts on the outside, but with cloth-canopies on the inside.
[He] causes the volition for merit (*puññacetanā*) of all beings to enter within, into the interior.
Because the Blessed One was also his son, it is said, "the other three sons. "Without being scattered" means not being dispersed by defeat, that is, without fleeing.
"He closed [the door]" means he did so thinking, "I am unable to give [it away]. "They took [him] because of his truthfulness" means because of the truthfulness of the royal family.
They chose their own boon.
"To turn back" means to return after having given one's word. "In the interval" means having died precisely within the time limit set by you.
An area measuring twenty-eight cubits is called an *usabha*. "In an *usabha*" means in a space measuring twenty-eight cubits.
“Engaged at the head of the almsgiving” means occupied with it.

“He” refers to the Blessed One. For such is the miracle of the Buddhas’ teaching that the meaning grasped through the teaching becomes manifest and stands before one as if directly perceived. Therefore he said: “Of these... I shall teach. “Certainty” (sanniṭṭhāna) means—
He reached the conclusion that the teaching on the discourse of burning was suitable for those who had long been acquainted with the fire of passion.
"Blazing" (*paditta*) means set ablaze, having become a single mass of flame by means of the eleven fires; hence he said, "thoroughly inflamed" (*sampajjalita*).
The characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) has been explained because suffering is described by way of the state of being ablaze through the eleven fires of the eye and so forth.
The commentary on the *Ādittasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Addhabhūtasutta*: 29.
Since the word *addha* has the same meaning as the word *adhi*, he says, “*Addhabhūtan* means *adhibhūtan*,” and so forth. The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Addhabhūtasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Samugghātasāruppasutta*. 30.
"Conceitedness" (*maññita*) means that which is grasped by craving, conceit, and views. "In all conceitedness" means all conceitedness whatsoever.
Its eradication is the destruction of the bridge; it is that which brings about the eradication of all conceivings (maññita) in a manner appropriate thereto.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the second method is stated: "Conceiving arises only in relation to the eye and so forth, not elsewhere. "Suitable" means appropriate and non-contradictory.
"Here" means precisely here in this teaching, because such [a method] does not exist elsewhere. "[Of craving, conceit, views, and conceivings]"...
In order to show the three types of conceiving (*maññita*)—along with their opposites—by applying them to one’s own and others’ continuums, it is said:

“‘The eye is I,’ etc. Therein, by the phrase “the eye is I,” he shows the conceiving of views regarding internal objects, because this illustrates the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*) and the conceit of “I” (*ahaṃkāra*).
By the word “mine,” he shows either the conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññita*) or the conceiving of pride (*mānamaññita*), as well as [conceiving] by way of possession (*pariggaha*).
This is because conceit arises from this [identification]. In the remaining two phrases as well, the analysis of conceiving (*maññita*) should be understood according to this same method.
"I" is simply the self (*attā*); and since that [self] exists dependent upon the eye, one does not conceive of it as "other. "Mine" refers to the impediment of possessiveness (*kiñcana-palibodha*);

since this is obtained when the eye exists, one does not conceive of it when it is absent, because such conceiving destroys its conditions. This same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.
"I have emerged from the eye"—thus one should say "I," because this being is perceived there in a subtle manner as having emerged from the eye.
"My possession and impediment have emerged from the eye," because it is perceived only when that [eye] exists.
The same method applies to the other two [ears and nose] as well. In that context, "another" means another being. He does not conceive, "The eyes are mine."
That eye [is empty] because there is an absence of anything that could be called "I" in relation to it. "Becoming mine" means being a cause for the notion of "mine.

The rest is self-evident. Thus, in this sutta, there are seven sections concerning the eye-door by way of the eye, visible form, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
likewise for the ear-door and so forth, making six sets of seven, which is forty-two. Furthermore, by way of the five aggregates of clinging (*sakkāya*):
By the statement beginning with “he conceives nothing of all,” thirty-nine [factors] are indicated.
Again, taking the round of existence in the three planes as “the world,” it is said, “he grasps nothing in the world”; thus there are forty-four.
In this way, it should be understood that insight is explained as having brought about Arahantship in forty-four places in every respect. “In one hundred and forty-four” [refers to this].
In some manuscripts it is written [differently], but that is a scribal error.
The commentary on the *Samugghātasāruppa-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Paṭhamasamugghātasappāya-sutta*.
31. It is "beneficial" because it brings that [result]. "From that" means from the mode of conceiving. "That" refers to the object of conceiving.
"In another mode" means that while one conceives of it in terms of modes such as impermanence, it exists in a different mode than those—namely, impermanence and so forth.

"Change into another state" means transformation; it is a change into another state due to its nature of arising and passing away, and it is to be transformed in two ways by means of aging and death. By approaching that...
Subject to change, even after having become thus, the world—clinging to states of existence whose nature is aging and dissolution—rejoices further in existence itself.
Having summarized exactly what was taken up below, [the text says] "he does not conceive the eye," and so forth;
that is, having taken together as one under the various designations of aggregates, elements, and bases—the aggregates and so on—which were previously mentioned below, it further...
It shows the basis for conceiving (*maññanāvatthu*). At the conclusion, together with the phrase stated as “therefore that comes to be,” there are eight [factors] in each section;
thus it is said, “in forty-eight places.
The commentary on the first *Samugghātasappāyasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Sutta on What is Conducive to Eradication (Dutiyasamugghātasappāyasuttavaṇṇanā) 32.
"Having shown": here, this particle *tvā* is used in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) or in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

For the Teacher’s teaching, characterized by the three turnings (*tiparivaṭṭa*) contained within the mental continuum of beings since beginningless time, has that [continuum] as its object; it proceeds for the sake of the very abandonment of that [continuum]. [The result is] Arahantship.
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Having brought [the subject] to completion, insight (*vipassanā*) was taught; thus, all four paths were taught together with insight.
The commentary on the *Dutiyasamugghātasappāyasutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Sabbavagga* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Nature of Birth (Jātidhammavagga), §§ 33–42.

"Having the nature of arising" means having the nature of originating through causes and conditions. "Having the nature of aging" means having the nature of decaying upon reaching maturity immediately after arising.
"Wherever the eye and so forth exist, right there [is] disease," characterized by its origination from discordant factors.
It has the nature of disease by way of being a condition for arising. It has the nature of death, meaning the nature of destruction.

It has the nature of sorrow, meaning the nature of suffering from being consumed by such things as the loss of kinsmen. It has the nature of defilement, meaning the nature of being defiled by craving and so forth.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Nature of Birth is concluded.
5. Explanation of the Chapter on All is Impermanent (Sabba-aniccatā-vagga), Verses 43–52.
The full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*) is included by way of its object, because it illuminates the phenomena that constitute that object.

It should be understood that the other two—the full understanding through examination (*tīraṇa-pariññā*) and the full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*)—are likewise included, since their objects are the phenomena to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-dhamma*) by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

And because of the possibility of the full understanding consisting of investigation and abandoning. The construction is as follows: in the category of the "to-be-fully-understood," only the full understanding of investigation is mentioned;
in the category of the "to-be-abandoned," only the full understanding of abandoning is mentioned. Yet the other two are also included, since there is no accomplishment of the goal without them.

It must be made directly evident through penetration of the object without delusion. Even though not explicitly stated, they are indeed included within the act of thorough comprehension (*parijānana*).
It is precisely for the purpose of abandoning. The meaning of "non-one-pointedness" (anekagga) is the state of being dissociated from a single nature.
The meaning of "afflicted" (upahata) is the state of being struck within by a disease-like affliction.
The commentary on the entire section on impermanence is finished.
The First Fifty. 6.
Commentary on the Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga), §§ 53–62.
Ignorance regarding the Four Truths is the delusion that conceals them. One finds what should not be found; one does not find what should be found.
"Because one does not find [it]," ignorance is indeed the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*). When true knowledge has arisen, ignorance is abandoned without remainder;
showing this, he said: "True knowledge is the true knowledge of the path of Arahantship. He further stated:

"Not only by means of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) does emergence from the path occur, but also by means of the other contemplations," thus saying: "...suffering... is indeed abandoned."
He said: "In all cases" refers to the subsequent suttas. Furthermore, it includes those suttas spoken by way of the characteristics of that meaning as well.
For even those were spoken with the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) of individuals who would understand them in such a way.
The commentary on the Chapter on Ignorance (*Avijjāvagga*) is finished.

Regarding the statement that "eye-consciousness has the function of seeing," it is said that "they have become desirable objects" because they are to be seen by the eye-consciousness already mentioned.

“Kamanīyā” means they are to be desired. Because they bring satisfaction to the mind, they are called “manāpā”; thus he says, “they increase the mind. “Piyarūpā” means their intrinsic nature is to be loved.
“Kāmūpasaṃhitā” means connected with sensual desire. Here, “upasaṃhitā” refers specifically to the state of being taken as an object;
therefore he says, “having made them an object,” and so forth. “Taṇhānandī” is delight consisting of craving, not merely the delight of contentment. “Nandiṃ... [he says].

[This is used] as in such passages as “he wanders,” etc. “Gāmantan” means the vicinity of a village. Having stated “a place not within the precincts,” he shows that by means of the words “where,” etc.

it is also a seizing (*gāha*). Because they have the nature of impermanence and so forth, formations (*saṅkhārā*) are not fit to be seized by that adherence, misapprehension, and seizing.
Formations themselves are the "signs of formations" (*saṅkhāranimitta*) because they serve as the cause for the occurrence [of existence]. Whatever [clinging] there is toward formations...
The aspect of self is to be seen through a misapprehension that has not been fully understood; [to see] that "it does not exist" is the aspect of non-self, which one sees as distinct from that.
"Misapprehension that has been fully understood" means a misapprehension that has been delimited and known by means of the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*).

Alternatively, "misapprehension that has been fully understood" refers to the misapprehension of insight that has been fully understood. "Insight" refers to that which is to be fully understood by insight according to the sevenfold set of formless [insights].

87. It is called *paṭisallāna* because one secludes oneself from all signs by means of it; it is the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
A "sword that takes away life" is so called because it carries off life and because it slays and harms living beings. "Attended upon" means waited upon.

“Anupavajja” means not to be reproached by others. This is because, in this case, there will be no future rebirth; thus he said, “without further occurrence.

By saying “This is not mine,” and so forth, he spoke while including [the state] within Arahantship. He speaks while illustrating the very state of an ordinary person (puthujjana) by way of showing that his task was yet unaccomplished.
Although the Elder had included the question asked within the context of Arahantship—

He spoke; however, when he said, "I do not perceive anything," he did not state any result. Therefore, having introduced this with the words, "This too should be kept in mind," the connection [is established].

"Tranquility of the defilements" (kilesapassaddhi) means the subsiding of the fever of the defilements. "For the sake of existence, again for the sake of existence" (bhavatthāya puna bhavatthāya). "Attachment to a resting place" (ālayanikanti).
"Overtaking" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) refers to the state of being overtaken by attachment (*nikanti*) and the underlying tendency (*ālaya*) known as longing for another existence.
"In the absence" means while it is non-existent. "Coming" (*āgati*) is the arrival here from another existence by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"Going" (*gati*) is the departure by way of death; that is, the transition from here due to passing away. "Destination" (*gati*) is the movement to a corresponding state; neither of those two exists. [This is] "death and rebirth" (*cutūpapāta*).
There is no passing away by way of successive existences, nor is there rebirth by way of re-arising; both of these do not exist.
Thus, when there is no passing away or rebirth, one does not exist "here," that is, in this world; nor does one exist "yonder," that is, in the other world.
For that very reason, one does not exist in both places. This alone is the end: this very non-existence in this world and in the other world is the final cessation of suffering.
“This very one” means exactly as it has been stated—here, in this reading, it refers to the meaning that has come down through tradition and serves as an authority.

“But those who” refers to those who maintain the correct doctrine. They assert an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), thinking, “In this way, the connection between one existence and another existence would be possible.
[The opponent replies: “It is purposeless,” because there is no such thing as an intermediate state for anyone. For immediately after the aggregates of death...
It is only the manifestation of the rebirth-linking aggregates. Therefore he said: “The intermediate state... is indeed rejected.
In that context, “existence” (bhāva) means presence. It is precisely rejected in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise of the Abhidhamma.
If this is so, how is it that the word “in between” (*antarena*) is used? To this he says: “‘In between,’ etc. This refers to another alternative interpretation distinct from the previous one. Its—

The statement "without an interval" (*antarena*) serves as an illumination. It does not illuminate an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because such a thing is not perceived and because there would be no purpose for it.

For wherever a condition exists for the resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*), there the physical basis (*vatthu*) that serves as its support and the co-existent aggregates (*khandha*) must also exist;
thus, consciousness arises together with its own support, and therefore there is no need for its arising [to be explained] separately.
The distance [of the person] should be understood. Beyond the two alternatives stated as "neither here nor there," there is another alternative by way of possibility, namely "not both";
the intention is that even in that case, it simply does not exist. Alternatively, *antarena* is a particle synonymous with *vinā*;
therefore, the meaning is: "neither here, nor there, nor even without both."
“He brought it forth” means he took it up by way of cutting. Therefore he said, “He cut the windpipe. “Grasping” means contemplating.

He was “fully extinguished” (parinibbuto) because of his long-standing application and devoted practice in insight meditation (vipassanā). “The blameless monk Channa brought forth the knife”—he spoke thus as if making a declaration (byākaraṇa), as one would at the time of attaining the state of an Arahant (asekkha).
"By this" means by the statement "families that are blameworthy. "The Elder" refers to the Elder Sāriputta. "Thus" means:
suspecting that he might have lived in close association during earlier times and would later attain *arahantship*, he asks. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Channa Sutta is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Puṇṇa-sutta, etc. (88–89).
“That” refers to the dyad of eye and form. Therefore he said, “the eye and form. “From the arising of delight” means:

from the arising of delight—that is, from craving, which is the cause of the remaining factors—the arising and convergence of delight is the “arising of delight”; therefore, it is said, “from the arising of delight.”

Therefore he said, "by the convergence of craving. Because suffering—consisting of the five aggregates—is shown together with its origin, meaning that it arises and proceeds through the convergence [of those aggregates], it is said, "having brought the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) to its culmination.

Because cessation is shown together with the means to its cessation, it is said, "having brought the turning away from the cycle (vivaṭṭa) to its culmination. [This applies] to the connections between questions and so forth.
He said, "There is no other [connection]," meaning that there is a separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhī*).
*Caṇḍā* means wrathful. *Duṭṭhā* means full of hatred; such is the meaning. *Kibbisā* means evil-doers. *Kakkhaḷā* means cruel.
*Ghaṭikamuggarena* means with a short-handled club upon which a small ball has been attached to one side. It is called a weapon (*sattha*) because it causes beings to suffer (*sasanato*).

Precisely because it takes away life, the weapon is called a "taker" (*hāraka*). Restraint of the sense faculties is called "taming" (*dama*) because of the taming of the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
Wisdom is called "taming" because of the taming and pacification of those who indulge in the defilements.
The observance of the *uposatha* is called "taming" because of the taming of the unruly [mind] arising through the doors of the body and so forth.
“Patience” should be understood as “taming,” because it tames and pacifies impatience. Therefore he said: “‘Tranquility’ is a synonym for that very thing.
“Therein” means in the Sunāparanta country. “These two” refers to these two brothers: this Elder Puṇṇa and his younger brother.
“He stood pressing against [him]” means having generated a sublime joy directed toward the Buddha. “Having roared seven lion-roars” means...
Having thus uttered seven lion-roars— namely, demonstrating the absence of contentment in enduring breast-cutting, verbal abuse, and threats;
and demonstrating the absence of contentment in enduring blows with the hand, blows with a clod of earth, blows with a staff, blows with a weapon,
and the taking of one’s life— he did not specify a dwelling place in the Canon because he had resided in four different locations.
Having done so, it was simply stated: “He dwells in the Sunāparanta country.
“In four places” means in these four locations: on Mount Abbuyhattha, at the Samuddagirivihāra, at Mātulagiri, and at the Makula-kārāma-vihāra.
Regarding that: there was no monk capable of walking up and down upon that walkway (caṅkama).
Because of the inability to maintain mental attention for meditation due to the great danger from the ocean. *Uppātikaṃ*: having raised a great upheaval that causes a sudden tempest.
*Sammukhe*: in the region of the wind. *Paṭivedesuṃ*: they announced. *From the time it was begun*:
from the time the earth was measured for the construction of the circular hall (*maṇḍalamāḷa*). By *Saccabandha*.
To complete the number of five hundred, it is said, “of four hundred and ninety-nine. “The Fragrant Chamber” (Gandhakuṭi) refers to the Great Fragrant Chamber in the Jetavana Mahāvihāra.
“Named Saccabandha” means that because he had resided for a long time on Mount Saccabandha, he received the name “Saccabandha.

“He attained arahantship” means that he reached the state of arahantship accompanied by the five supernormal powers (pañca-abhiññā). Therefore, he said: “His supernormal powers came along with the Path itself.”
The great multitude gathered there became, some stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arhats.
Among them, some were possessors of the three knowledges, some possessed the six supernormal powers, and some had attained the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).

With reference to this, it was said: "A liberation from bondage occurred for the great multitude. Furthermore, those who there undertook the going for refuge, the five precepts, or the ten precepts...
Because they had received this favor, and by virtue of those deities, it is said that "there was a great clamor concerning the Buddha.
However, he caused the dawn to break right within the Great Fragrant Chamber (Mahāgandhakuṭī) for the sake of favoring the deities and for the prosperity of the clans. [He thought:
"Someone has been led onto the path to the states of deprivation; there is a sustainer of the world, and through his power, the processes of its evolution and dissolution occur."
"By him alone this generation has a protector; he applies himself to each respective task"—thus [the Buddha spoke] to dispel wrong graspings.
He requested that [the Teacher] be attended upon, saying, "I must dwell here for a long time.
The sixth is the Bāhiya Sutta; it is self-evident because it follows the method already explained below.

It "moves" (*ejati*), meaning it trembles at the sign of the six objects; thus it is called *ejā*. Therefore he said, "in the sense of moving. In the sense of afflicting...

92–93. "Dvaya" means a dyad (*duka*). Since the presentation in the text is by way of eliding the repetition (*āmeḍita*), he says: "two sets of two parts."
"Thus it is, thus": this refers to the dyad consisting of the eye and visible form as being impermanent and so forth.
"It moves" means it flickers due to instability. "It trembles" means it quivers because of aging and death. It is a "cause" because it is the sign for the arising [of consciousness].

And because there is no such thing as a "conjunction" (saṅgati) apart from the phenomena that are conjoining, nor likewise any "assemblage" (sannipāta) or "coming together" (samavāya), contact (phassa) produced by way of those [phenomena] is described in that manner. Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth.

"Basis" (vatthu) means the eye, by way of being the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) and so on. "Object" (ārammaṇa) means visible form, by way of being the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and so on.
The three co-nascent aggregates beginning with feeling [arise] by way of being co-nascent conditions and so forth.
"This is the cause" means this threefold cause. Regarding the phrases beginning with "by contact," this is the summary of the meaning:

because while contact performs its own function of touching upon a visible-form object, feeling likewise performs its function of experiencing, and perception performs its function of perceiving; therefore, "by contact..."

In order to demonstrate now, by way of reference to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), the very same meaning already stated in the passage beginning with "touched" (*phuṭṭham eva*), the words beginning with "touched" (*phuṭṭho*) were spoken.
The Blessed One has described the five aggregates (*pañca khandhā*) in thirty ways. To the question "Why?", he said "How," and so forth.
Just as the designation "tree" applies to the branches of a tree, the designation "aggregate" applies even to each individual phenomenon. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
—“Consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness.
