10. The Chapter on the Six (Saḷavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Untamed and Unguarded (Adanta-agutta-sutta) 94.
"Untamed" means not brought to subduing, which is the state of being free from habitual tendencies. "Unguarded" means not protected by the fence known as mindfulness.
"Uncovered" means not covered by a door-panel. By all four words, he expresses the non-obstruction of the sense-faculties.

"Carriers" (adhivāhā) means those that carry [suffering]; "carriers of suffering" (dukkhādhivāhā) means those that convey suffering. "Nerayika" refers to that which arises in the hells. By the word "etc.
(ādi), he includes the remainder of the canonical text.

*Saḷeva*: the letter *sa* is substituted for the letter *cha*, while the letter *ḷa* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). *Yattha*: this is the locative case used in the sense of a cause or condition (*nimittatthe*).

*Anavassutā atintā*: not drenched, meaning not moistened by lust (*rāga*). *Assāditaṃ*: reached, having gone toward enjoyment (*assāda*). Therefore he said, "possessing enjoyment" (*assādavantaṃ*). *Sukhadukkhaṃ*: the desirable and the undesirable.

*Anvayatīti anvayo*: that which follows is a consequence; it is a cause (*hetu*). He said "consequent upon contact" (*phassanvayaṃ*) because contact is its consequence—meaning "having contact as its cause" (*phassahetukaṃ*).
“Aviruddha”: this is a designation formed by the elision of a case ending.
“Papañcasaññā” refers to perception conjoined with craving and the like. Therefore he said: “Having become what is called ‘papañca-perception’ through the perception of defilements.
Those people possess papañca-perception; thus they are “papañcasaññā. They are so called because they cause proliferation (*papañcayanti*).
They create proliferation (*papañca*) and delay in *saṃsāra*. "Possessing perception" (*saññino*) means they possess perception based on the perception of a household life.
"Mental-made thought" (*manomayaṃ vitakkaṃ*) refers to wrong thought conceived solely by the mind. "He moves" (*iriyati*) means he moves—that is, he practices—the practice (*iriyaṃ*).
"Well-developed" means well-cultivated; thus it is "developed from development. "His mind touched" means his mind is touched by that aforementioned contact.
"Does not waver anywhere" means it does not tremble toward any object, whether desirable or undesirable.
"Go to the further shore" means become those who go to the further shore.
The commentary on the *Adantāgutta Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Māluṅkyaputta Sutta* 95.

“He disparages” means he rebukes. “He exalts” means he praises. This elder, it is said, was Māluṅkyaputta. “Having neglected” means having neglected by not applying systematic attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).

*Yatra* is a personal pronoun used here as an ornamental expression. *Nāma* is used in the sense of disbelief when it belongs to the side of disparagement (*apasādana*), but in the sense of belief when it belongs to the side of praise (*ussādana*).
"What kind of birth? means: "What is the use of that state of being old?";

he speaks thus while not regarding even the state of being old as worth a blade of grass. Therefore he said: "If... [omitted] ...not favoring. *Anuggaṇhanto* means not considering. For those like me...
Praising the instruction now as something that brings benefit, he says, “The Blessed One’s instruction is helpful.

The illustration stated by way of supposition— beginning with “not seen, never seen before”— is for the purpose of applying the method [of analysis] such that “just as desire and the rest do not exist in these [five aggregates],
so it is with the others once they have been fully understood,” because those [other aggregates] must also be treated in the same manner as these.
Therefore it was said: “Sensual pleasures are like a dream.
Regarding the phrase “only what is seen by eye-consciousness”: this refers to the mode of apprehension of the visible base (rūpāyatana) by eye-consciousness;
it is only as much as that. What is its measure? It is to be personally experienced and cannot be shown to another; it is a mere conceptual construct.

It is form (*rūpa*). Therefore, he says: “Eye-consciousness,” and so forth. “Form” means the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). “Merely form” means merely the sense-sphere of form distinguished by blue and so on, but not [the specific qualities of] blue and so on themselves;
for this word *matta* (merely) serves to exclude particularities. If this is so, what is the purpose of the particle *eva* (only/merely)?
For although eye-consciousness occurs in relation to the sense-sphere of form, [it does not grasp] the specific qualities such as blue, thinking, “This is... [etc.]”
One does not apprehend it as "this is called blue" or "this is called yellow.

The inclusion of the particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of excluding even that which is connected [to the object], such as its nature of being permanent or impermanent. Therefore he said, "not the nature of permanence, etc.

"By the other consciousnesses" means by the impulsion consciousnesses (*javana-viññāṇa*). That which is called "seen" is so designated because eye-consciousness is the seeing of the visible base (*rūpāyatana*). Therefore he said, "the discerning of form in regard to form."
"Only eye-consciousness" means: "All my consciousness shall consist of nothing more than that which is merely the apprehension of the visible object by eye-consciousness.
Alternatively, the reading is "free from lust and so forth. "The seen" (diṭṭha) refers, in terms of the meaning of the word, to the visible form seen by eye-consciousness.
"Right there" means: in the visible form merely seen by eye-consciousness. [This refers to] the triad of consciousnesses.
"Merely seen" (diṭṭhamattaṃ) means that it proceeds free from lust and other defilements, just like eye-consciousness. Therefore he said, "Just as that," and so forth.
"Known" (viññātaṃ) refers to the object cognized by mind-door adverting consciousness; it is intended as such because it is to be known free from lust and other defilements.

Therefore he said, "Just as by adverting," and so forth. "At that time" (tadā) means at that moment, not from that point onward; this is the meaning here, which he shows by the phrase beginning with "merely seen."
Those [defilements] such as lust (*rāga*), etc., whose cessation is intended, are referred to by the pronoun "that" (*ta*) in the phrase "by that" (*tena*);
thus it is said, "one who is impassioned by that lust," and so forth. In the word "therein" (*tattha*), the locative case denotes the object;
and since the state of being an object must be understood through its connection with the subject, it is stated, "bound," and so forth.

“Mindfulness” (*sati*) is the clear observation of the specific nature of form. Because it does not arise due to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward an attractive sign, it is said to be “not seen” and “not occurring. “Clinging” (*ajjhosāya*) means having clung; that is, by swallowing, by finalizing, and by making [the object] one’s own.
Regarding the phrase “by covetousness and by ill-will,” he says “by covetousness and by ill-will” because the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
He says “by covetousness and ill-will” because there is a change of grammatical case according to the sense. “Of one who accumulates” means of one who increases [kamma-formations].

"Mindful" (*paṭissato*) means being mindful, endowed with mindfulness in all circumstances. Regarding the phrase "and for one who cultivates," here the word *ca* (and) and the word *api* (even/also) are mere particles;
thus, the meaning stated is simply "for one who cultivates.
The commentary on the Mālukyaputta Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Parihāna Sutta 96.

"The nature of decline" (*parihānasabhāva*) means the nature of declining from blameless qualities. "Overpowered" (*abhibhavitāni*) means they have been overcome by way of their state of being rendered ineffective.
"Intentions based on craving" (*sarasaṅkappā*) refers to intentions that are unstable with respect to this or that object.
"Conducive to fetters" means that which is to be fettered. For one who allows the arising of defilements again and again provides an opportunity for the fetters;

thus, it is called "tolerating the class of defilements. Defilement itself is the "class of defilements. However, when one makes an object the focus of the mind, it is called "tolerating" that object.
One does not abandon the object by abandoning desire and lust, but rather [abandons it] by bringing about the state of non-arising of the defilement.
Thus it is. The "base of mastery" (*abhibhavitam āyatanam*) was spoken of in terms of endurance and so forth.

Having asked about the Dhamma with the words, "And how, bhikkhus, is one subject to decline?", the Blessed One, in analyzing that, showed the Dhamma by way of a person through the passage beginning, "If that bhikkhu endures it," and so on.
The commentary on the *Parihāna-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Pamādavihāri-sutta* 97.
"Not having closed the faculty of the eye" means not having closed it, not having covered it while standing. "He sprinkles" means [he sprinkles] with defilements (*kilesa*).
He sprinkles especially. "Saturated with defilements" means moistened by defilements. "Weak rapture" is tender rapture that has not yet reached full strength.
"Powerful rapture" is rapture that has reached the state of uplift and pervasion. "Tranquility of distress" is tranquility characterized by the subsiding of distress in body and mind.
They do not arise because the succession of conditions has not been established. "And how, monks, does one dwell in negligence..."
Having questioned about the person with the words beginning, “Does it exist? and so forth, and with the words beginning, “There is no joy;
joy arises,” and so forth, the person is shown by way of the Dhamma through the phrases, “one who dwells in negligence” and “one who dwells in diligence.
The commentary on the *Pamādavihārīsutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta 98.
"And what, bhikkhus, is non-restraint?"—this is the statement.

"By way of explaining the states that are to be abandoned" means that it is the very teaching of those states to be abandoned that is being stated. "And how, bhikkhus, does non-restraint come to be?"—this refers to the Dhamma.
Having asked, [the Buddha] analyzed the Dhamma itself by saying, "Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye," and so forth.
The commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta.

99. “By means of one-pointedness of mind” means by means of one-pointedness of mind through the vehicle of serenity (*samatha*). “While it is declining” means while it is declining due to the non-attainment of that [one-pointedness]. “The meditation subject” (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to the meditation subject of insight (*vipassanā*), or indeed serenity itself.
7. Commentary on the *Paṭisallāna Sutta* (Discourse on Seclusion) 100.
“The meditation subject” means the meditation subject of both serenity and insight.
8–9. Commentary on the First *Na tumhākaṃ* Sutta, etc. 101–102.
"Having surrounded the simile" means having encompassed the simile. "By way of the bare [text]" means solely by itself, without the simile.
10. Commentary on the *Udaka* Sutta.
103. *Udakoti* is its name. *Vedaṃ* means knowledge. One who has conquered all is *sabbaji*. *Avakhaṭaṃ* means dug in.
*Ucchādanadhammo* means having the nature of being smeared. *Parimaddanadhammo* means having the nature of being rubbed. *Parihato* means carried away.
It should be stated [in full] with the phrases "accumulation of rice and gruel," "smearing," and "rubbing. *Ucchādanaṃ*...
Or, having considered it as merely rubbing, it was not included.
The commentary on the Udakasutta is finished.
The commentary on the Saḷavagga is finished.
The Second Fifty. 11.
The Chapter on the One Who Has Attained Security from Bondage (Yogakkhemivagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the One Who Has Attained Security from Bondage (Yogakkhemisutta-vaṇṇanā).
104. "By the four bonds" means by the four bonds beginning with the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*). "One who is secure" means one who possesses security, that is, one who is skillful.

"That which has become the cause" means that which has become the cause for the means to be performed. It is called a "method" (*pariyāya*) because it makes known both the process of proceeding and the process of returning;
it is a "Dhamma-method" (*dhammapariyāya*) because it is both the Dhamma and a method due to its being the Dhamma of the scriptures. One should follow that Dhamma-method.
But because that [Dhamma] is the cause for its attainment, it is therefore called the "cause of the Dhamma" (*dhammakāraṇa*).
"The method" (*yutti*) refers either to the states of serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā-dhammā*) or to the states of the Four Noble Truths (*catusacca-dhammā*).
Having extracted the word "therefore" (*tasmā*), he asks the reason by posing the question "why?", and then asks analytically: "Is it because of being declared, or rather because of being abandoned?"

However, since the abandoning of desire and lust is the cause for the state of one who has attained security from bondage (*yogakkhemibhāva*), and not the mere speaking of it, therefore the words "because they have been abandoned" and so forth were spoken.
The commentary on the *Yogakkhemisutta* is finished.
2–10. Commentary on the *Upādāyasutta* and others.
105–113. "Pleasure and pain as feeling" refers to what is designated as feeling—that is, pleasure and pain—so it has been said.

Because of the statement "internal pleasure and pain," and because both the bliss of liberation and the suffering of the six sense bases have been mentioned, it can be understood that the bliss of turning away (*vivaṭṭasukha*) is also indeed included here.
Granted, in the *Khandhiya-vagga*, the teaching is presented by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).
Not by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, the matter that should be stated here is exactly according to the method already explained in the Khandhika-vagga.
The commentary on the *Upādāya-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the Yogakkhemi-vagga is finished.
12. The Chapter on Worldly Qualities of Desire (Lokakāmaguṇavagga) 1–2. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Snare of Māra, etc. (Paṭhamamārapāsasuttādivaṇṇanā) 114–115.
It is called an "abode" (āvāsa) because the defilement-Māra dwells therein. The "qualities of desire" (kāmaguṇa) are the internal and external sense bases (āyatana).

He has gone to the dwelling of the defilement-Māra (kilesamāra) and has fallen under its power. "Of the threefold" means of the threefold Māra, which is reckoned as the perception of conceptual proliferation (papañca).
From this very fact, it can be understood that he has also fallen under the power of the Devaputta-Māra.
The commentary on the first discourse, the Mārapāsasutta, etc., is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Lokantagamanasutta 116.

“World” (*loka*) is that wherein the bodies of beings, the groves of elements, and so forth, are dissolved; it refers to the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). Alternatively, conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are called “world” in the sense of being broken down and disintegrated.
“End” (*anta*) means the limit. “Having brought together with the knowledge of omniscience” means having made them coincide with the range of the knowledge of omniscience.
"Without contradicting. "I shall praise" means I shall commend.
"Thus accomplished" means it is thus perfected; this is my request that it should be seen in this way. Therefore he said, "the meaning is 'of such a kind.
"Knowing, he knows" means that by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he indeed knows whatever is to be known. For...
One established in partial knowledge knows all that ought to be known.
For, by the term "knows" (*jāna*), used here in its highest sense and as an inclusive designation, the entire range of knowable objects (*ñeyyajāta*) is encompassed without exception;

thus, it is appropriate that the instrument for the act of knowing those objects is precisely the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). This is understood through the context and by the proximity of the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*).

And this meaning must be clarified: "He sees only what is to be seen" means that he indeed sees with the eyes of knowledge known as the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*), the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*), the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

Alternatively, "he knows what is to be known" means that unlike others who, being subject to perversion (*vipallāsa*), know even while knowing through the influence of perversion—those who propound a thorough understanding (*pariññā*) of sense-desires and form—the Blessed One does not do so. The Blessed One...
However, because he has abandoned the perversions, the meaning is that knowing, he simply knows; and because there is an absence of the seeing of [wrong] views, seeing, he simply sees.

It is "become the eye" in the sense of being a guide for seeing, both because it accomplishes the seeing of things as they truly are for the world—just as the physical eye guides and accomplishes the seeing of beings—and because it consists of the eye of wisdom (*paññā*).
Or, he is "one who has become vision" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he has become one who possesses the eye of wisdom through self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*).

The meaning of "one who has become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*) should be understood in exactly the same way. Alternatively, he is "one who has become the Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) because he has attained and realized the Dhamma that is not shared with others, since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) have arisen within him and because he brings about their arising in the world. "Brahmā" is said in the sense of being supreme.

He is one who possesses the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*); because he has arisen by means of that, and because he brings about its arising for the world, and because he has attained it through self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), he is "become sublime" (*brahmabhūta*).
He speaks the Dhamma of the Four Truths, thus he is a "speaker" (*vattā*). He speaks while causing the penetration of the Truths to proceed for a long time, thus he is a "proponent" (*pavattā*).
"Having extracted the meaning" means having drawn out the meaning of suffering and so forth; or, he is one who leads others to the ultimate goal (*paramattha*), which is Nibbāna.
He is the "giver of the Deathless" because he bestows the Deathless upon beings by causing them to realize it.

He is the "Lord of Dhamma" because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) are dependent upon him. One is said to "revere" when one makes someone heavy by repeatedly entreating them, and likewise when one speaks after having made the matter difficult to understand.
One perceives the world by means of the eye while it exists, not when it is absent;
for there is no conventional designation of a "world" apart from the internal sense bases. Therefore he said, "The eye, indeed, is the world," and so forth.

One whose views are not abandoned—that is, one who has not eradicated the view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and is unable to effect the analytical resolution of the compact—perceives both the whole and its parts as "the world."
And he conceives [it]. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), the triad of phrases—"he perceives it as 'the world' and he conceives it"—is drawn in.

"Of that" refers either to the worldling (*puthujjana*) or to the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). For the worldling perceives the eye and so forth, together with their spatial location, as the "world-system.
"By going" means by walking on foot. It is not possible [to go] because of their infinity. "In the sense of breaking up" (*lujjanaṭṭhena*).
This was said in order to show the end of the world by way of the world of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).

Its "end" is Nibbāna, because it is possible to reach it since it is to be attained through right practice. However, there is no such thing as an "end" to the world-system of the universe (*cakkavāḷa*), because it cannot be reached by traveling.
"By these words" means by these words which are divisions of sentences.
Since those [words] have the characteristic of being a collection of syllables, he says "by the combinations of syllables.
"By individual syllables" means by syllables that are grasped separately by the mind, each having its own fixed position within its respective word.
Wisdom (*paññā*) is called "penetration" (*paṇḍā*) in the sense of going; one who has gone from here and reached [the goal] by means of that is "penetrating" (*paṇḍita*), that is, wise.
Great wisdom should be understood by way of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*); thus he said, "in great matters," and so forth. Regarding the word *tanti*:
in the first alternative, *tanti* is a mere particle; in the second alternative, however, it is a demonstrative pronoun. Thus he said, "that has been explained."
The commentary on the Lokantagamanasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kāmaguṇasutta: 117.
"By the mind" (cetasā) is a genitive used in the sense of an instrument. He said, "Contact by means of the mind is experience," thus: "by the mind."
“...experienced before. By way of conformity to the three seasons, there were three palaces; by way of those, there were three varieties of theatrical performances.
These were presented as objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) merely by virtue of their being delightful, not by virtue of actual sensual desire.
For indeed, after his Great Renunciation, no thoughts of sensual desire had ever arisen in the Bodhisattva. Therefore, the Evil Māra said:
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step;
yet I could find no opening in the mindful Sambuddha.
The passage beginning with “He named Metteyya,” etc., is merely a vision of the future; it does not arise in the Bodhisatta himself in this manner.

“Attarūpa” means that which has a self as its beloved form; thus, by the elision of the first member of the compound in the latter term, the meaning is stated as “by one who is desirous of his own welfare.
Alternatively, “attarūpena” means by one whose essential nature is seized by joy and gladness—by one who is satisfied, exultant, and uplifted.
“Appamāda” means non-negligence, the state of acting without breaking [the precepts] regarding wholesome qualities; thus he says, “constant practice. “Avossagga” means...
The non-release of the mind from the strands of sensual pleasure is the failure to leap forward [into them].
The former alternative is shown by way of performing wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*), while the latter is shown by way of not performing unwholesome states. "Two states" refers to two states:
heedfulness (*appamāda*) and mindfulness (*sati*). Heedfulness and mindfulness should be understood as the four aggregates of wholesome states occurring in such a manner.
"Should be performed" means they should be set in motion.
"In that sphere" means in that cause known as Nibbāna, which is the penetration [of truth]. "That cause" is the cause of the six sense-bases.
Nibbāna is called the cessation of the six sense-bases because the six sense-bases cease therein. Thus he said.
“Nibbāna. It is with reference to that,” and so forth. “In nibbāna” means in nibbāna.
The commentary on the *Kāmaguṇasutta* is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the *Sakkapañhasutta*, etc.
118–119. *Diṭṭhe* means in what has become directly perceived. *Dhamme* means in the phenomena of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
For therein, the perception and view that "this is self" constitutes the perception of selfhood (*attabhāvasaññā*). Therefore it was said: “In this very life, in this very selfhood.
Regarding the phrase “dependent on that,” the word “that” (*taṃ*) refers back to what was stated previously by way of the synonyms beginning with “delight” (*abhinandanā*).

He said, "dependent on craving," because craving is what has been clung to. That which has that [craving] as its clinging is "clinging to that" (*tad-upādāna*). Therefore he said, "grasping at that," and so forth.
Grasping, which is designated as craving and clinging, belongs to this; thus it is "grasping at that. The sixth [section] is self-evident, as it follows the method already stated in the fifth.
The commentary on the *Sakkapañhasutta* and others is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Sāriputtasaddhivihārikasutta*: 120.

"He will connect" means he will establish a connection between what precedes and what follows. "Interruption" means the cessation resulting from the arising of conditions that are contrary to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
8. Commentary on the Rāhulovāda Sutta 121.

Those qualities which, when rightly developed and cultivated, lead to the realization of liberation and Arahantship—namely, the requisites beginning with faith—are intended here as "those that bring about the ripening of liberation. They "bring it to ripeness" means...
They bring about ripening and transformation. "Dhammas" refers to the factors that act as causes.

"By way of being a cause for purification" means by way of their state of being a cause for purification; that purification, moreover, arises from the power of the faculties such as faith (*saddhindriya*).
Just as, for example, a noble prince of pure birth attains complete purity through the removal of adversaries, the gathering of allies, and the excellence of his station.
Showing that it should be viewed in this very way, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth.
Persons who lack faith and so on lead only to the decline of those with faith and so on, whereas faith and so on lead only to their fulfillment;
likewise is the reflection upon discourses that inspire confidence (*pasādaniya-suttanta*), for "discourses that inspire confidence" refers to such texts as the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*.
"In the *Sammappadhāna* [discourses]" means in the *Sammappadhāna Sutta*. "In the *Satipaṭṭhāna*" means in the four foundations of mindfulness.

"In the *Jhānavimokkha*" means in the discourses delivered with reference to both the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the liberations (*vimokkha*). "In the *Gambhīrañāṇacariya*" means in the discourses connected with the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

"Such things as good friendship" refers to good friendship, restraint by virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), talk on effacement (*abhisallekhakathā*), the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambha*), and penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*).
These five qualities, beginning with having virtuous friends, are those spoken of in the Udāna: “Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has virtuous friends,” and so forth.
“While surveying the world” means while the Venerable Rāhula was observing the ripening of the faculties of those deities.
Then [he thought]: “There will be a great assembly at the Andhavana grove for the midday rest.”
For it will be said: "There is no limit by way of counting, such as 'this much'.

Those who dwell on trees and mountains are earth-dwellers; those who inhabit celestial mansions that move through space are sky-dwellers. These should be understood as the "Dhamma-eye" in the sense of seeing the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.
The commentary on the Rāhulovāda Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Worldly Qualities of Desire is finished.
13. The Chapter on Householders. 1–3.
Commentary on the Suttas beginning with Vesālī.
124–126. Regarding "Dvīsū" (In Two): in this section on householders, the meaning is that the textual passages stated in the first, second, and third [suttas] are exactly as previously explained;
there is nothing new. 127–128. Commentary on the Bhāradvāja-sutta and others:
Granted, other renunciants also wander about for alms at the appropriate time, yet this one has eaten his fill.
Showing that he has gone forth for that very reason, he said, “Carrying his alms-bowl,” and so forth.
“Rubbing” means that he places the bowl on the ground while rubbing it. “Completely worn away” means worn away all around. A nāḷika... [as before] ...has arisen;
because the placing of an extra bowl is prohibited, he does not take another. “The cultivation of the faculties” means the cultivation of the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
Some say that the intention is: "having thus established an inclination toward insight (vipassanā) and having further developed that insight.

Others, however, say: "having established an inclination toward insight by means of the five faculties beginning with faith, and having developed the faculty by way of accomplishing the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the abandonments (pahāna) through that happiness."
Regarding the phrase "he approached": in order to show how that king approached, starting from the moment of his arrival, the passage beginning with "The Elder, it is said...

has been commenced. "A great drinking bout" (*mahāpāna*) refers to seven days of drinking liquor by those devoted to drink, without performing any other work, accompanied by a retinue suited to that activity.
Therefore he said: "having drunk what is called a great drinking bout. "With parched rice" (*sālithusehi*).
"With red rice and peas": [they were struck] by the painful sensations arising from the bites of ants, as if they were being burned. "They pierced them with mouth-spears out of affection":
for that king was lustful after women. "The tradition" (*paveṇi*):
their lineage of undertaking, the continuity of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "They maintained it": they brought it to fulfillment.
“An object of reverence” (garukārammaṇa) means an object that should be revered; the meaning is an object that should not be transgressed against. “Of him” (assa) refers to the king.
“Without entering the mind” (cittam anotarantaṃ) means not entering or approaching the cognitive process of serene confidence (pasādavīthi). “To harass” (viheṭhetuṃ) means to afflict.
Because greed arises repeatedly, it is expressed in the plural as “states of greed” (lobhadhammā). It is also said, “they arise.”
It is precisely for this reason that a state of greed (*lobhadhamma*), when arising, functions—that is, proceeds—by as if grasping and making known its own causes and conditions.

In the phrase "this very body" (*imaṃyeva kāyaṃ*), the word *kāya* here refers to a collection in the sense of a totality, because it has as its object the collection of phenomena arising in locations such as the womb and the abdomen;
however, the others [the sense-bases] should be understood as "body" (*kāya*) by virtue of being characterized by a body.
It is indeed clear because it follows the method explained below.
The commentary on the Bhāradvāja-sutta and others is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Ghosita-sutta.
129. "And forms that are agreeable" means that form-phenomena (rūpadhammā), such as blue and so forth, exist as pleasing and lovely to the mind;

this is for the purpose of showing the essential nature of contact to be experienced as pleasure. Likewise, in the passage "and forms that are agreeable [to be experienced] as equanimity," it should be stated accordingly.
It is said: "Eye-consciousness... [etc. ...contact. This is by way of decisive support (upanissaya).
For eye-consciousness-associated contact is to be experienced as pleasant by way of its own occurrence, not by way of its co-nascent factors. Therefore he said:
"Dependent on a single contact, a pleasant feeling arises through the process of impulsion (javana). Regarding the "remaining sections":
these refer to the five divisions mentioned in the passage beginning, "There exists, householder, the ear-element."

Twenty-three elements have been explained by way of the six doors through the method of analytical inclusion. "Supported by the physical basis" means supported by the heart-basis. There are twenty in the five doors and three in the mind door; thus, there are twenty-three.
The commentary on the Ghosita Sutta is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta, etc.
130–131. “That is ‘this’”: the meaning is that whatever visible form has been seen by the eye, that is "this.

"That is to be experienced as pleasant" refers to both the eye-consciousness which serves as a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for a pleasant feeling, and whatever [other mental states] are respectively related to it by way of decisive support, or by way of immediate succession (*anantara*) if they are immediate, or by way of association (*sampayutta*) if they are co-nascent.
Or, contact is the condition for pleasant feeling; the construction is: "In dependence upon that contact to be experienced as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises.
This same method applies everywhere in all the remaining seven sections. Or, "the mind-element alone" is according to the Abhidhamma method;
however, according to the Sutta method, it is in the sense of emptiness, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul.
And it indeed receives the designation "mind-element" (manodhātu). The eighth [sutta] is self-evident, as its method has been explained below.
The commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta and others is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta.
132. These were spoken of specifically as *māṇavaka*s (young men), not merely as *brāhmaṇa* youths. *Selyyakāni* refers to mutual games involving leaping over stones.
Those who carry an elephant (*ibha*) for the purpose of attending to it are called *ibbha*; they are elephant-keepers.

However, because they take charge of the property of a low-status household and assume the status of a householder (*gahapati*), they are also called "householders" (*gahapatika*); thus he said "householders. *Kaṇha* means...
"Of dark birth. "Supporting the kingdom" means they support the tax-revenue of the kingdom in which they dwell, or they are supporters by maintaining their own households.
"Wandering about" means they play while moving all around. "Those for whom virtue is foremost" means those who are preeminent in virtue;
those who remembered the past were the ones most excellent in virtue. "Gates" refers to the gates of the eyes and so forth.

"Having departed" means having gone away and being separated [from them]. "Uneven" means devoid of evenness, having the nature of misconduct. "Various kinds of punishments" refers to the infliction of various types of penalties.
"Without food" means not eating anything at all. Like mud is mud, it is a stain (*mala*).

Regarding "tooth-mud," by the elision of the first word, it is called "mud"; thus it is said, "mud is the stain on the teeth. Not performing what ought to be done by goats, without disturbing [the order].

A *vata* (vow) is by way of formal undertaking. This same method applies to the others as well. "Hypocrisy" (*kohañña*) means concealing the faults existing within oneself and proclaiming non-existent virtues;
thus it is said: "Concealed... and hypocrisy. "The appearance of requisites and belongings" (*parikkhāra-bhaṇḍaka-vaṇṇā*): "requisites and belongings" refers to barber’s tools.
And these are made for the purpose of one’s own livelihood, for the sake of a small amount of food, and for the purpose of binding oneself and not being released [from the world].
"Entirely" means being free from the mental obstructions (*cetokhila*) by way of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Therefore, he said: "pliant and not stiff.

"Resolved" means engaged and devoted through a sense of delight. "Narrow-minded" means one whose mind is limited or broken on all sides. "Immeasurable-minded" means one whose mind is capable of resisting the question, "Who is this?
The commentary on the Lohicca Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verañjakaṇḍa Sutta (Verañcānisuttavaṇṇanā) 133.
Exhorting the brahmin woman to listen to the Dhamma, the young man said, "Yagghe. Therefore it is said: "'Yagghe' is a particle used in the sense of exhortation.
The commentary on the Verañjakaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Householders is finished.
14. The Chapter on Devadaha. 1.
The Commentary on the Discourse to Devadaha.
134. "Delighting the mind" means occurring by way of being pleasing and desirable to the mind when it has come into the range [of the senses].
2. Commentary on the Kṣaṇa Sutta. 135.
"Consisting of the six bases of contact" means experienced as undesirable through the six bases of contact. "The discernment of contact at the six doors."
Through all six doors, there is indeed the experience of an object for the purpose of experiencing suffering in its entirety.
"Tāvatiṃsapura" refers to the great city of Sudassana. There is no absence [of pleasure] because of the complete experience of happiness.

By the term "niraya," the other states of deprivation (apāya) are also included under the general category of miserable existence (duggati-bhava). The dwelling in the holy life of the path (maggabrahmacariyavāsa).
By the phrase "unable to remain," it should be understood that all places of deprivation are included.
"In this very world" means in this human world alone. A "state of loss" (apāya) is recognized because one occasionally experiences suffering similar to the suffering of the states of loss.
A "heavenly realm" (sagga) is recognized because one occasionally obtains prosperity similar to the enjoyments of the gods.
“This is the land of action” means that this human world is called the “land of action” for the performance of manly exertion, because it is the suitable place for such things.
In that context, showing the primary action, he said, “herein, the cultivation of the path. “Bases” means causes. “Arousing of spiritual urgency” means producing a sense of urgency;
there are many [such bases], beginning with birth. For instance, birth, aging, sickness, death, and existence in the states of misery—
Therein, having reflected upon many objects of spiritual urgency— such as the cause for rebirth in hell, the cause for rebirth among animals, the cause for rebirth in the host of non-heroic spirits,
the basis of the round in the past, the basis of the round in the future, and the basis of the search for nutriment in the present— you,
being stirred by a sense of urgency and having given rise to that urgency, should apply yourself to systematic exertion.
"Saṃvega" means: "you should attain a sense of spiritual urgency.
The commentary on the Khaṇa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the First Rūpārāma Sutta.
136. *Sammuditā* means having attained joy; *pamoditā* means having become joyful. *Dukkhitā* means possessing suffering, those in whom suffering has arisen;
thus he said "suffering. *Sukhito* means one who has this happiness (*sukha*); thus he said "happy.
"Whatever phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) exist in the world"—this is what is meant by "those who see" them, that is, seeing them correctly through the penetration of the Truths (*sacca*).
Having said, "It is contrary," the passage beginning with "For the world... was stated in order to demonstrate that state of contrariness.
The word "are called" (*āhu*) is to be supplied to connect it with "the unattractive" (*asubhā*).

"All this" refers to what was stated: "Happiness is seen by the Noble Ones... [etc. ...the Noble Ones know that as happiness. All of this was spoken with reference to *nibbāna* alone; for it is *nibbāna* indeed—
It is called absolute happiness.
The fact that there are ninety-five heretics (*pāsaṇḍin*) has already been explained in the *Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā*.

"Enveloped by the hindrances of the defilements" means that the aggregates of defilement are the "hindrances of the defilements" (*kilesanīvaraṇa*); they are those who are obstructed by that. The vision of Nibbāna...
The Noble Path; by means of that, its penetration is like the lunar disk obscured by a dark cloud.
"Having delimited" means having delimited it through the delimitation of its impure nature and through right discernment and vision. "Of the path-dhamma" means of the dhamma of the Noble Path.
"By those who have not entered" means by those who have entered step by step without leaving [the practice]. He shows: "Who else is worthy to know? No one else knows."
The commentary on the First Discourse on Delighting in Form is finished.
4–12. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Delighting in Form, etc. (137–145).
Having treated it as a simple [discourse], [these are presented] solely by way of prose phrases, without being composed in verse. Likewise...
Thus, having joined the internal and external sense bases with the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristics of suffering and non-self,
[this was taught] by way of vision.
The commentary on the second *Rūpārāma-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the Devadaha Chapter is finished.
15. The Chapter on the New and the Old. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Cessation of Kamma.
146. Since both the eye that exists and the karma that produced it are intended [by the term "old"], the statement “the eye is not old;

only the karma is old” was made. To show how the designation “old” applies to that eye, he said: “But from karma,” and so forth. It is called “old” by way of its condition because it was accomplished in a previous birth.
By the name of the karma that has become the condition for what is to be said. "Thus spoken" means it is spoken of as "past karma.
"Produced by coming together through conditions" means produced by having come together and met face-to-face with conditions such as craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā).
"By volition" means by karmic volition (kamma-cetanā). "Fashioned" means intended. "By feeling" means...

[It is] of the feeling that occurs by depending on and taking as its object the self (*attā*). "Basis" (*vatthu*) should be seen through the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) as the cause of production and the place of occurrence.
"By the cessation of karma" means by the cessation of karma established through the non-arising and cessation of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"He touches liberation" means he attains the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. [The self] becomes the object...
Cessation is Nibbāna; it is called “the cessation of kamma,” having been understood as “kamma ceases herein.
Because it was said, “Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be negligent,” it is stated that “preliminary insight has been explained.
The commentary to the Kamma-nirodha Sutta is finished.
2–5. Commentary on the *Anicca*, *Nibbāna*, and *Sappāya* Suttas (147–150).
“Of Nibbāna” means of the attainment of Nibbāna, or of the Nibbāna that is the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa*).

“A beneficial course of practice” means a course of practice that brings about benefit. “In the four” refers to the four beginning with the second [sutta]. It is taught that these are courses of practice conducive to Nibbāna.
Having done so, it was stated: "The four paths are taught together with insight.
The commentary on the *Anicca*, *Nibbāna*, and *Sappāya* suttas is concluded.
6–7. Commentary on the *Antevāsika* and other suttas.
151–152. The word *anta* (end) occurs in the sense of proximity, as in expressions such as “the edge of the water” (*udakanta*) or “the edge of the forest” (*vananta*).

However, because the defilement dwells very close by, owing to its internal residence, it is called “one who dwells within” (*antevāsika*), with the case ending elided, just as in the cases of “skilled in the forest” (*vanekusala*) or “trees on the bank” (*kūlerukkhā*).
Therefore he said: “‘Not one who dwells within’ means free from the defilements that dwell within. [It means] free from the defilements that practice [within].
Free from the defilements that manifest in conduct. "Dwelling within him" means they dwell and operate within the internal mind of this person.
"They overcome him" means those defilements, having overpowered this person, bring him under their own control.
Therefore he said: "They overwhelm or they instruct. "By those teachers" means by those...
By the teachers who, through those things termed "defilements," establish beings within their own destiny. The seventh [section] is exactly according to the method explained below;
for while the teaching below has come down by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), here it is by way of the bases (*āyatana*)—this alone is the distinction.
The commentary on the *Antevāsika-sutta* and others is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Atthi-nukho-pariyāya-sutta* 153.
It is called a *pariyāya* because it goes around (*parigacchati*) or encompasses the fruit; thus he says, "A *pariyāya* is a cause," as in the phrase, "that which they encompass, that reason.
Faith that operates toward an object seen directly and not erroneously is "direct faith" (*paccakkha-saddhā*), just as...
“The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded. Such is the manner of conviction that arises through hearsay (*iti kira*), which is a semblance of faith (*saddhā*).
“This” refers to the statement, “except by way of faith. “Having found it pleasing” means having found some matter agreeable according to one’s own judgment.
“Having made it acceptable” is a synonym for that same term; it means having made the mind thus acceptable. Therefore he said:
“‘It exists’ is the mode of apprehension. Regarding the meaning handed down through tradition, “thus indeed it is” is the oral transmission (*anussavana*).
“Of one who reflects on the reason” means of one who reflects on the logical connection (*yutti*). “The reason presents itself” means it stands before one’s own mind as “well said.
“It exists” is the mental apprehension that “this very reason is thus consistent with this meaning. “Investigation of the mode” (*ākāraparivitakka*)—

The conceptualization of reasoning (*yuttiparikappanā*). "Adherence" (*laddhi*) means grasping with certainty; however, that should be understood as nothing but ignorance, because it is a view characterized by grasping what is not as it truly is.
"That" refers to the adherence. "It exists" means this adherence has arisen in me and is found to be plausible.
This mode of grasping is called "acceptance through the contemplation of views" (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*), which is designated as the adherence that has first arisen.
“Reflection on views” (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*) means the mode of acceptance through the contemplation of views.
“Five grounds” refers to the five causes previously mentioned, beginning with faith. “Having released, not having grasped”:

this is the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) of those in training (*sekkhā*), referring to the absence of lust and so forth—which are to be abandoned by the lower paths—thinking, “There is no lust, hatred, or delusion within me. Completely...
It was said, "The reviewing of those beyond training (asekha) is with reference to non-existence," meaning:

"The reviewing of both those in training (sekha) and those beyond training has been explained. It should be understood that the reviewing of those in training is explained by the passage beginning, "Or whatever exists internally," and so forth, while the reviewing of those beyond training is explained by the passage beginning, "Or whatever does not exist internally," and so forth.
The commentary on the Atthinukhopariyāyasutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Indriyasampannasutta and others (Suttas 154–155):
In passages such as, “Monks, dwell possessed of virtue,” the word *sampanna* here has the sense of being complete (*paripuṇṇa*).
He said, "one whose faculties are complete. The connection is that one is called "complete in faculties" because of being endowed with the faculties.
Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, it would merely state the perfection of possession, he said, "or the eye and so forth," and so on.
"With reference to that" means with reference to the meaning stated by the second alternative. In the preceding Khandhiya-vagga, [it was] by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).
The teaching has been presented; here it is stated "in the same manner as previously described" by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
The commentary on the *Indriyasampanna-sutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the *Navapurāṇavagga* is concluded.

156–159. *Atthato* means "by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*). It is called "meaning" (*attha*) because it is noble through knowledge and because it is to be known; thus, it is the intrinsic nature.

For in this way, that which has the intrinsic nature of being "well-known" is "delight" (*nandī*) in the sense of rejoicing, and "lust" (*rāga*) in the sense of coloring. "By way of liberation" means by way of the attainment of liberation. "In this" refers to this first sutta.
"In the second and so forth" refers to the second, third, and fourth suttas. They are "clear" precisely because they follow the method already stated below.

For those lacking concentration, who are attaining one-pointedness of mind; and for those lacking seclusion, who are attaining physical solitude.
The construction is: "and those who obtain one-pointedness of mind. "It becomes manifest" means it appears clearly (*vibhūta*).
"It is disclosed" and "it is made evident" is said because the appearance of the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths through their state of being manifest has been described;
thus it is said: "In both cases... they have been explained."
The commentary on the *Jīvakambavana-samādhi-sutta* and others is concluded.

The contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth are indeed called the "states that ripen liberation. At that time, the Elder’s faculties such as faith had not yet reached maturity; through these teachings, the Elder attained the maturation of his faculties.
The commentary on the *Koṭṭhika-anicca-sutta* and others is concluded.
10–12. Commentary on the *Micchādiṭṭhi-pahāna-sutta* and others (165–167).
“Individually” means separately. “In the same manner as stated above” means precisely according to the method explained previously, since there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Abandoning of Wrong View and others is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Destruction of Delight is finished.

1–60. Commentary on the *Ajjhatta-anicca-chanda-sutta* and others (168–227).
“Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein desire should be abandoned”—thus, sixty discourses were spoken according to the inclinations of various individuals;
and these [discourses] were taught by way of a formulaic summary (*peyyāla*).
Regarding the phrase "ascended," it is stated: "There is what is called a 'set of sixty recitations'. Therefore he said, "But those which here...
and so forth. The commentary on the *Ajjhatta-aniccha-chanda-sutta* and others is finished.

18. The Chapter on the Ocean (Samuddavagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on the Ocean (Paṭhamasamuddasuttavaṇṇanā) 228.
If the ocean is called "samudda" by these two meanings—namely, "in the sense of being difficult to fill" and "in the sense of being a gathering place"—then...
In order to show that, in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*), this [designation] is appropriate only for the eye, the passage beginning with "If" was stated.

Therein, "in the sense of being difficult to fill" means by way of its incapacity to be filled. "In the sense of being an ocean" means by way of receiving [water] piled up higher and higher on all sides;
for even though the ocean receives the great floods of water from the Mahāgaṅgā and other great rivers every year, it remains an ocean.

It does not reach fulfillment; and whatever area of ground it covers, it leads that very place to the state of an ocean, or it reaches non-existence once the ocean water has receded, or it remains as it was, having attained a state of being waterless.
Granted, this sense of being difficult to fill and the sense of being an ocean are found in the word *sāgara*; nevertheless, both of these [meanings] apply specifically to the eye.
Showing that [it] is obtained, he says “for him,” and so forth. “Converging” means approaching from all sides by way of the blue and other parts;
the meaning is that it comes into the range of perception. It is unable to do so because it is difficult to satisfy.

It proceeds with a movement of hatred because it causes the continuity of the sentient being to become corrupt. And its state of being corrupt should be understood by way of craving associated with the eye-door.

Just as the force of waves rolling one after another in the ocean is called "the ocean," so too the object-base of visible form—classified as blue and so forth—which rolls one after another before the ocean of the eye, deserves to be called "of the eye" because it is not shared by anything else;
thus it is said, "a surge consisting of visible form. "Without regard" means in the sense of correct seeing.

Having grasped at the state of being agreeable and the state of being disagreeable in a visible form, the "non-examination" is the grasping of one who does not reflect, thinking, "This indeed has been seen by me," but grasps it merely as a compact mass. "Endures" means it overcomes [the object];
it does not undergo any alteration on account of that cause.
"Ūmī" refers to waves. "Āvaṭṭa" (whirlpool) refers to water that moves by way of swirling. "Gāha-rakkhasa" (crocodile-demon) refers to crocodiles, demons, and so forth.
Just as waves in the ocean, rolling one over another, overwhelm the person who has fallen into them and lead them to ruin and disaster, so too do the whirlpools and the crocodile-demons.
In this same way, these defilements such as lust, when they arise within a being, [lead them to ruin].

Having overwhelmed them, they lead beings to ruin and disaster. Because it is the cause for the arising of defilements in beings and thus a cause for their falling into ruin and disaster, the ocean of the eye is described as "with waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and rākṣasas," by way of being the object of that fear of waves.
Here, "fear" (*bhaya*) means that which one fears; "fear of waves" (*ūmibhaya*) means a fear like a wave. In the sense of being agitated...
Anger (*kodha*). That very same [anger] is "distress" (*upāyāsa*) in the sense of its arising by way of crushing the mind and in the sense of being a firm affliction.

In this context, the similarity of anger and distress to a wave should be understood through their production of ruin and calamity by repeatedly occurring and overwhelming beings, not allowing them to lift their heads.
Likewise, the strands of sensual pleasure overwhelm beings who are conquered by the defilements, just as pride does.
The similarity to a whirlpool should be understood through the act of causing ruin after having whirled one around within the self—
conceived as the objects such as form— in such a way that even the thought of renunciation, which exists outside of that, does not arise;

for when a house-dwelling *rākṣasa* overcomes and seizes a man who has come to its own hunting ground and is devoid of protection, it carries him off even though he stands in a place that is not its usual range.
Having led [the victim] into its range and rendered him incapable of self-defense by means such as displaying terrifying forms, it then enters him, deprives him of his beauty,
strength, wealth, longevity, and happiness, and brings about great ruin and calamity; in the same way, a woman also—
lacking wise attention and having overcome a man who is not a hero by means of her own physical beauty and other charms— seizes him.
Or, even if one is of a heroic nature, by means of feminine gestures, personal charms, and amorous displays, he may become possessed by feminine deceit;

or, rendering himself unable to accomplish the qualities of virtue and so forth that are beneficial to him, he deprives himself of the praise of his own virtues and brings about great ruin and calamity.
In this way, the female sex should be regarded as being like a house-demoness.

The phrase "fearful of waves" is a term of definition. For just as a wave is called "fear" in the sense of being something to be feared, so too are whirlpools, crocodiles, and sea-monsters; thus the meaning should be understood as "fearful because of the fear of waves and the like.
One who has gone to the end, the limit, is said to have "gone to the further shore," which is Nibbāna.
The commentary on the first Sāgara Sutta is finished.
2–3. Commentary on the Second *Samudda Sutta*, etc. (229–230).

It is said, "in the sense of moistening" (*temanaṭṭhena*), because it brings about a state of wetness (*allabhāva*) for the defilements (*kilesa*). "Noble disciples" (*ariyasāvaka*) refers to non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

For they are not "swollen" (*samunna*) by way of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). "The three deaths" (*tayo maccu*) refers to the Māras of defilement (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of a deva (*devaputta*).
"By means of the three acquisitions (*upadhi*)" refers to the three acquisitions consisting of defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and sensual qualities (*kāmaguṇa*).

However, he is not "without acquisition" (*nirūpadhi*) with respect to the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandhupadhi*), because he has attained only *nibbāna* with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*). "Gone" (*gata*) means gone by way of the progress of practice.
The commentary on the second *Samudda Sutta* and others is finished.
4–6. Commentary on the *Khīrarukkhopama-sutta* and others (231–233).
"In the sense of not having been abandoned" means by way of not having been eradicated by the Path. "It exists" means it is present.
When the conditions are present, because it performs its function, the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) is slight; it is called "limited" (*paritta*), like the poison of a rat.

Because of its limited power (*appānubhāvattā*). "Even such as this" means even a small amount. "Of one" refers to one who has not abandoned the defilements (*appahīnakilesassa*). "Excessive" (*adhimattānaṃ*) refers to desirable and enticing things;
by way of the object-base (*vatthu*), even a slight desirable object is indeed excessive. Therefore he said: "even the size of a fingernail's surface," and so forth.

"Young," and so on—these are three words. "Should violate" (*ābhindeyya*) means should break. "Both of those" (*taṃ ubhayaṃ*) means both that eye and the visible form; both of these sense-bases (*āyatana*).
The commentary on the Khīrarukkhopama Sutta and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Udāyī Sutta: 234.
"In this way too" means by this reason as well. By "the impermanent," the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) is explained through the state of impermanence.

Because consciousness arises through causes and conditions, and since there must be cessation once there has been arising, consciousness is impermanent by virtue of its nature of arising and passing away.
Furthermore, if it were a self, it would have to be established independently of conditions; yet it is not so established.
Therefore, by means of its impermanence, the selflessness of consciousness is stated as: "Consciousness is non-self."
The commentary on the Udāyīsutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Ādittapariyāyasutta: 235.
Because they arise clearly, following upon each defilement (*kilesa*) as its specific manifestation and as a condition for its arising, they are called "sub-defilements" (*anubyañjana*).
He says, “hands, feet, and so forth are the parts,” in the passage beginning with “hands are beautiful.
“Grasping at signs” (*nimittaggāha*) means grasping that which serves as the sign for the arising of defilements.

“Grasping by combining” means grasping together as one—such as “woman” or “man”—after having brought the parts together. “Grasping by analysis” means grasping exhaustively through differentiation. “Like a crocodile” (*kumbhīlasadisa*)...
It is like a crocodile’s grip. Therefore he said: “It seizes everything,” meaning it seizes each respective part, such as the hands and feet, by dividing them up.

It is like a leech’s grip, similar to a blood-sucker. The statement that these are obtained even in a single cognitive process (*javana*) refers to the mind-door impulsions (*manodvārika-javana*) that arise following the eye-door.
"Bound by attachment to the sign" means bound—that is, fettered—by grasping at gratification in the sign as previously described.
"By the life-continuum alone" means by the fundamental life-continuum (*mūla-bhavanga*) itself.

"Showing the danger of the defilements" means that if, while such defilements are arising, the death-consciousness were to be interrupted by an unwholesome state of mind, one would certainly [be reborn] in hell or in the animal realm.
He says this to show that one must fear the arising of defilements.

Having stated, "It was said thus according to the occasion," he explains that meaning by saying, "In the case of the eye-door," and so forth. "Or with a lustful mind" means with a mind colored by passion (*rāga*).
How can there be an experience of the flavor of the object (*ārammaṇarasa*) with a mind that is corrupted? [The answer is: It is through the arising of a feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*).
In this way, the experience of the flavor of the object (ārammaṇarasa) should be understood. "At this time" means at the time of death.
"Cutting with a razor-edged saw" refers to the cutting performed by a saw with eight teeth situated between the two nostrils.
"A long-handled axe" means a large axe with a long handle. By the phrase "having lain down and fallen into sleep," he excludes the sleep of nodding.
For in that state, there might occasionally be an opportunity for the arrows of wrong thoughts to intervene;
but this is certainly not the case when one has lain down and fallen into a deep sleep. "Thoughts" refers to wrong thoughts.
The commentary on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the First Simile of the Hand and Foot Sutta, etc. (236–237).

Regarding the ninth [sutta], he says, "When it is said 'it is discerned' (*paññāyati*), it is spoken according to the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) of those who understand," and so forth: "In the tenth, when it is said 'it does not exist' (*na hoti*)," and so on. For this much alone is the distinction between the two suttas.
The commentary on the First Simile of the Hand and Foot Sutta, etc., is concluded.
The commentary on the Samuddavagga is finished.
19. The Āsīvisa-vagga (Snake Chapter). 1. Commentary on the Āsīvisopama-sutta (The Simile of the Venomous Snake).

238. Among those bhikkhus who were then seated surrounding the Blessed One, some lived alone, some with one companion, some with two companions, some with three companions, and some with four companions, dwelling in forest retreats;
thus it is said: "those who wander alone... up to those who wander in groups of five. They were of similar inclinations and lived in concord.

To one who is devoted to the practice of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), there are those who assist them; for that very reason, there are those who are appropriately engaged in that task. By means of the disposition of the individual (*puggalajjhāsaya*) acting as the cause, it becomes a supporting condition (*paccaya*), meaning it serves as a prop.

Beginning with the words, “Just as, monks,” and continuing up to, “the brahmin has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land”—this is the presentation of the summary matrix (*mātikānikkhepa*). The following is the detailed explanation (*vitthārabhājana*) of that matrix.

"It will be a carrier of latent tendencies" means it will bring about latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). "As if lifting up Mount Sineru," and so forth, is a demonstration of the extreme difficulty of this teaching due to its uniqueness compared to others.

Just as the term "bed" is applied to those on a bed, here the word "mouth" is intended to refer to the poison located in the mouth. This is because [the poison] is brought to a state resembling dry wood.
“Kaṭṭha” is said [to mean wood]; thus, one whose mouth is like wood is *kaṭṭhamukho*—a snake that, by means of its bite and so forth, produces a state resembling wood.
Alternatively, it is *kaṭṭhamukho* because poison (*visa*) is placed in its mouth, making it resemble wood.
In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well. “These four” refers to these four according to the classification of their poisonous functions.
Now, in order to show the distinction between their respective functions, the passage beginning with “Among them” is stated.

“As if pierced by an iron spike” means as if an iron spike had been driven into the interior. “Like a rotten, putrid jackfruit” means like a jackfruit that has been cooked and then, with the lapse of time, has become putrid.
“In a caṅgavāra” refers to the alkaline straining vessel of washermen or the straining vessel for liquor.
Or: by cutting it off entirely, like a place struck by lightning. "By a great bite" means by a large incision.

"By the transformation caused by the force of the poison" means by the change brought about through the onset of the poison's power. "By the wind" means by the wind rising up after touching the body of that snake;
however, there is no need to speak of the wind from the nostrils. "By way of designating a person" refers to those very [beings].

There are sixty-four types of snake venom based on the names of individuals, such as *āgatavisa* (the one whose venom has arrived), because each of the sixteen snakes possesses four distinct varieties.
*Āgatavisa* means "one whose venom has arrived," which signifies that its venom acts very rapidly. *Ghoravisa* means "fierce venom," referring to venom that is difficult to treat.
This [type] is like cold water in its quality of being extremely difficult to release once it has gripped.
For it is said that the water-snake (*udakasappo*) indeed possesses a terrible venom: "like the venom of water-snakes and the like.
It is "perceived" (*paññāyati*) by way of swellings, pustules, and so forth. The *aneḷakasappo* is a great *āsīvisa* (venomous serpent).

The *nīlasappo* is a tree-snake, green in color, which frequents the tops of trees and similar places. "By this means" refers to those whose venom is discharged only when they have bitten upon pieces of wood.
The fourfold nature is stated by means of this method, beginning with the words, “‘āgataviso,’ ‘no ghoraviso,’ and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “those whose venom is in the mouth of the stick,” there are three types: those whose venom is in the mouth of the stick (*kaṭṭhamukha*), those whose venom is in what is touched (*phuṭṭhavisa*), and those whose venom is in the wind (*vātavisa*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that in the cases of the putrid-mouthed (*pūtimukha*) and others, there are likewise four types each, beginning with those whose venom is in the mouth.
"Each one" means each single [set] out of the sixty-four. "In four ways" means having divided them into four by way of the classification as egg-born and so forth.

"Fifty-six" means fifty-six plus [something]. "Of the path traversed" means that when the path traversed according to the aforementioned number is condensed in reverse order, they gradually become only four.
"By way of lineage" means by way of the species such as the "mouth-of-wood" (*kaṭṭhamukha*) and so forth.
Their state of being touched by poison (*phuṭṭha-visatā*) is like having poured it over their entire bodies; thus, they are said to have "wind-poison" (*vāta-visatā*).

"In this way" refers to the passage beginning with "those whose poison is poured out" (*āsitta-visā*). Here, the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) of the word *āsīvisa* (venomous snake) should be understood according to the method of philology (*nirutti*).

"With exalted heat" (*uggata-tejā*) means possessing intense heat; or, it refers to their fierce nature through the power of their own venom. They are those whose poison is difficult to suppress (*dunnimmaddana-visā*).
"Poisoned foods that cannot be neutralized by antidotes. Regarding the phrase "four venomous snakes," here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*).
By this, it includes the remainder of the canonical text.
Regarding the term "venomous snakes," it should be understood that these venomous snakes possess poison in their bites. "Only in the bodily hairs"—by that person...
It should be understood that they did not show it to them because they had not done anything undesirable for anyone, and because their lifespan was still remaining.

He asked because he wished to have it explained as it truly is. "Difficult to attend upon" (*durupatthāhā*) means difficult to serve. "The path of safety" (*sotthimaggo*) is the means for attaining well-being.

"One who moves within" (*antaracaro*) refers to one who moves among [the group], like a trusted servant who betrays confidence; therefore, he is called a "murderer" (*vadhako*). Now, regarding those...
The words beginning with "first" were spoken to show the reason for sending [the messenger].
It is as if it had come face-to-face; for even such a verbal construction is observed in the world, just as in the expression, "he places a man in the presence.
Therefore, "come face-to-face" means that it has arrived facing him. A plank of crooked shape [was placed] at the foot of the tree for those who came and went.
Spread out for the purpose of sitting.
It is called a *santāraṇī* because a person with empty hands crosses over by means of it. An *uttarasetu* is a bridge for crossing from this shore to the further shore.
A *rukkhasetu* is a wooden bridge that can be traversed by one or two people. A bridge suitable for travel by foot-soldiers is a *jaṅghasattha-setu*.
A "jaṅghasetu" (a bridge for the legs) is a cart-bridge that can be traversed by a cart. This brahmin does not exist in the ultimate sense;
however, showing that its meaning is possible in a figurative sense, he said, "because of having warded off so many adversaries.
"Teaching" refers to the teaching by way of enumeration. "Turning back" means withdrawing. It was not obtained.
"Vatāsī" means "alas, it was not obtained.

It is like a king because it exercises sovereignty over beings through its governance of karma. [The comparison to] a king... [and so on]... applies to the worldling (*puthujjana*) because of his transgression consisting of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

"By the fleeing of knowledge" refers to the fleeing of knowledge that has arisen by way of the desire to become disenchanted with, detached from, and liberated from the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
[This is] precisely by means of the fleeing of knowledge (*ñāṇapalāyana*) established through the attainment of the path.
In this way, the correlation of the simile is brought to its ultimate conclusion here. With the words "Just as... and so forth, the illustration of the whole by means of a part is commenced.

He supports the aforementioned statement with the words of the Aṭṭhakathā masters by means of the passage beginning with "He becomes rigid" (*patthaddho bhavati*). In that context, the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by means of the mouth of a stick" (*kaṭṭhamukhena vā*)...
The meaning is "like a wooden-mouth. Just as one bitten by a snake with a wooden mouth becomes rigid, so too, through the provocation of the earth element, that body becomes like a wooden-mouth;
the meaning is that it becomes rigid as if it had entered a wooden mouth. Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It should be connected by bringing it over as: "or through the provocation of the earth element."
This is the meaning here: even when bitten by a woodlouse, the body becomes rigid solely through the disturbance of the earth element;
therefore, that body, as long as it is not separated from the earth element, remains like something bitten by a woodlouse.
Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness. In this case, the meaning is: the body bitten by a woodlouse becomes rigid.

Or else, it is not by means of mantras or medicines. However, due to the provocation of the earth element, that body—devoid of mantras and medicines—becomes as rigid as a piece of wood placed in a furnace, being absolutely stiffened.
In this context, "body" refers to the natural body. "Putrid" means decomposed. "Heated" means entirely heated, having reached a state of great burning.
"Cut to pieces" means entirely severed, reduced to a state of dust and fragments. When...
When the body has reached a state of rigidity and so forth, the meaning is that the person is like one standing in the mouth of a snake with a wooden head or similar [venomous] creature.

"By way of distinction" means by way of the distinctions such as the wooden-headed [snake] and by way of the distinctions of the elements such as earth and so forth. "Because of the perception of harm, etc.

and so on is for the purpose of producing spiritual penetration (*nibbedha*) by showing how harm and other [unpleasant states] are directly experienced even in insentient beings, just as they are in sentient ones.

It has begun. In this context, "from their abode" means from the place of their occurrence. "Of these" refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Similarity" refers to their similarity by virtue of having an anthill as an abode, a hollow as an abode, a thicket as an abode, and a heap of refuse as an abode.
"By way of individual characteristics" means by way of their respective distinct characteristics.

The similarity should be understood as being like the effect of a poison’s potency: it consists in the production of a transformation in earth and the other elements—such as their state of hardness—and in the production of a state of hardness and so forth in the person possessing them.

"Disaster" (*anattha*) means calamities. "Disease" (*byādhi*) refers to diseases such as leprosy (*kuṭṭha*). "Those who delight in birth within existence" (*bhave jātābhinandino*) are those whose nature is to take pleasure in being born within the various realms of existence. For indeed, delighting in birth within the five aggregates (*pañcavokāra*) is nothing other than delighting in the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

"More difficult to attend to" (*durupaṭṭhānatarāni*) means more difficult to remedy. "Difficult to approach" (*durāsada*) means difficult to draw near; they are unable to come close, thinking, "I shall attend to them.
"We recognize their names as karma," yet there is no such thing as a benefactor. "Because of infinite faults and misfortunes" (*anantadosūpaddavato*).
"Because it is the cause of immeasurable faults and calamities. "A single side" means a single suffering.
When the aggregate of form breaks up, it breaks up only by taking along the four immaterial aggregates, because the immaterial aggregates have a single cessation.
They also break up by taking along the physical basis (vatthurūpa), when the immaterial aggregates have broken up in the five-aggregate plane.
Because there is an absence of stability in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). "To this extent" means merely by the arising of greed.
Wisdom (*paññā*) is called the supreme limb of the person, because wholesome states have wisdom as their pinnacle; and since wisdom does not arise when defilements arise, it is said:
"To this extent, it is said that wisdom has fallen away. It leads [beings] to the various wombs (*yoni*) by means of the kamma-condition that leads to those [wombs].

Regarding the category of existence (*bhāva*): the twenty-five great fears mentioned in such passages as "fear of birth, fear of aging, fear of death, fear of thieves," and so forth, as well as the thirty-two tortures mentioned in such passages as "he cuts off even the hand," are indeed included here because the cause is established therein.
It is stated that "delightful lust is the aggregate of volitional formations" because it is comprised within the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
This is found in the Pāḷi itself in the passage beginning, “If, monks, they do not catch him by way of the eye,” and so forth.

The phrase “not obtaining anything” was not mentioned separately because the statement that the robbers did not obtain anything to seize in that empty village already implies that the man obtained no refuge for himself;
here, the monk represents the person, while the external sense bases represent the robbers.

"Having adhered" means having performed an act of insight-adherence (*vipassanābhinivesa*). It is stated "by way of the meditation subject of derived form" because the teaching is presented by way of the internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*).
"Of external things" refers to the external sense bases. "Five functions" refers to the five functions that must be performed by thieves at that time.
*Hatthasāraṃ* means valuable goods that can be grasped with one's own hands. They handle them by touching with the hands through methods such as throwing them down.
*Pahāraṭṭhāne* means at the place where they have been struck. They say it is "instantly," meaning at that very moment.

Having abandoned the wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*) that brings one’s own happiness, one becomes possessed of the unwholesome which brings suffering; having abandoned the goods that bring happiness, [one goes] outside.
"Like the departure" is said because that [state] is a basis for happiness. The time of reaching the state of being "at the hands of others"... [etc.]...
is because the body of qualities (*guṇasarīra*) was then afflicted by negligence. The time of the "blow"... [etc.]... is because the body of qualities was afflicted even more severely than that.
The time of being "struck by the blow"... [etc.]... is because it is like the attainment of death for the body of qualities. By the use of a slave by the rest of the people... [etc.]...
The state of being enjoyed is stated as an illustration of the attainment of a different condition, namely, the reaching of the state of a householder. The construction is as follows:

"That very object which was mentioned as 'having come into the range of the six doors'—it is by depending on that very object that the mass of suffering pertaining to future lives is to be understood.

"Material form and so forth" refers to visible forms, sounds, odors, and tastes. "Of these" refers to the primary elements and derived material forms as previously described. "By way of lightness and so forth" [is explained as follows].
By way of their lightness and so forth. "The sense of being difficult to cross" means the state of being impossible to cross, which is the sense of a flood (*ogha*).
"By the method already stated" refers to the method stated in such passages as, "Associated feeling is the aggregate of feeling.

"By the four great elements and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the derived aggregates (*upādānakkhandha*) and others are included. "For the purpose of showing mental activity" means for the purpose of showing the application of the mind.
