“Precisely the effort that has been stated” refers to that which is called “right effort” in the Noble Path. “The *Bhaddekaratta* and so forth” refers to the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta* and others, stated as beginning with: “One should exert oneself this very day.
“A man with clubbed feet” means one who, having had his feet severed, is impaired in locomotion. “It binds the mind” means it fixes the function upon that consciousness.

It binds. The firm resolve of the mind toward that [path], thinking, "This noble path is my means for crossing the flood," its further engagement therein, and the exertion of energy, constitute the binding of the mind.
Taking these—namely, delight, lust, craving, ignorance, and so forth—as the conditions for that name-and-form (nāmarūpa), they are a portion of the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).
And it is a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) here, being free from craving for the Noble Path and Nibbāna.
"By sixteen modes" means by the sixteen modes beginning with oppression (*pīḷana*). "By sixty thousand methods" is according to the method set forth in the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*.

At the conclusion of the teaching... they were established; here, those of "attainment through expansion" (*vipañcitaññū*) are distinguished as having attained specific distinctions by way of grasping [the teaching]. They...
For at that time, they were seated in the presence of the Teacher as recipients of the Dhamma.

However, since the specific attainment of those who understand through a condensed teaching (ugghaṭitaññū) and those who require guidance (neyya) is not established in the commentary, it has not been included here.
The commentary on the Āsīvisopama Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Rathopama Sutta (The Simile of the Chariot) 239.

For one who dwells with the sense faculties well-restrained, knowing the proper measure in food, mindful, and clearly comprehending, the suffering arising from the signs of defilement does not find entry;
rather, an abundance of happiness and gladness is said to arise. Just as fruit mixed with that [honey] becomes sweet.
"Yoni" means a source; it is the decisive cause. "Assa" refers to the bhikkhu. "Paripuṇṇaṃ" means complete, without deficiency.
"Āsavakkhaya" means that which exhausts the taints without remainder; it is the supreme path. "Yaṃ yaṃ" refers to whichever mode of going among the slow, medium, or swift.
"Rakkhaṇatthāya" means for the purpose of protection from the thieves that are the defilements. "Veganiggahaṇatthāya" means for the purpose of suppressing the force [of the defilements].
For the purpose of restraining the force of the faculties caused by the defilements. "For the purpose of non-indulgence" means for the cessation of indulgence and agitation.
"For the purpose of the subsiding of the defilements" means for the gradual calming and pacification of the defilements.

What is called "the delight of the recluse" refers to the bliss of serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala). Just as even for well-trained thoroughbred horses, there is the charioteer...
Thinking that there might be some slight degree of attachment through the manner of application, he says "sending after having made it free from attachment" in order to show its absence.

"Knowledge goes" means it proceeds without clinging; this is all the more so because the cultivation of the faculties has already been performed and the suppression of the defilements has been easily accomplished.
The donor's intention may be noble or base. The measure of the object to be given—
Vessels, both small and large.

The site for the Great Pavilion (*mahāmaṇḍapa*) refers to the location where a great pavilion must be constructed in front of the Lohapāsāda, sufficient to accommodate the assembly of the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "The vessel for receiving" refers to the serving bowl used for receiving portions.

A lay supporter (*upāsaka*) who has attained the status of a meal-preparer by nature. By means of the three types of cooking known as soft, medium, and hard, or alternatively, those known as burning, roasting, and frying.
“Having purified” means having cleared away his unworthiness for a king. He threw it on the ground [thinking], “I have not given this to the monks;
I have placed it in my own mouth. He took it with his mouth to demonstrate that he was free from fault.
He wiped it to show the proper measure. When asked, “From where have you come? he fell into negligence. “The remainder” means the portion left over.
*Idamatthiyaṃ* means "this purpose. *Itaraṃ* refers to knowing the proper measure of food, even though it is not mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
*Sayanaṃ* means "lying down"; the lying down of those who enjoy sensual pleasures is "the reclining of sensual pleasure-seekers" (*kāmabhogiseyyā*).

There is no such thing as "lying on the right side," because one must perform the duties to be done with the right hand. *Tejussadattā*—this [epithet] applies specifically to the lion, who is fearless.
This was said in order to show "lying down. For the statement, "having placed both forefeet in one place and the hind feet in another," demonstrates how the feet are kept from being scattered.
By "the reclining posture of the fourth jhāna," he refers to the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) belonging to the fourth jhāna; for Tathāgatas generally [do so].

They lie down only after having attained the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). And they say that this [attainment] occurs for them after emerging from the fourth jhāna and because of the completion of the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).
Here, the lion’s posture (*sīhaseyyā*) is mentioned; it is considered a posture characterized by not abandoning the previous position when placing one foot over the other.
Therefore he said, "For this," and so forth. "In this way" means he makes his bed in the manner described by the words "on the right side," and so on.
How is one mindful and clearly comprehending while falling asleep? For the intention is that falling asleep occurs through the *bhavaṅga* (subconscious) consciousness.
By the phrase "without abandoning," it should be understood as not abandoning that state due to being intent upon it.

Likewise, at the beginning and end of the descent into sleep, there is mindfulness and clear comprehension that has not been relinquished. Therefore he said: "Even while descending into sleep, one is mindful and clearly comprehending."
"But this," he says, refers to the method already stated: "even when falling asleep, one is mindful and clearly comprehending.

"They did not approve of the 'element of knowledge'" means that the ancient masters did not accept the view that even during sleep, the nature of consciousness is simply the occurrence of knowledge as it is during wakefulness.
[They held that] while the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses proceed uninterruptedly, mindfulness and clear comprehension cannot possibly exist.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). For according to the former method, it is the non-restraint of mindfulness and clear comprehension that is meant, not that of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

The intended meaning is that by means of these three factors—restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and devotion to wakefulness—all such things as avoiding the signs and secondary characteristics belong exclusively to the side of insight (*vipassanā*).

“Those very same” refers to the faculties and so forth that occur at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*). The teaching should be explained in detail up to the stage of *arahantship*. However, in the Canon it is stated in brief: “The basis for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been undertaken by him.
The commentary on the *Rathopama-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Kummopama-sutta*.
240. “A skeleton” (*aṭṭhikummam*) means a tortoise with sharp bones on its back. “Bound by tendons” (*tantibandho*) means bound together.
Having placed it within his own skull as if in a casket, he “places it together” (*samodahanto*), meaning he places it correctly, contemplating it only internally.

“In the skull of the object” (*ārammaṇakapāle*) means in the basin of the object. “Placing it together” means that because he grasps only what is seen, he correctly applies his mental reflections right there.
“Turning away”: for he does not allow it to proceed by way of that object. “Five things”: when it is said, “I will speak at the proper time,” and so forth.
The commentary on the *Kummopama-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Paṭhamadārukkhandhopama-sutta*.
241. As if sporting upon reaching the ocean. "With branches bent within" means with branches leaning toward the bank of the Gaṅgā.
"It moistens" means it becomes drenched. Because it stands like a bridge of poles fallen across [the river], it became a support for the great multitude;
likewise, due to its vast size, there was no need for entering the current of the Gaṅgā and so forth.
“This person” refers to the individual mentioned immediately prior. “Having descended upon the noble path” means having entered the fourfold course of the noble path.
The connection is that, having reflected with the words “The mind, indeed,” and so forth, he does not relinquish the bonds of the householder’s life.
“To one who frequents him” means to one who associates with him. “Expenditure” (payoga) refers to fields, lands, and so forth, because they are to be employed for the sake of livelihood.
Then, regarding the income arising from such activity: although it provides the physical sustenance for the monks, it is for the sake of their alms-food.

"A broken jar" (*muṇḍaghaṭa*) refers to a jar with a split rim. "On the shoulder" (*khandhe*) means on the shoulder. "Property belonging to the Saṅgha" (*saṅghabhoga*) refers to going to a village that is the property of the Saṅgha.
"They speak thus in meaning" means that because the sense [of the matter] arises in that way, they are as if speaking thus.
"Thinking it is rice-gruel when it is merely rice-gruel": having drunk the rice-gruel, he swallows another portion of rice-gruel while that [first] is still undigested—this is the connection.

"Stained by defilements" means his mind is indeed followed by defilements due to the absence of proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). "Having pulled out his eyes" means that, under the influence of anger, making eye-salve from his own eyes, he will wander about having pulled them out. He is agitated and unpacified.

A "follower of wrong views" (*diṭṭhigatika*) refers to one within the Dispensation who, having thus emerged through improper attention, has made the Dispensation contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.
He who illuminates [this] is like Ariṭṭha. Therefore he said, “For he,” and so forth. There is form (rūpa) in the immaterial realm (arūpabhava);

otherwise, for one who has passed away from there, how could there be the arising of the aggregate of form? In the non-percipient realm (asaññībhava), there is mind (citta)—the same principle applies here as well.

The supramundane path (lokuttaramagga) consists of many moments of consciousness, according to such statements as, “One who would develop these four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) for seven years.”
The underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is dissociated from the mind; otherwise, there would be the simultaneous arising of both blameworthy and blameless phenomena.
Furthermore, those beings wander and transmigrate; otherwise, there would be no connection between kamma and its fruits.
Thus he speaks, having adopted such a false doctrine.
Like a *temana* tree... [and so on]... and a person who rarely hears the Dhamma does not wither away because of the moisture of faith.
"One who has practiced discipline" and "one who has trained in discipline" are like the term "one who has mastered the sciences" (*katavijjo*).
"Examine it for those who preach the Dhamma" means: examine this gift for the noble ladies who preach the Dhamma, according to their respective suitability, by way of entrusting it to them.
Having said this: a "speaker of the day" (*divākathika*) is one who speaks in the evening; a "speaker of the night" (*rattikathika*) is a person who speaks during the first watch of the night.
"Delightful as the Nandana Grove" means as charming as the Nandana Grove. "The monks who carry his burden" refers to the preceptors and others who perform his duties.
"Having heard the discourse while sitting comfortably" means having heard the conversation seated together, preceded by polite greetings.

“Stationed” means stationed by way of its very stationary configuration (ṭhitasaṇṭhāna), that is, by way of its stationary form; the meaning is that it is not moving. The construction is: “The paintings, roots, and so forth, are stationed by way of their stationary configuration.

“By way of softness” means by way of having a soft heart and being full of concern. “The path” refers to the practice of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). “Having illustrated” means having made manifest, having explained, having made clear.

“Arising there” (tatruppāda) refers to the arising of life-span produced therein; he speaks with reference to the field. “With oil... hands” means with hands holding jars of oil, jars of honey, jars of molasses, and so forth.

They departed because of their misconduct. Regarding the word "filled": the past tense expressions used here and there below were, it is said, spoken because they have come down in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
Approaching and not approaching, etc., refers both to the approaching and non-approaching of the near shore and the far shore, as well as to the sinkings in between.
"Penetrated" means to know. "This" refers to the aforementioned nature of the eye. "Grief" refers to the grief that serves as the condition for its state of dullness.
Even one who "falls into" it is said to "approach" it because the defilement caused by that sign has been produced.
"Of the three characteristics" refers to [the characteristics of] non-existence after having been, having a beginning and an end, being temporary, and being the negation of permanence, and so forth.
By way of characterizing the three characteristics. "From the left" means wrongly; "from the right" means rightly.

Just as the internal bases are spoken of as the "near shore" because they constitute the state of being this side for each respective being, so too the external bases [are spoken of as the "far shore"] because they constitute their state of being the other side.

The [terms] on the far side have been explained. Because it is the cause for wandering in the midst of the states of deprivation (*apāya*), delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*) alone is called "the sinking in the middle" (*majjhe saṃsādo*).

"Puffed up" means having attained arrogance through such thoughts as "I am superior. In the context of self-exaltation, because one burns oneself by means of the practice of wearing rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*), it should be understood as taking on another form.

It is said to be like a log of wood that is mistaken for a stone or a stump. It becomes pulverized due to the powerful force of the whirlpool. "In the four states of deprivation" refers to the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
A fallen person, even in the world of humans, undergoes a state of being pulverized and scattered for a long time through the destruction of his body of virtues;
this is because he has reached such a state. Indeed, it is thus that he is born in such realms of misery (apāya).
There is no such thing as "corrupt" virtue; therefore, the word *du-* here has the sense of non-existence, which is why he is called "one devoid of virtue" (*nissīla*). "Evil" (*pāpa*)...
In passages such as "by evil it is easily done," the word *pāpa* is a synonym for what is inferior; thus he says, "a base state.
"Not pure" means not pure in body, speech, and mind. "Or by suspicion" means that through one's own suspicion, one recalls or suspects the conduct and actions of others.
Therefore he says, "For him," and so forth. "He enters into those actions" means [he associates with] those who perform those actions.
"He enters within": by the state of putrefaction of virtues means by the attainment of a defiled state of those virtuous qualities (sīladhamma) that were previously grasped as virtues.
"Become like refuse" means having refuse produced within, or having become refuse itself.

"The going-forth of the debtless" means the going-forth of one who is indeed debtless. Because it illuminates such things as approaching or not approaching the near shore and so forth, the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭavivaṭṭa) have been described.
The commentary on the First Simile of the Log is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Simile of the Log: 242.
Any offense that leads to rehabilitation and leads to confession is defiled from the moment it is concealed.
It is called "defiled" (saṃkiliṭṭha) by virtue of being an obstacle. However, it is called "undefiled" (asaṃkiliṭṭha) because it stands in a state where there is no offense;
thus it is said: "For him, its manifestation is comfortable. Such a thing is defiled either by way of being concealed or by way of its being a grave matter (duṭṭhulla).
The commentary on the second Simile of the Log of Wood is finished. 6.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Series of Terms Concerning the Lustful (Avassuta-pariyāya-sutta).

243. "Santhāgāra" means a hall for deliberation. Therefore he said: "At times such as when preparing for a military expedition," and so forth. By the word "etc. (ādi), [he includes] auspicious ceremonies and great festivals.
The gathering (*saṅgaha*) is to be understood [in this sense]. "They gather" (*santharanti*) means they rest; the meaning is that they dispel fatigue.

"Together" (*saha*) means in one place by way of assembly. Regarding the term *santhāgāra*: it should be understood that because there is instruction on the matter (*atthānusāsana*) together in that house (*agāra*), the letter *ttha* is changed to *ntha*, thus it is called a "hall of assembly" (*santhāgāra*). First, it is so called by way of deliberation therein.
The meaning is that they spread out and investigate.
Since the word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka will indeed have arrived, by way of the arrival of the Buddha’s word, the arrival of the dhammas of the noble fruits has also been stated.
For those dwelling there throughout the three watches of the night, there is the enjoyment of the attainment of fruition.

And since within that Saṅgha of bhikkhus there were those of virtuous character and virtuous worldlings who were exerting themselves in insight (vipassanā), the noble path-dhammas also indeed arrived there.
"With fresh cow dung" means with clear, fresh liquid cow dung. "Having smeared" means having plastered. "With four kinds of scents" means...
With the fragrances of saffron, turuṣka, yavana-flowers, and tamāla-leaves. "Of various colors" means having various colors by way of blue and so forth;

"of various shapes" means having various forms according to the particular walls [they adorn]. Regarding "the great back-covering rug (mahāpiṭṭhika-kojava)," they say it refers to a rug that has received the conventional name "great back-covering" because it is to be spread upon the backs of elephants and the like.
However, this was said with reference to a *kuttaka* (a small rug or carpet).
Some also say that "mahāpiṭṭhika-kojavas" are rugs made of wool that are more than four finger-breadths thick.
*Hatthattharas* (elephant rugs) and *assattharas* (horse rugs) are rugs to be spread upon the backs of elephants and horses, decorated with the forms of elephants and horses.

*Sīhattharakas* (lion rugs), however, are rugs decorated specifically with the forms of lions and so forth. A *cittattharaka* (patterned rug) is a rug decorated with various figures as well as various floral designs and the like.
*Upadhāna* means a pillow. *Upadahitvā* means having placed it in a manner suitable for serving as a pillow. A *gandhadāma* is a garland made of fragrant substances.
A *pattadāma* is a garland made of *tāla* leaves and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes garlands made from vermilion, *takkola*, nutmeg, cloves, and other such items.
A *pallaṅkapīṭha* is a seat constructed in the shape of a couch (*pallaṅka*). [This refers to] one side among the three sides...
Thus, there is a leaning-back support with a backrest, and a backless support with a seat. "A league in circumference" means in an area measuring a league in perimeter.
"Having arranged" means having made the corner portion of the inner robe and the other portions equal, having prepared them. Therefore he said:
"as if drawing a lotus with a knife," and "covering the three circles. Because for the Buddhas...

Just as his perfection of form, so too his perfection of deportment had reached the highest excellence; therefore, showing that at that time the Blessed One would have shone in such a way, he said, "With a golden girdle," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "with the peerless appearance of a Buddha" and so on, [it is shown that] because there was no reason for the Blessed One to conceal his Buddha-majesty at that time, [he appeared before] the gods, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandhabbas, and others assembled there.
This shows that he entered Kapilavatthu solely by his own natural disposition in order to inspire confidence.
Since the bodily radiance of Buddhas naturally extends over a space of eighty cubits, it is said that "he occupied a space of eighty cubits.
The rays of a Buddha are six-colored, consisting of blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and crystal-clear.
"Sabbapāliphulla" means blossomed and fully opened on all sides, from the roots up to the tips of the branches.
"Arranged in succession," and so forth, is a metaphorical comparison (*parikappūpamā*); just as another [object] shines when it is adorned... [as described]... so did it shine.
Because it was fashioned by the thirty paramis, it is said that it shone in such a way. "By twenty-five... [etc.]
They say that the great Gaṅgā, having become one hundred mouths, entered the ocean along with twenty-five very large Gaṅgās.
In the *Papañcasūdanī*, it is stated as "of twenty-five rivers," meaning twenty-five great rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and ending with the Candabhāgā; for this is a figurative expression.
“Sambhijjāti” means having reached a state of commingling and mixture at the gateway of the mouth, that is, at the place where it has entered the ocean.

“Of nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and so forth” is stated by way of a figurative description. “With a thousand” means with a thousand verses; the meaning is: with a composition the measure of which is a *bhāṇavāra*.
“Shaking the earth” means making the earth resound with the proclamation of one’s own special qualities; even while being such, [he recited].
Not harming living beings; because of the circumambulation of all Buddhas, he lifts his right foot first;
he touches the earth evenly due to the characteristic of having well-placed feet. Even though he touches the ground evenly, he is not defiled by dust because of the delicacy of his skin.
"The low places rise up," and so forth—this refers to the attainment of the mark of a Great Man known as the well-placed feet of the Buddhas.
The fruit of the outflow (*nissandaphala*). "He lifts [it] not too far away" means he does not lift it to place it at a distance that is too great.

And "he goes forth without setting it down too near or too close" means he proceeds without placing it in a spot that is either too near or too close. "Causing laughter" means gladdening the world together with its devas.
"He moves with four feet" means he is one who moves on four feet (*catucārī*).
Because it has proceeded by way of manifesting the majesty (*anubhāva*) of the Buddhas, this is called "the time for praise.
Whether the physical beauty of the body or the praise of their qualities is being recounted, it cannot be said that it is poorly told. Why? Because the Blessed Buddhas possess immeasurable beauty;
when the qualities of a Buddha are praised, they enter precisely into the description as it was begun by one who knows them. [The phrase] "with a *dukūla* cloth-pillow" means...
"With a fine linen cloth fastened [around his waist].

"Moving with the majestic stride of an elephant-king" means his placement of footsteps was like that of a noble elephant. "Possessing the marks of a hundred merits" means he possessed the marks of a Great Man produced by many hundreds of merits.
"Like the radiant Maṇi-jewel" means shining and gleaming exceedingly, surrounded by eighty-four thousand gems.
Like a gem. Some say there is a gem called *verocana*. Like a great *sāla* tree, or like a large tree such as the *koviḷāra* standing in its purity.
"Just like the *paduma* and the *kokanada*" means like the great *paduma* known as the *kokanada*, or like a blossoming lotus.

"Like one bringing down the Ganges from the sky," and so forth; this introductory narrative demonstrates both the extreme difficulty of this task for others and its quality of bringing ultimate happiness to those who hear it. "Like one pulling up the essence of the earth":
this is like one who, having set a water-wheel in motion, pulls up the sap of the great earth from its lower surface with the opening facing upwards.
"Yojanika" means measuring one yojana. "Madhubhaṇḍa" means a honeycomb.
"Mahanta" means vast or sublime merit. "All gifts have been given" means that every kind of requisite has indeed been given by the donor of the dwelling.
For instance, having wandered for alms through two or three villages and received nothing at all—

Even for one who has arrived, after entering a monastery endowed with shade and water, bathing, and lying down for a moment in his lodging, when he rises and sits up, strength seems to have been restored to his body as if it had been injected.
Furthermore, while wandering outside, the element of beauty (*vaṇṇadhātu*) in the body suffers from wind and heat; but having entered the lodging and closed the door for a moment—
For one who is seated, the dissimilar continuity subsides, and the similar continuity becomes established; it is as if the element of beauty has been brought and placed therein.
For one wandering outside, thorns pierce the feet, stumps strike them, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise. Having entered a dwelling and closed the door—
But for one who is seated, none of these dangers exist. For one engaged in recitation, there arises the happiness of the joy of the Dhamma;
for one attending to the meditation subject, there arises the happiness of tranquility due to the absence of external distraction.
And for one wandering about externally, sweat breaks out on the body, the eyes twitch, and at the moment of entering the lodging, [one encounters] beds, chairs, and so forth.
They are not visible; however, when one has been seated for a moment, it is as if the clarity of one's eyes has been brought back and restored.
Doors, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth become visible. Furthermore, seeing someone dwelling in this monastery, people respectfully attend to them with the four requisites.
Therefore it was said: "When a gift of a dwelling place is given, all gifts [are fulfilled]."
“It becomes exactly as given. Regarding the eight grounds... [as before] ... “it is not possible”—this meaning should be illustrated by the *Mahāsudassana* narrative.
“The mother’s womb is unconfined”—this meaning should be illustrated by way of the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence.
“Cold” refers to the cold that arises either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the change of the external seasons.
"Hot" (*uṇha*) refers to the heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood as arising from forest fires and the like. "Repels" (*paṭihanti*) means he repels it.
He acts in such a way that, by means of both [cold and heat], no affliction strikes his body and mind.

For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a monk whose mind is distracted is unable to apply himself with wise effort (*yoniso padahati*). "Fierce beasts" (*vāḷamiga*) refers to fierce beasts such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
For when you have entered a well-guarded lodging and sat down after closing the door, there are no dangers for you.
"Reptiles" refers to any crawling creatures that move by slithering, such as long-bodied snakes and others of that kind. "Gnats" is merely an illustration;
by this term, the inclusion of stinging insects and the like should be understood. "In the cold" refers either to the cold season or to periods such as the seven-day rains.
"And when the touch of cold arises. "Showers" is to be construed as: whenever they arise, he wards off the falling rains.
"Terrible wind and heat" refers to the wind—distinguished as dusty or dustless—which is terrible because it acts by uprooting and breaking trees, shrubs, and so forth;
and the sun’s heat, which is terrible because it arises during the seasons of summer and feverish heat. "Is warded off" means it is repelled.

“For the sake of a shelter” means for the purpose of delighting in seclusion by turning the mind away from various objects. “For the sake of comfort” means for the purpose of living at ease through the absence of the aforementioned dangers.
“To meditate” means to meditate by way of concentrating the mind upon any one among the thirty-eight meditation subjects after having bound it there.
“To see with insight” means to comprehend conditioned phenomena by way of their impermanence and so forth.
“Vihāra” means a dwelling place. “Kāraye” means he should have them built. “Ramme” means delightful.
“Vāsayettha bahussute” means that after having them built, he should cause those who are learned, virtuous, and of noble character to dwell there.
Furthermore, while causing them to dwell, he should provide food, drink, clothing, and lodgings in such a way that those learned ones do not suffer from a lack of requisites.
And one should give to those who have become upright and are endowed with noble aspiration, with a mind serene through faith in the fruits of kamma and the qualities of the Triple Gem.
Now, in order to show the mutual assistance between householders and those gone forth, he spoke the verse beginning with “Te tassa.
Therein, “te” refers to the learned ones; “tassa” refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*). “Desentī dhammaṃ” means they teach the Dhamma which dispels the entire suffering of the cycle of existence.

They preach the Dhamma that leads to liberation. "Having understood that Dhamma here" means that a person, having understood the true Dhamma in this teaching through right practice, becomes free from taints (*anāsava*) by attaining the supreme path and attains final Nibbāna.
"In the dwelling" refers to the gift of a dwelling. "Blessing" means profit. By way of honor and respect, the first watch of the night was spent [in listening] to the Teacher.
Since only a small portion of the middle watch of the night remained when the teaching of the Dhamma was concluded, it is stated in the Pāḷi as “most of the night”;
thus he says, “more than one and a half watches. It does not fit into a formal compilation because of its vast extent.
For even the Buddhas’ expression of gratitude after a meal, if spoken by expanding it slightly, becomes long and of middling length. Thus, for example:
The lip-covering is very bright; the tongue is slender; the dwelling in the life-continuum is brief;
there is no gasping, no stretching, and no distracted mind; omniscient knowledge is fully established, and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are inexhaustible.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "having shown," "having shown" means having delivered a Dhamma talk connected with the gift of a dwelling. Then...

Furthermore, O Great King, having correctly shown them the qualities of virtue and so forth—namely, "Virtue is thus, concentration is thus, wisdom is thus"—and having manifested them directly as if grasping them by the hand, he "incited" them; that is, he incited them so that they would correctly adopt those qualities of virtue and so on, thinking:
"Virtue should be undertaken in this way; by one established in virtue, concentration and wisdom should be developed in this way."

Having had [them] grasp it in that way. "Having encouraged" means: having encouraged them so that the virtue they have undertaken becomes thoroughly purified, and so that when serenity and insight are cultivated, being well-purified, they bring about successive distinctions; thus, having encouraged them and having cleansed them by means of reflection.
"Having gladdened" means: [having gladdened them] at present with the qualities of virtue and so forth, established according to the instruction.
Having gladdened the mind with the benefits and advantages already attained as well as with the specific fruits yet to be attained above,
and having thoroughly satisfied it by means of the flavor of what has been gained— thus is the meaning of these words to be understood.
For the most part, the Śākya kings found satisfaction and established their footing in the Blessed One’s teaching through his discourse on the Dhamma.
Because prefixes have multiple meanings, the prefix *abhi-* can also share the same meaning as *ati-*. Thus it is said: "Abhikkantā means atikkantā.
In that context, the phrase beginning with "it is said" (*tatra kira*) and so forth is not a fixed formula; therefore he says, "This is not a reason," and so on.

The statement "lightness of body and mind, etc., arise" is an explanation of the cause for the transformation of body and mind; [this occurs] through the attainment of the unsurpassed hearing when lightness and the other qualities have arisen.
This is because of the attainment of the knowledge of the meaning and the Dhamma as they are acquired. For it has been said:

“In whatever way, friends, the Teacher or a certain venerable fellow-celibate teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, in that very way he gains knowledge of the meaning in that Dhamma, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma,” and so forth.
Backache arose because the body was subject to the clung-to (upādinnaka) state and because suffering follows due to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Or, regarding the statement "this is not the reason," in order to clarify that very intention with which it was said, "he is able," etc., was stated.
He is able to sit in a single cross-legged posture just as he did in the village of Veluva. "In this much space" means in this much...
The construction is: "In each instance, the instance is accomplished. And "that" refers to the fixing of the perception of emergence in the mind.
"Hearing a discourse on the Dhamma" means out of reverence for the Dhamma.
"Of one who is lustful" means by way of lust and so forth, which constitute the state of being lustful. "The cause of being lustful" means the cause of the state of being moistened [with passion].
"By way of being intent upon defilements" means by way of the defilements, that is, by way of their agitation. "Like extinguishing" means like the subsiding [of a fire].
"Of those free from indulgence" means of those devoid of agitation.
The commentary on the sutta in the manner of the *avassuta* (lustful) section is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Dukkhadhamma-sutta* 244.
"Of things that are suffering" (*dukkhadhammānaṃ*) means of the causes of suffering. Therefore he said, "of things whose nature is the origination of suffering," and so forth.
Therein, in order to show both what suffering is and what the things that are suffering are, it was stated: "In the five [aggregates]," etc. "They" refers to the five aggregates.
"Because they have the nature of producing suffering" means because they are the causes for the arising of suffering. "Of that" (*assa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrument.

"Sensual pleasures" (*kāme*) refers to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesa-kāma*). Again, "of that" (*assa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of possession. "Movement" (*cāraṃ*) refers to the movement of the mind.
"Dwelling" (*vihāraṃ*) refers to the dwelling of the movement occurring at the five sense doors; some also call it "single-pointed. For this very reason, [it is said] "having followed after..."

"Thus it is said regarding one who is wandering. "Having followed after" means having followed step by step from the occurrence of the process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*) up until the third impulsion (*javana*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "leaping in and so forth," the suffering involved in the pursuit of sensual pleasures by means of agriculture, cattle-herding, and other such activities is included.

"Dāya" means that which gives [pleasure]; it is a forest. Hence he says "the wilderness" (*aṭavī*). "A thicket of thorns" refers to a forest resembling a small enclosure or hut. Since a noun requires a verb, he supplies the verb "he pierced" (*vijjhī*) as the remainder of the sentence.
“Dandhāyitattaṃ” (sluggishness) is the persistence of arisen defilements. Therefore he said, “merely having arisen,” and so forth.

“By that” means by mindfulness. “Some defilements” refers to the fact that among the fourteen functions of consciousness, it is specifically during the function of impulsion (*javana*) that the defilements of the mind arise;
thus it was stated in that way. They remain suppressed by virtue of being unable to proceed. Therefore he said:
“Unable to remain steady. This is stated because the eye-door is mentioned first in the text;
by that same principle, the remaining doors are also included. [This occurs] during the first impulsion-moment when lust and other defilements have arisen.

It is so called because it can be obtained through reflexive mindfulness (*paccavekkhaṇasati*) once one has recognized, through a lapse of mindfulness, “Defilements have arisen in me. Therefore he said:
—“It is not surprising that this. Having turned [the mind] over means having turned it over in a way that is not based on reason (*ayoniso*). Regarding “in the case of adverting and so forth”:

because a desirable object has been obtained precisely through those [turnings] when adverting and so forth arise in an irrational manner, it is attained and fit for occurrence due to the fulfillment of conditions.
Having turned back means having turned back the arising of defilements even during the second impulsion (*javana*) moment. How?
He said, "For those who have initiated insight," and so forth, to show that this can indeed be attained by him.

"Established in development and reflection" refers to the state of the yogi being firmly grounded in both meditative development (*bhāvanā*) and reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). This is its benefit:
even though the defilements have found the opportunity to arise through the acquisition of conditions, they are suppressed in various ways by the power of the development previously practiced.
Having been suppressed, they simply turn back; wholesome states, having found an opportunity, increase further and further.
*Abhihaṭṭhunti*: having brought forward. *Anudahantīti*: they are as if burning along with it. *Anusentīti*: here too, the method is the same. *Anāvaṭṭanteti*:
not turning back from the state of asceticism (*sāmañña*); this is the intended meaning. Thus, the power of insight (*vipassanā*) alone is illustrated.
Because the attainment of the path and its fruits has not yet arisen.
The commentary on the *Dukkhadhamma Sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Kiṃsukopama Sutta*.

245. It is said that there is "various seeing" by way of function, in the sense of the manifold vision [attained] through the full understanding (*pariññā*) and clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths; for it is stated:

"Vision is a designation for the first path. This is because the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is conventionally established for the subsequent paths, and because this [first path] is the first vision of Nibbāna.

Therefore he said, "The first path," and so forth. Someone, not understanding the meaning as it has been stated—that is, without error—might suspect an over-extension of the term *ñāṇadassana* (knowledge-and-vision) by way of its taking an object; in order to preclude that, he said, "But the change-of-lineage," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "It is not called 'seeing,'" they cite the example of "the king's seeing. All four paths, however, are indeed seeing.

In the sense already stated, the method of development (*bhāvanā-pariyāya*), however, refers to the manner in which the three subsequent paths proceed by means of the development that serves as the means for the first path.
"Purification by seeing" (*dassana-visuddhi*) means that purification through seeing exists therein; thus it is *dassanavisuddhika*, [referring to] Nibbāna.
One who has the sphere of contact (*phassāyatana*) as his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is called a "meditator on the sphere of contact. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"In a portion of formations" means in a part of formations. They say that the discernment of form is accomplished when, at the minimum limit, one sees mere phenomena such as earth and so forth;
and the discernment of the formless is accomplished when one sees mere phenomena associated with that, such as eye-consciousness and so forth.
"He spoke only of the path he had himself realized" means that he explained to him precisely that method by which he had applied himself to insight (vipassanā).

"But this one," refers to the monk who is asking about the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Of these" is a statement concerning those whose meditation subjects are the bases of contact (phassāyatana) and those whose meditation subjects are the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha).
Having stated, "They do not coincide with one another," he makes that same point clear by saying, "By the first," and so forth.
Because there is no formation for one who is liberated from the five aggregates, it is said, "without exception.
"In the same way" means that just as with the meditation subject of the bases of contact, so too, having asked about this meditation subject of the five aggregates, [the answer follows].
"The elements proceed evenly" means that the bodily elements, such as taste and the rest, proceed evenly, not remaining in a state of disequilibrium.
They were. Therefore he said, “a body fit [for practice], having attained strength. The passage beginning with “past formations” is stated by way of an application of insight (*vipassanā*).
Comprehension (*sammasana*) must be maintained in all instances. “The ground for wandering” means the place of one’s range of activity.
“The state of being a doer” means the state of being devoted to cultivation (*bhāvanā*). “A man with jaundice” means a person afflicted by jaundice. “Ariṭṭha” means...
The Sutta. "Having prepared medicine" means having prepared a medicinal compound. "I will make" means I will prepare medicine.
"Like a burnt stump" means like a charred stump, because it is covered with a network of creepers and because it is overspread with a succession of young sprouts.
"In the village near the southern gate" means in the village in the vicinity of the southern gate. "Red" means red-colored. "Recently grown" means...
"Like one with a long robe hanging down" means as if wearing a robe that has slipped off. "One who has taken up a hatchet" means one who has seized a small axe. "Dense shade" means thick shade.
Because the branches of that tree are not sparse but possess thick foliage and stand joined together with one another, its shade is likewise;
therefore it is said: "Dense shade means shade standing joined together," that is, thick shade.
This is the meaning. The passage beginning with "Therein" (*tattha*) and so forth is the correlation of the simile.
"To those who are intent upon this or that aspect" means to those who are practicing insight through various modes of application—such as the six bases of contact—and who are intent upon Nibbāna.
It is "well-purified" by virtue of the accomplishment of the full understanding of the three characteristics and so forth.

“In that very same manner” means in the manner of one’s own inclination. Now, in order to demonstrate those various modes in conjunction with similes, the passage beginning with “Just as” is commenced; this is easily understood.
“This” refers to the city simile. “If that has been observed” means if the collection of meanings illustrated by the *kiṃsuka* simile has been observed.
"Of that bhikkhu": for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, that is, for the further development of the specific distinction gained by means of the meaning as it was clearly perceived.
"Of that very meaning": of that meaning known as the purification of vision (*dassanavisuddhi*).
"There is no fear of thieves" because of the tranquil state of the kingdom of the Middle Country. "Three men high" means measuring three men in height.
They were variegated with various wall-paintings, and above the pillars they were delightful, marked by the shapes of bows and diverse floral designs.
Therefore, he said, “for the purpose of adorning the city.
Because they must be installed to ensure the stability of the city gate, it was stated, “they also serve to ward off thieves. *Piṭṭhasaṅghāta* refers to the door-post.

“He is endowed with wisdom known as discernment (paṇḍicca), which consists of the knowledge that recognizes: ‘These are the residents, these are the newcomers; here too, there is need for these people for the sake of the city and the lord of the city, and through them there might be harm.
He is endowed with proficiency (veyyattiya) consisting of skillfulness in removing what is unknown. Regarding the phrase ‘consisting of situational wisdom (ṭhānuppattika-paññā)... therein...”
In that matter of state business, [it was] by means of what is termed "instantaneous presence of mind.
A "royal official" (*rājāyutta*) is one appointed or commissioned by the king; it refers to a person stationed in various places to perform duties for the king.
"In just a few days" means that in only a few days, his position became unstable because he had performed improper acts. Thus it is understood.
It is said: "Having removed all the grounds for legal decision and so forth.
"Cut off his head" means: cut off his royal duty in that regard, which is the head—the supreme limb—standing in the place of the head.
Otherwise, if its ordinary meaning were taken, it would constitute an order for the taking of life. For... [it is not so].
A universal monarch (cakkavattirāja) issues such a command because he restrains others from it as well.
Alternatively, by saying "cut it," he shows himself as if cutting off his own head by my command;
thus, having fulfilled the instruction therein, he would descend, and such indeed is the practice recorded further on. "Therein" means in this frontier city.
"Arising" means arising in the meditation subject of serenity (*samatha*).
"Of that very [city]" is to be connected by supplying the words "are called the gates" with reference to the city designated as *sakkāya*.
The construction is: "the pair of swift messengers. Because the physical heart-base is grasped as being in the middle like a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*).
It is said: “of the great elements that serve as the support for the heart-base.

If this is so, and only the physical base (vatthurūpa) should be taken, why is there a mention of the great elements instead of taking that very base? To answer this, he says: “For of the physical base,” and so forth.
“Of such a kind” means of the same kind as the path of insight previously described by way of right view and the other factors. “This too, because it is endowed with eight factors...”
Having said, "It is just like that," the Noble Path is called the "path as it has come. "This, first, is here" means:
herein, in this sutta, this is the correlation with the aforementioned simile brought forward for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
"This correlation" refers to the correlation with the simile that will now be explained. The simile of the city master is by way of the five aggregates.
It is brought forth to show one who has attained purification of vision and whose taints are destroyed.
The construction is as follows: "The simile of the crossroads is brought forth to show one who has attained purification of vision and whose taints are destroyed by way of the four great elements.
Having stated, "Only the Four Truths were spoken," and having set them forth to demonstrate those truths, it was said, "Even by the whole [of this]," and so on. Here, the equipment for the city—
The six doors and so forth. For by that, the six bases of contact and so forth are illustrated.
And since these are included within the truth of suffering, it is said: "By means of the components of the city, the truth of suffering itself is explained.
The commentary on the Kiṃsuka-sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Vīṇopama Sutta (The Simile of the Lute) 246.
Regarding the phrase "of a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī," although only these two assemblies are mentioned in the text, this Dhamma-collection is common to all;
it includes the remaining assemblies as well as other gods and humans—this is the intended meaning.

The passage beginning with “Just as if” (*yathā nāma*) was commenced in order to demonstrate by means of a simile. “Sacrificing” (*yajanto*) means giving. “To be found” (*vinditabbo*) means to be obtained; the sense is that it is to be attained.
“Desire” (*chando*) refers to the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chando*). Therefore he said: “Weak craving is not able to delight him. This occurs because it arose previously.
They first arose with respect to a single object. For that [faith], being without prior cultivation, is weak. "He" refers to desire (*chanda*);

it is unable to take delight because it has not received such cultivation. "Hatred" (*dosa*) is so called because it defiles the mind. "Those" refers to the taking up of sticks and so forth. "Rooted in that" means:

those rooted in greed (*lobha*), such as deceit, hypocrisy, conceit, arrogance, wrong view, restlessness, and so on; and those rooted in hatred (*dosa*), such as enmity, malice, spite, envy, stinginess, stubbornness, and aggression, and so on.

Defilements rooted in delusion— namely, shamelessness (*ahirika*), fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*), sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and distorted attention (*viparītamanasikāra*)—
are indeed included here because they are rooted in that [delusion]. Furthermore, since all defiled phenomena are comprised within the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arisings,
the phrase "desire or lust" (*chando rāgo*) is stated here to demonstrate that these [other defilements] are also included therein.
It is "full of danger" (*sabhaya*) in the sense of being something to be feared. It is "terrifying" (*sappaṭibhaya*) in the sense of being formidable.

It is "thorny" (*sakaṇṭaka*) in the sense of obstructing the side of wholesome states. It is "overgrown" (*sagahana*) in the sense of being difficult to penetrate by means of wholesome and blameless qualities.

It is a "wrong path" (*ummagga*) because it does not lead to the attainment of fortunate rebirths or to Nibbāna. It is a "bad path" (*kummagga*) because it leads to the lower realms. "Wandering" (*iriyanā*) means turning about or proceeding.
Defilement itself is the path of defilement because it leads to states of misery. The intention is that it is not possible to go to a state of prosperity, much less to attain Nibbāna.
By the phrase "through the contemplation of the foul, etc.," the word "etc. should be understood as including the attention to impermanence and so forth. The mind turns away;
a mind possessed of lust does not arise because it has been dispelled by the application of its opposite. Regarding the "neutral object":
Regarding an object that serves as the basis for equanimity toward the unknown: "for one who adverts to the recitation... [etc.

...to the questioning" means for one who adverts to the recitation by way of causing it to be recited, to the questioning by way of causing it to be questioned, and to living with teachers by way of dwelling in their presence.
"The mind" refers to the mind through the accomplishment of inclination toward it by way of reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge and associating with persons possessed of wisdom.
The ignorant mind ceases.
Just as it is said that "merit is the fruit arising from merit," so too, because it arises from grain, it is called "grain"; thus he says, "Grain means the crop grown in the place of grain.

By "yoke" (ghaṭā), a pair of horns is intended here; thus he says, "between two horns. They say that "yoke" (ghaṭā) is a conventional term for the space between the horns of oxen and the like. By "nose-rope" (nāsārajjuka), he means the place where the nose-rope is fastened.

*Dameti*: it restrains [the mind] from various objects. *Taṃ*: that is, the mind. *Yaṃ suttaṃ subhāsitaṃ mayā tadassa*: "That which was well-spoken by me, let that be for him"—that is, for that bhikkhu.
*Ārammaṇe*: in the object, namely the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). *Sudujitaṃ*: conquered by means of making it free from turbulence. *Sutajjitaṃ*: conquered by means of driving it far away;
and since what has become thus is called "conquered" (*tajjita*), it is so stated. *Gocarajjhattaṃ*: an object that has become internal.
For the object of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is called "internal" because it is devoid of external objects such as visible forms.

"Guarded by serenity" (samathānurakkhanaṃ) means that serenity protects this [virtue]. The meaning is that it is spoken of in such a way that the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara-sīla) becomes a protection for serenity. For just as the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties is a condition for serenity, so too...
"Tranquility (samatha) is also a condition for him":
when the lute is being played, it "delights the mind," thus it is called "delighting" (rañjana). Because it binds the mind through its non-releasability, it is "binding" (bandhanīya).
A "veṭṭhaka" is a peg for striking the strings. A "koṇa" is so called because of its scraping or because it produces sound from the lute.
A *koṇa* is a wooden staff that has received its name; it is a small stick made from any material such as horn and the like. Therefore he said, "a square, solid staff.

Because that king or royal minister did not understand the sound according to its true nature, the words beginning with "I shall see the sound" were spoken specifically to demonstrate his state of ignorance regarding it.
The phrase "it is indeed non-existent" (*asatī kira*) is stated in the text with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*); thus, speaking according to the actual gender, one says "non-existent" (*asā*).
He said: Having stated that "‘Asati’ is a term for what is base,” he spoke the words “Women in the world are called ‘asati’” in order to demonstrate its application there;
the meaning is that women in the world are indeed *asati*. He states the reason for this: “No fixed time (*velā*) exists for them.
In the world, by nature, there is a fixed time or boundary (*velā-mariyādā*) such as “the elder brother,” “the younger brother,” or “the maternal uncle,” but no such [fixed] time exists for them.
Why? Because those who are lustful and arrogant fall into the disposal of all [possessions] by way of enjoyment.
How? Just as fire consumes everything. Therefore it was said:
"All rivers flow crookedly; all forests are made of wood."
“All women commit evil when they obtain a man who is well-protected.

Furthermore, there are other stringed instruments such as the square-shaped drum (*ambaṇa*) and so forth. The five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*) are like a lute because they consist of a collection of many phenomena (*dhamma*). The practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is like a king because he seeks the phenomena connected thereto.

“Of him” means of the practitioner. The word “destiny” (*gati*) is used for other states of existence besides hell; therefore, it is said “the destiny of destinies” (*gatigati*) for the sake of specification.
“Suffering-suffering” and “form-form”: the meaning is that which is designated as a destination (*gati*), namely, the place of occurrence.
Therefore he said: “In this interval, one wanders and revolves. A destination is a place of birth; thus it is a “destination of birth” (*sañjātigati*).
Furthermore, that destination is shown by way of the womb, which is a directly perceived basis for the agitation of beings.

“This is his body,” and so forth, has been stated. The "destination of its own characteristic" (*salakkhaṇagati*) means that for a material phenomenon, its own characteristic is its destination and its consummation;

beyond that, there is nothing else. "Non-existence" (*abhāva*) is absolute non-existence. "The destination of dissolution" (*vibhavagati*) is the cessation of the continuity [of the stream], because it is the state of being the consummation of that.

"Dissolution" (*bhedo*) refers to momentary cessation; here too, the term is used by way of its being the consummation of that. "As far as the peak of existence" (*yāva bhavagga*) means as far as the highest point of all existence.

The distinctions regarding the dissolution of specific characteristics and the modes of existence have already been explained by the phrase "this is the same method," and thus they are not included here.
For that one whose taints are exhausted, these do not exist because they have been utterly eradicated by the supreme path.

Virtue (*sīla*) has been discussed because it was taught as the means for warding off desire and other defilements toward form and the rest. In the middle, the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*) has been discussed.
Because it is illuminated by the statement, “It settles within itself… [and] becomes concentrated,” and because Nibbāna is described at the conclusion by the words,
“And that which for him… does not exist.
The commentary on the Vīṇopama Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Chappāṇaka Sutta (The Simile of the Wounded Man) 247.

*Vaṇasarīro* means one whose body is wounded. *Pakkattā* means because of being putrefied. Regarding the expression "the designation *sara* for arrows," since the word *kaṇḍa* is a synonym for *sara*, he says:
"A *saravana* is a thicket of arrows (*kaṇḍavana*). ... [The passage] beginning with *Arugatto* should be understood as follows... [etc.]... it should be understood.

Because of the defects of fragmentation, unevenness, and disintegration throughout the lower, middle, and upper parts of the body of qualities (guṇasarīra) due to broken and flawed moral conduct (sīla) and so forth;

here, "kusa" is intended to mean "thorns" because of their similarity to thorns, or the specific portion of the kusa grass itself is called "kusa-thorn" because it possesses the aforementioned characteristics.
“In the sense of piercing those who live in villages” means in the sense of afflicting them by receiving their offerings while being unworthy.

“A winged one” refers to the *hatthiliṅga* bird. It is said that its mouth resembles an elephant’s trunk; therefore, it is called the “elephant-trunk bird. “He should release it” means he should release it exactly as it was tied with a rope.
“With his own bodily possessions” means with the parts of his own body. “Having bound himself into a circle” means so that his body takes the form of a circle.
"Stands" means having acted in this way. "I will sleep" means I will descend into sleep. "Desirous of flying" means desirous of soaring upward.
"Direction after direction" means from one direction to another direction.
The six sense bases are like six creatures because of their differing inclinations; and their differing inclinations are due to their being directed toward various different objects.
They are to be seen as follows: craving is like a strong rope because it binds them; ignorance is like a knot in the middle because it is the cause for the bond being difficult to untie.
The object is powerful both by virtue of its attractiveness and because of the firmness of the adherence of craving toward it.

Or, in the context of providing an illustration through a similar comparison, "absorption" (*appanā*) means a linking together. In the text itself, the simile is applied with the words "just so," and so forth. The eye has a distorted inclination because it is bent unevenly toward visible forms, consciousness, and so on. This same method applies to the others as well.
“Ear-hole pit” (*kaṇṇacchiddakūpaka*) refers to the cavity known as the ear-hole. “It is a condition for that” means it is a decisive support (*upanissaya*);

for without it, there would be no apprehension of sound. Having stated, “Even the non-cavity space is indeed suitable,” the passage beginning with “inside a cave” was spoken to demonstrate its status as a condition.
“Striking a succession of elements” (*dhātuparamparā ghaṭṭento*) means striking a succession of primary material phenomena (*bhūta*).
"Thus being" means when sound comes within the path of the ear by way of such a succession of occurrences, there is the state of the ear having its object present.
Just as with the nose and other [senses], the cognition "the sound is distant" would not be possible because of the nature of apprehending what is present.
Such-and-such a mode of knowing occurs due to the specific mode of grasping belonging to mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). This is the occurrence of ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).

However, in both cases, the conditions are indeed the same. It should be understood that even a sound situated at a distance becomes a condition for echoes and the like in such places, just as iron is a condition for the movement of iron.
"Dhammatā" means the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhamma-sabhāva*); the meaning is that this is the inherent nature of sound.
Hearing [the sound] from here and there occurs because of obtaining the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) designated as space.

If, however, the ear were to grasp only what is present [at the moment of contact], then sound produced by mind (cittasamuṭṭhāna-sadda) would not be an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for ear-consciousness.

Furthermore, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated without qualification that "the sound-base (saddāyatana) is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of being an object-condition," and there is no occurrence of sound produced by mind externally.
Alternatively, sound produced by mind [reaches the ear] through a succession of elements (dhātuparamparā).
It strikes the ear-sensitivity; that sound which proceeds by way of succession is not born of consciousness. For it is born of the primary elements (utu).
Therefore, one must conclude here that the sound, as soon as it has arisen, comes within the range of the ear-sensitivity while remaining right there.
Hence it was said: "Its objective field is indeed that which has not reached [the sense organ]."
At that time, it attains one-pointedness of mind due to the absence of dangers.

Because it functions in dependence on the space reckoned as the nostril-cavity, the nose is said to have space as its resort (*ākāsajjhāsaya*). Since the apprehension of odors is impossible without air, its range of objects consists of odors supported by air (*vātūpanissayagandhagocara*).
Therefore, he said: "For thus," and so forth.
The food obtained from a village is called "the village"; because of its inclination toward that [food], it is said to have a village-orientation.

Likewise, for the sake of life, flavor is "life" (jīvita); because of its inclination toward that [flavor], it is called the tongue (jivhā). It is not possible to know the flavor of what has not been moistened by saliva;
therefore, the tongue has as its object the flavor supported by water.
"Outside of a fresh cemetery. "Inclined toward the appropriated" (*upādiṇṇakajjhāsaya*) means leaning toward the appropriated.
Consciousness arises there only when the tangible object has come into contact with the earth that serves as the physical basis for the body-faculty (*kāyapasāda*), and not otherwise;
thus it is said, "having the tangible object supported by earth. "For in this way," and so forth, [is stated] because of the body's inclination toward the appropriated.
It is effective. "Internal and external" means either internal or external. "Of it" means of the body.
"Well-spread," and so forth, shows its state of being a condition for the earth.
"Diverse inclination" means leaning toward various objects; by this, he shows the mind's lack of stability, like that of a monkey.
Therefore he said, “Even though previously seen,” and so forth. By the mention of the *mūlabhavaṅga* (root-life-continuum), the *piṭṭhibhavaṅga* (aftermath-life-continuum) is excluded.
“Of that” refers to the mind. Thus, consciousness should be understood as consisting of functional activity (*kiriya*). “Diversity” means differentiation.

It is with respect to those who are bound by the prevention of proceeding according to their own desire. “The state of being without indulgence” refers to the cessation of the agitation known as restlessness (*lolatā*).
“Non-existence. “It does not drag along” means it does not drag along the mental continuum toward its own object, namely the visible form, nor the person endowed with that [continuum].
Only the preliminary stage of insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) is spoken of here, because it was stated by way of the sense bases: “In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The commentary on the Chappaṇakopama Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Yavakalāpi Sutta* (Sutta 248).
A "heap of barley" (*yavapuñja*) is a collection of well-ripened barley. "With clubs in their hands" (*kājahatthā*) means with staffs in their hands.

"They would thresh" (*potheyyuṃ*) means they would thresh it so that the grain known as barley is separated from its stalk. "Having scattered the barley" (*yave sāvetvā*) means [having scattered it] from the tip of the stalk.
Having released and separated them by threshing with a pestle;

the six sense bases (āyatana) are like a crossroads because they are the place where one is struck by the sticks of objects; the sentient being is like a sheaf of barley because he is struck by those [sticks];
and the six types of conflict (byābhaṅgiyo) are like [the stalks], for in their own nature each is threefold according to the desirable, the undesirable, and the neutral.
The eighteen objects [are so called] because they strike a being who stands like a heap of barley.
The plural expression "defilements that are the aspiration for existence" (*bhavapatthanā-kilesā*) is used with reference to the repeated arising [of beings] through the aspiration for existence.

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the aspiration for existence and the defilements that serve as its conditions are together "the defilements that are the aspiration for existence. This is because the suffering of the round of rebirth for sentient beings—
Indeed, all that is rooted in the aspiration for existence (*bhavapatthanā*); therefore it is said, "In this way, beings," and so forth.
"Defilements of the aspiration for existence" refers to the defilement rooted in the aspiration for existence.
"In the vicinity" (*bhummam*) is used in the sense of proximity. Hence he says, "at the gate of Sudhammā. "Not done" means not producing suffering.
"Not done. "Like a pig feeding on fresh dung" means like a pig that eats fresh dung. "By the mind alone" means by the very mind of one who is bound.
"Therefore" means because it is like the release from the bond of Vepacitti’s bondage;
therefore it is called "Vepacitti’s bondage. "The bond released by knowledge" means the bond that is released by means of knowledge.
"Conceiving" means conceiving by way of craving as "this is mine," by way of view as "this is my self," and by way of conceit as "I am this.
Since there is no basis for conceiving apart from the aggregates, it is said, "conceiving the aggregates.
"Of Māra" refers to the genitive case "of Māra. "Bound by the defilement-Māra" means bound by that very same defilement-Māra.
Bound by the fetter of defilements. The same principle applies here to the word "freed.
When there is the conceit of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*), there is no possibility at all for the conceits of views and pride;

thus, just as the conceits of views and pride are expressed by the term "I am" (*asmīti*), so too is the conceit of craving expressed by that same term. Therefore it is said: "By the term 'I am,' the conceit of craving [is expressed]."
"...is said. By the phrase "this I am," there is the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhimaññita*) by way of the very objects of views currently available.
By way of the conceptualization of objects of views yet to come, there is the conceiving of views. For the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) for the most part embraces the future.
The connection is made by bringing in the phrase "the conceiving of views itself by way of annihilationism" (*ucchedavasena*).
The words beginning with "possessing form" (*rūpī*) are [epithets] that illustrate the various manifestations of the very grasping at eternalism (*sassata*).

Since what is conceptualized (*maññita*) is a disease by way of being an affliction, a boil by way of being an internal corruption, and an arrow by way of being a piercing pain, therefore, through these defilements such as craving, they both "quiver" (*iñjanti*) by way of manifest movement and "tremble" (*phandanti*) by way of unmanifest movement. This is what is elaborated upon.
"Longing in saṃsāra" should be understood as the prolongation of the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*). "Attaining the mode of negligence" means attaining the mode of infatuation.
"Of these" refers to the defilements of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*). "For the purpose of showing the mode" means for the purpose of showing the mode of their occurrence.
What is called "conceit" (*māna*) is the occurrence in the mode of intoxication, such as "I am superior," and so forth. "By way of the conceit associated with craving" means...
Why was this said? Is it not the case that all conceit (*māna*) is associated with craving (*taṇhā*)? For when there is ambiguity, a qualification is required. This is true;
however, there is craving that serves as a condition for conceit, and there is craving that does not serve as a condition for conceit;
therefore, conceit is said to be indeterminate. Thus, in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "Dependent on a fetter-dhamma, [arises] a fettered..."

Regarding the statement, “A phenomenon arises with a root-condition,” here, having demonstrated the conjunction by joining the fetters with the fetters as they occur— stating, “dependent on the fetter of sensual lust,
there is the fetter of conceit and the fetter of ignorance,” and “dependent on the fetter of sensual lust, there is the fetter of ignorance,” and “dependent on the fetter of conceit,
there is the fetter of lust for existence”— [the text continues: “dependent on the fetter of conceit, there is the fetter of lust for existence.”
Having stated, "the fetter of ignorance," it is further said: "the fetter of ignorance [arises] dependent upon the fetter of craving for existence.
Herein, the indeterminate nature of conceit with respect to the fetters of sensual lust and craving for existence is made clear.
In that context, this was said—"by way of conceit associated with craving"—referring to that craving which is powerful. [It refers to] that which is associated with powerful craving.
For conceit (*māna*), having itself become powerful, proceeds with a particular degree of inflation in the form of "I am.

"By way of views" means by way of views rooted in conceit. For when a person who is frequently possessed of conceit—such as "I am superior"—directs it toward one [of the aggregates] such as form, the view arises, "This is I," because conceit has not been abandoned.
Conceit also arises right there, in each respective instance. Thus, with reference to a view rooted in conceit, he says: "It was stated by way of the view 'I am this'.
However, the objector, not understanding this point and grasping at the meaning of association even though it is not actually found, challenges [the author] with the words "But is it not...
and so forth. The other [the author], accepting that point by saying "Yes, it is not," [continues] regarding conceit...
He states the resolution with the words beginning "But... and so forth. Its meaning has already been explained.
The commentary on the *Yavakalāpi Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Āsīvisa Vagga* is finished.
The Fourth Fifty.
The commentary on the *Saḷāyatanasaṃyutta* is finished.
2. The *Vedanāsaṃyutta*.
1. Sagāthāvagga 1.
Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta 249.

“And he understands feelings” refers to the understanding of feelings as they are spoken of in the context of the full awakening to the Truths; such understanding is preceded by an especially eminent concentration.
Since it was said by the Blessed One, “one who is concentrated,” he said, “concentrated either by access or by absorption.
“Feelings” refers to the three kinds of feeling. “By way of the truth of suffering” means by way of the state of being the truth of suffering; the meaning is, by way of full understanding.
“Origination” refers to the cause of arising, which is divided into craving, ignorance, karma, contact, and so forth. Therefore he said, “by way of the truth of origination.”

"...understands. "Wherein" (*yattha*) means by way of which cause; it refers to that [condition] by depending upon which the cessation of craving for sense-pleasures, ignorance, and so forth, leads to the cessation of feeling.
This is their cessation. For it is said that Nibbāna is the cessation of feeling because the Noble Path arises with Nibbāna as its object.
"It goes to destruction" (*khayam gacchati*) means it leads to destruction (*khayagāmi*); thus, it is "leading to destruction. "Chāta" is a term for craving for sense-pleasures.
Because it proceeds by way of the desire to eat, and because hunger has been utterly cut off, there is no hunger (*chāta*) in this state;

thus he is "without hunger" (*nicchāto*). Therefore he said, "free from craving" (*nittaṇho*). "Feelings pertaining to the course of comprehension" (*sammasanacāravedanā*) means feelings pertaining to the access of comprehension. "By two phrases" refers to these two:
"composed" (*samāhito*) and "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*). However, the word "mindful" (*sato*) is [a qualification] of the phrase "clearly comprehending" itself.
The intention is "to augment. By the remaining four [terms], the Four Noble Truths are explained; by the other two, however, only the awakening to the Four Noble Truths is explained.
"Comprehensive" means that which encompasses all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature. Therefore he said: "The delimitation of the phenomena of the four planes has been stated.
The commentary on the Samādhi Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Sukhasutta* 250.
"It is not suffering" (*na dukkhaṃ*) means non-suffering (*adukkhaṃ*); "it is not pleasure" (*na sukhaṃ*) means non-pleasure (*asukhaṃ*). The letter *m* serves to join the words.

"Neither-suffering-nor-pleasure" (*adukkhamasukhaṃ*) is a neuter designation in view of the word "feeling" (*vedayita*). This is said with reference to [feelings] occurring within one's own and others' continuums.
"Grasping internally and externally" was said [by the Blessed One] as "one's own and another's. By this, it should be understood that all feeling whatsoever is included.
"Having the nature of perishing" means having a nature that cannot be seen after its dissolution due to its momentary duration.
It is "perishable" (*palokina*) because disintegration (*paloka*) or breaking up exists for it; hence he said, "having the nature of breaking up. Having touched [this] with knowledge...

"Having touched" means: having touched it repeatedly through the succession of paths—first by way of the object with the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) in the prior stage, thinking "it is impermanent, it is subject to dissolution," and subsequently by way of non-delusion; thus, seeing its passing away.

"He becomes dispassionate" means he becomes dispassionate through the fading away (*virāga*) that is the path. This teaching regarding the feeling associated with the mode of comprehension is given from the perspective of those who have begun insight meditation. [This applies] to both the mundane and the supramundane.
Thoroughly understanding, penetrating, and touching with knowledge according to reality by means of various knowledges is "contact with knowledge.
The commentary on the *Sukha-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Pahāna-sutta*.

251. He cut off all craving, which is divided into one hundred and eight types, by means of its abandonment through complete eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*). Therefore, he said, "He completely cut off" (*samucchindī*).
To the extent that craving was entirely eradicated, to that same extent were all fetters (*saññojana*) [eradicated];

thus he said, "The tenfold [fetters] as well," and so forth. "Thoroughly" (*sammā*) means "well. Furthermore, abandonment is abandonment by means of the right method and the correct principle (*ñāya*).
He said: "By way of cause and reason. "The clear realization through seeing" refers to penetration characterized by non-delusion.
For when the path of arahantship arises, it proceeds precisely while shattering the delusion that conceals its own nature;
thus, pride becomes truly seen for what it is—this is its "clear realization through seeing. Just as, when the sun has risen, darkness is being shattered...
When the path of arahantship arises, that [defilement] is completely abandoned; it no longer finds a footing within that continuum.
This is its "realization through abandonment" (*pahānābhisamaya*). Therefore, it is said: "The path of arahantship," and so forth.
"By way of function" means by way of not failing to accomplish the function of seeing, which consists in penetration free from delusion.

The connection is: "these four ends. "An end defined by a boundary" means an end that is reckoned as a boundary. This same method applies to the remaining three as well. Regarding the phrase "in those": it refers to the four ends. The construction is as follows:

he made that which is reckoned as the fourth limit—the end and the delimitation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra—by seeing and abandoning conceit through the path of Arahatship. "Samussaya" means the personal existence (attabhāva).
“He does not abandon” means he does not separate from it, he does not relinquish it. Therefore he said, “he does not forsake clear comprehension”;

the meaning is that he does not discard clear comprehension.
