Regarding the phrase “he does not come into reckoning,” when explaining the meaning by way of the statement “taintless in this very life,” he said “the lustful, the hateful” with reference to *nibbāna with residue remaining*. “He does not come into reckoning” means...

Or, in the case of one who is taintless in this very life, established in the Dhamma, and a master of knowledge, he does not conform to the designation "human" or "deva" after the breakup of the body;
thus the meaning should also be stated by way of Nibbāna without residue.

And here, since the underlying tendencies such as lust are mentioned in relation to feelings like pleasure respectively, it is said: "In this sutta, the underlying tendency toward the object is explained."

For that which is liable to arise in relation to desirable objects and so forth when there is a convergence of conditions such as lust, and which has not been abandoned by the Path, is called the "underlying tendency of lust" (rāgānusaya) and so on.
Its meaning is "not yet abandoned," and it is to be abandoned by the Path; its meaning is not "overcome by an active outburst" (pariyuṭṭhāna).
The commentary on the *Pahāna-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Pātālasutta* 252.
Regarding the phrase "where there is no absolute foundation," the intended meaning here is that it is not sufficient for a great, absolute abyss;
thus he said, "there is no foundation here. "The sense of non-origination" means not the sense of having originated.
"Musāti" means "loses. "So" refers to the uninstructed worldling (*puthujjana*). The construction is: "that water which falls [into the ocean].
Because a great wind, similar to the *veramba* wind, arises here and there upon the surface of the ocean and causes the water of the great ocean to surge upward;
that [wind], having sometimes gone toward the world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*) and sometimes toward the base of Mount Sineru, strikes against it.

Therefore it was said: “The mouth of the powerful [wind] of the great ocean,” and so forth. “Leaping forward with speed” means leaping forward with the very same speed by which it was tossed up by the great force of the wind.
“Like a fall into a great hell” means it is like falling into a deep chasm or abyss that is a yojana in length, breadth, and depth.
“Of such a kind” means capable of dwelling there. “Non-existent” means unreal. By way of purpose...
For speech is indeed called "unreal.
"It did not find a footing" means it did not obtain a foundation. "Unbound" means anything that is without a basis. "One of weak knowledge" means one devoid of the power of wisdom.
Having stated "the uninstructed worldling," because it is then said "the instructed noble disciple," [it follows that] the "stream-enterer..."
It is said, "the yoke. Regarding the other noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), there is simply nothing further to be said; for by them, feeling has been thoroughly understood (*supariññāta*).
A practitioner with powerful insight (*balavavipassaka*)... [and so on] ...even a mere beginner (*yogāvacara*) qualifies, because of having partially understood feelings.
The commentary on the *Pātāla-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta 253.
“It should be seen as suffering by way of change” means that although it may be pleasant, the state of suffering through change (*pariṇāmadukkhatā*) is nonetheless absolute for pleasant feeling.
“In the sense of piercing” means in the sense of piercing the personal existence (*attabhāva*) by way of oppression.
"Having been" (*hutvā*) means having arisen through the coming together of conditions. By this, the acquisition of self-existence preceded by the state of being cooked (ripened) is expressed.
"In the manner of non-existence" (*abhāvākārena*) means in the manner of passing away into destruction. By this, the state of dissolution is expressed.

Through both [phrases], he shows impermanence that has reached its peak by virtue of being delimited by arising and passing away. And this very manner of non-existence after having been is indeed found in the other feelings as well.
Moreover, there is an excess of the nature of suffering in these two.

Because the preceding feelings were shown as being to be seen by way of their painfulness, the manner in which the subsequent feeling is to be seen is likewise shown here. "He saw" (addā) means he perceived by realizing it through the course of knowledge;
for this "seeing as suffering" is itself the movement of knowledge. It has a peaceful nature because its form is tranquilized with respect to both pleasure and pain.
The commentary on the Daṭṭhabba-sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Salla-sutta 254.

"In two kinds of persons" means in two kinds of persons: the one who has heard [the teaching] and the one who has not heard it. "Following the previous penetration" refers to the penetration that occurred previously.
*Anugatavedhaṃ*: with a following penetration; having become twice as strong, by way of a more firm occurrence. *Evameva*: just so;
just as the subsequent penetration of the pierced man is stronger, even so. Concentration, the path, and the fruit are the "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) by way of suppression, eradication, and subsidence.
Here, both jhāna and concentration are included under the heading of "concentration. He does not know because it has not been attained. He knows it as the escape.
It is indeed non-escape from those feelings of pleasure and pain that have been attained. It is not dissociated from them because the defilements have not yet been abandoned.
"Of one who has discerned the dhammas" means of one by whom the four aggregates have been fully understood through the wisdom of discernment. Therefore he said, "of one who has weighed the dhammas.
In this sutta as well, as in the previous one, only the underlying tendency toward the object is discussed; and that is in the same manner as explained there.
It is to be understood. Because the abandoning of attachment and aversion has been stated, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is the primary subject.
A non-returner (anāgāmī) is also suitable, as the abandoning of aversion is attainable by him.
The commentary on the Salla Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Sick (Paṭhamagelaññasuttavaṇṇanā) 255.
“Thinking that they will believe that the sick should be attended to” is the construction. “Therein” means in that place.

“Those for whom the practice of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is suitable” means those to whom the meditation subject is appropriate; the meaning is that they delight in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
"Contemplating impermanence" means contemplating the impermanence of the feeling that has arisen dependent upon the body.
The same method applies to "contemplating vanishing," and so forth. "Vanishing" (vaya), however, refers specifically to its destruction. "Fading away" (virāga) means the fading of lust.
"Relinquishment" (paṭinissagga) means the relinquishment through abandonment, or alternatively, the relinquishment through leaping forward [into Nibbāna].
The "practice leading to arrival" (*āgamanīyapaṭipadā*) is the preliminary practice that serves as the basis for the arrival of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

It is exclusively preliminary and not supramundane (*lokuttara*). Full awareness (*sampajañña*) is likewise only preliminary. The three contemplations (*anupassanā*) are also only preliminary, because they are included within insight (*vipassanā*).
They are called "mixed" because they are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. The time for development is shown by the phrase: "for one who dwells contemplating cessation."
"Because it is said: 'For one who dwells contemplating relinquishment, the underlying tendency to lust is abandoned.
The commentary on the First Discourse on Illness is finished.
8–9. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Illness, etc.

256–257. Regarding the phrase "dependent on contact" (*phassaṃ paṭicca*): here, by the heading of "contact," the bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) are intended. For contact cannot arise without the bases of contact.
Therefore it was said: "In this context, the body itself is called 'contact,'" the intention being that it is spoken of under the heading of contact.
The ninth [section] is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained below.

10. Commentary on the Phassamūlaka Sutta: 258.
That which is beneficial to pleasant feeling is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasant. As for that state of being beneficial, he says it is by way of being a condition.

“Conditioned for pleasant feeling. In these two suttas as well—meaning in this ninth and tenth sutta—the term *sammasanacāravedanā* refers specifically to feelings that are objects of comprehension (*sammasanīyavedanā*), and not to supramundane (*lokuttara*) ones; this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the *Phassamūlaka-sutta* is concluded.
The commentary on the Sagāthāvagga is finished.
2. Rahogatavagga 1.
Commentary on the Rahogatasutta.
259. "Whatever is felt" refers to what has been called feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which is included within suffering;
the meaning is that it receives the designation "suffering" by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*). Therefore he said: "The meaning is that all of that is suffering.
In the passage beginning with "That which... and so forth, there is the mode of non-existence characterized as the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatā*).

The nature of destruction, the nature of perishing, and the twofold nature of transformation through aging and death—referring to this, I have said that "all feeling is suffering. This is the summary of the meaning.
"That" refers to the impermanence of formations (*saṅkhāra*). Feeling (*vedanā*) is also precisely impermanent because it has the same nature as formations. Their impermanence...
And indeed, having regarded death as "disintegration," there is no suffering greater than that; thus all feelings are called "suffering.
This is in accordance with such Sutta passages as, "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," and "The five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
"The four formless states" refers to the four formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*). "In this" refers to this section on subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).
The commentary on the Rahogatasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Agārasutta 262.
"Puratthimā" is an expression formed by the elision of a case ending; or it is a nominative singular used in the sense of the ablative. "By way of the first jhāna, etc. means:

By way of the first and second jhānas. "By way of recollection" is merely an illustration, since other types of non-sensual happiness accompanied by applied thought (*savitakka*) that are included within access-concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) are also obtainable.
Or else, in the phrase "of that too, the first jhāna, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be understood as including [the remaining jhānas].
For those who have fallen into suffering on account of sensual desire, the feeling of suffering is "with bait" (*sāmisā*) because of the bait of sensual pleasure.
Feeling (*vedanā*). The "supreme liberation" (*anuttara-vimokkha*) refers to the fruit of arahantship (*arahatta-phala*).

When one establishes a longing (*piha*), thinking, "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere?", and that longing remains unfulfilled, there arises a feeling of mental distress (*domanassa-vedanā*) conditioned by that longing.

Equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is called "unworldly" (*nirāmisa*) and "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhā*). However, to show it with particular distinction:
“It is said: ‘The feeling that has arisen by way of the fourth jhāna is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The commentary on the Agārasutta is finished.

263–266. It should be understood that these are taught according to the dispositions of those to be trained (*veneyya*), following the very same method explained below.

"In this context" refers to these four suttas. The first two [suttas] proceed by way of the teaching from the point where speech is stilled for one who has attained the first *jhāna*, up until the stilling of the defilements for one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

“They are said to be ‘possessing full tranquility’ (paripuṇṇapassaddhikāni). Because they were not taught until they had been made complete [in that respect], it was said: ‘The latter [suttas] possess half-tranquility because of the teaching,’ and so forth.

A staff-mallet (*daṇḍamuggara*) and a tip-spoon-mallet (*aggasoṇḍamuggara*). Inserting black thread (*kāḷasutta*) refers to a tube of black thread (*kāḷasuttanāḷi*).

It is called "five-limbed" (*pañcakaṅga*) because it possesses five components, such as the adze and so forth. It establishes the supports to be performed according to the method set forth in the science of site-determination (*vatthuvijjā*).
The carpenter. This refers to the Venerable Paṇḍita-Udāyi, not the Venerable Lāḷu-Udāyi. Regarding "two Ānandas," this is a citation from the commentary;
however, in the canonical text (Pāḷi), it says, "both Ānandas by me. Physical [feeling] is that which is dependent on the body, while mental [feeling] is that which is dependent on the mind.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) is simply pleasure in the sense of being predominant. "By way of mental application" refers to visible forms and so forth.
By way of wandering with equanimity (*upekkhā*). Regarding the past object. "In the present" refers to the present by way of time (*addhā-paccuppanna*). Thus, one hundred and eight is "eight-hundred.
A separate connection (*anusandhi*) means a single connection that is distinct and unmixed with others, such as the connection of questions (*pucchā-anusandhi*) and so forth.
Even a single feeling (*vedanā*) was spoken of by bringing forward [the passage]: "Therein, monks, the well-taught noble disciple... and then [stating], "With contact as condition, feeling arises."

Because the Blessed One, after speaking of the feeling of equanimity in the fourth jhāna, said, “There is, Ānanda, another happiness besides this happiness,” and so forth, he was indeed supporting the Elder’s argument. Therefore, that feeling of equanimity is called “happiness” precisely because its intrinsic nature is peaceful.
“More excellent” means much more desirable, more delightful. Thus he said.
“More beautiful” means more excellent, being brought to a state of preeminence; hence he says “more invigorating.

It is called “bliss” (sukha) because it thoroughly consumes its opposite, or because it easily provides space [for the mind]. Cessation is called bliss because of the total absence of arising and passing away.
Hence he says: “in the sense of bliss, which is defined as the state of being free from suffering.”

“In happiness alone”: he describes it as nothing other than happiness. “Making the attainment of cessation the head”: making the teaching on the attainment of cessation the head—that is, the foremost—of the discourse.
It is said to be “for the sake of the person who is to be guided” because, having raised up those intent on the summary of the teaching, it is explained in detail.
The tenth [discourse] has its meaning already explained, as it follows the method stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
The commentary on the Pañcakaṅgasutta and others is finished.

2–10. Commentary on the *Aṭṭhasatasutta* and others (270–278).

There are one hundred and eight feelings; because there is here a method (*pariyāya*)—that is, a cause (*kāraṇa*)—for that state of being one hundred and eight, it is called the "Method of One Hundred and Eight" (*aṭṭhasatapariyāya*), namely, the discourse (*sutta*). Therefore he said: "The cause of the [one hundred and eight] states" (*dhammakāraṇa*).
The cause is that which consists of the Dhamma as scripture (*pariyatti*). "Bodily" means belonging to the body of the five doors.

Therefore he said, "They are found only in the sense-sphere," meaning they belong to the plane of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*). They do not exist in the formless sphere; the meaning is that they belong to three planes. Therefore he said:
"In the formless realm, the third and fourth jhānas arise, and those are supramundane (*lokuttara*), not mundane (*lokiya*). As for the others...
Equanimity-feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*). "They range over" means they approach and reach. "Of those associated with it" means of those associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"By way of acquisition" means by way of having been acquired. "One who contemplates" means one who reviews or sees.

"The past" is that which has passed by transcending the three moments; it is ceased by having reached cessation; it is transformed by the relinquishing of its original nature. "One who recollects" means...

"For one who reflects": "connected with the household" means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). For here, the strands of sensual pleasure are spoken of by way of the household, as a synonym for things connected with the household.
"Change, fading away, and cessation": having understood change, the characteristic of fading away, and cessation.
"In the past": in the past. "At present": now, occurring in the present. "Seeing with right wisdom": with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).

"And by means of the wisdom of the path" refers to one who sees according to reality. "To cause them to exert themselves" means, having established insight (*vipassanā*), to lead them to the penetration of the path.
Because they proceed directed toward *nibbāna*, they are called "joy based on renunciation.

"Connected with worldly material things" means dependent upon the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "That sphere" (*tadāyatana*) means that sphere, that cause, which is *arahantship*. Among the unsurpassed...
"In the liberations" means in the states of the noble fruits (*ariyaphala*). "They long for" means they desire attainment.
"Equanimity" refers to the equanimity of ignorance devoid of mental joy. "Of the fool" because of his association with folly; for that very reason, "of the deluded worldling" (*puthujjana*).

"Of one who has not conquered the flow" because he has not conquered the flow of the defilements by means of the paths that conquer the flow. [This refers to] the result (*vipāka*) that proceeds beyond the seventh existence and so forth.

Because of being unconquered, [it belongs] to one who has not conquered the result. Because of not knowing the danger in the cycle of existence which has many dangers, [it belongs] to one who does not see the danger.
Because of the absence of proficiency in practice and penetration, [it belongs] to the uninstructed worldling (*puthujjana*).
It does not transcend, it does not go beyond, form—because of the absence of association with knowledge. "Comprehensive" means that which encompasses all phenomena. The third and so forth...
Up to the tenth [sutta], because they follow the method already explained below, their meaning is self-evident.

11. Commentary on the *Nirāmisasutta*.
279. They are "with the bait of defilement" (*sāmisā*) by way of their object and their association. "From the non-baity" (*nirāmisāyā*) is an ablative expression.

For that joy, since it proceeds within a continuum where the bait of defilement has entirely subsided, and because its domain consists of objects that are phenomena of ultimate nature, itself possesses an exceedingly peaceful mode of being.
Even among those [feelings] that are non-material in their occurrence, it is said to be more non-material. Therefore he said, "Is it not the case that...," and so forth.
Now, in order to establish this meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as indeed...," and so forth. *Appaṭihārikaṃ* means devoid of resistance (*paṭiharaṇa*), i.e., non-resistant;
the meaning is that it is unobstructed by anything. "In the remaining sections" refers to the sections on pleasure and equanimity.

The section on the liberations (vimokkhavāra), however, has not been extended [by analogy] because it differs from the others. Therefore he said: "But in the section on the liberations," and so forth.
"Connected with form" means connected with developed form. It is called "material" (sāmisa) because its activity is both bound up with material form and resembles material form;
therefore, it is called "the bait of form" (rūpāmisa), and by that bait of form, it is "material."

Regarding the phrase "having approached Nibbāna": here, "having approached" refers to one who is disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) and inclined toward the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra).
The meaning is: by one who has turned the mind away [from the round] through the lineage (gotrabhū), it is realized by means of the Path.

For when that [Nibbāna] is being realized, having attained it, and depending upon it as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and upon it as the predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya)—which serves as the foundation for the stabilization of formations that are liberated through the state of supreme consolation and for the state of the ultimate destination—one abides in what is termed destruction (khaya).
The path exhausts lust and the other defilements; however, because there would be no non-arising and cessation of lust and the others in the absence of its realization, it is said:
"By coming to Nibbāna, lust is exhausted.
"By this very sutta" means by this very Jambukhādaka Sutta. One might say that Nibbāna is merely the exhaustion of the defilements.
Because it is stated in the Sutta as “the destruction of lust,” and so forth; and because it is stated without qualification as “merely the destruction of defilements,” he asks, “Of what?
and so on. Indeed, he will say “of oneself,” for [one might think] that through the destruction of another’s defilements, the attainment of another’s Nibbāna would be illogical.
Furthermore, by taking Nibbāna as its object, the state of having reached the destruction of defilements at the moment of the lineage-change (gotrabhū) would be implied.
He asks: "But what if those [defilements] have not yet been exhausted? and so forth.

Is it not impossible to say that the exhaustion of defilements occurs merely by taking something as an object? For the mind takes all things—past, future, and so on—as its objects, not only those that have already been produced.
One might argue: "The change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū*) will also proceed by taking as its object that state of non-arising of defilements which is to be brought about by the Path?"
No, because for one who has not attained Nibbāna, there is no knowledge that takes Nibbāna as its object. For Nibbāna is not like other phenomena;

rather, due to its extreme profundity, it cannot be taken as an object by one who has not attained it. Therefore, that which is to be attained by the change-of-lineage consciousness must possess a profound nature that transcends the intrinsic characteristics of the three periods of time, or else it would have to be merely the exhaustion of the defilements.
The destruction of defilements must have been accomplished prior to the moment of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).

For if it were made the object [of consciousness] before the destruction of defilements had been attained, then even the moments of consciousness preceding the change-of-lineage would take it as their object.
Therefore, etc., is the conclusion of the very meaning already stated. And that is this Nibbāna. Material phenomena are non-material... [etc.]
Regarding the phrase "in 'dhammā' and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood as including supramundane, untainted states and others.

By its inclusion among formless phenomena (arūpadhamma) and the like, its status as a fully accomplished reality (pariniṣpannatā) is indicated. Therefore he said: "It is not merely the destruction of defilements.
For if it were merely the destruction of defilements, it would follow that there is a multiplicity of Nibbānas, such that "as many defilements as are destroyed, so many are the Nibbānas."
If it were non-existent by its very nature, its state of profundity and so forth, as well as its state of being unconditioned and so forth, would not exist; yet these have been predicated of Nibbāna.

Therefore, its status as a fully accomplished reality must be admitted. Furthermore, because an object that is conventional truth or an object that consists of conditioned phenomena is incapable of abandoning defilements through their total eradication—whereas sublime knowledge and insight-knowledge [are capable]—[Nibbāna must be unconditioned].

Or else, one abandons [defilements] by way of suppression or by way of partial eradication; therefore, the object of noble path-knowledge must be an object that has a nature contrary to conditioned phenomena comprised within conventional truth.
For it is said that this knowledge abandons defilements by way of their total cutting off;
thus, one should reach the conclusion here that Nibbāna is an unconditioned nature established in such a manner.

“He exercises mastery over cessation because of his state as a non-returner. “These are formations” refers to these: “body-formation, speech-formation, [and mind-formation].”
The three formations spoken of as "the mental formation" (cittasaṅkhāra) are mutually mixed both in terms of their verbal expression and their meaning;
for that very reason, they are confused, disordered, indistinct, difficult to discern, and hard to illuminate, being difficult to explain without confusion.
For instance, wholesome volition itself is called "bodily formation," "verbal formation," and also "mental formation."
In some instances, inhalation and exhalation are called "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*); applied thought and sustained thought are called "verbal formation" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*);
and perception and feeling are called "mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*). Therefore it was said, "For thus," and so forth.

In that context, "taking up" (*ādāna*) is drawing [something] toward oneself; "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) is placing it in one's hand once it has been obtained; "releasing" (*muñcana*) is letting go of what has been grasped.
"Having brought about and accomplished the movement and the pressing. "The pressing of the jaw" means that, by way of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), one first performs the pressing of the jaw;

Here, their dependence on the body should be understood as being due to their existing only when that [body] exists, and not by way of the body’s acting as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*).

Showing this, he said: "When the body is present, they are; when it is absent, they are not. And here, "the body" should be understood as the body composed of the four primary elements (*karaja-kāya*).
"Dependent on the mind" means having arisen by depending on the mind, having obtained it as a support-condition.

The phrase "I shall attain" (*samāpajjissam*), being spoken in proximity to the word "I am attaining" (*samāpajjāmi*), is rightly understood as referring only to the immediate future time, and not otherwise;
thus it is said: "By these two phrases, the time of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) is stated.
This was said because it ought to be stated in that way, but not because such a movement of consciousness is actually possible for him [in that state].

The same method applies even when one has attained [the attainment]. "By the former" refers to the two phrases: "I shall attain" and "I am attaining. "By the latter" refers to the phrase: "I have attained.
It is "developed" and "aroused" for the purpose of attaining cessation. This is by means of what is termed the attainment of successive attainments (*anupubbasamāpatti*).
Through the cultivation of cessation, that mind becomes cultivated. Therefore, he said, "That which... and so forth.
"In the second jhāna itself" means it ceases at the moment of the second jhāna. Because it does not arise there and because it is not produced, "cessation below" is what is intended.
The non-occurrence of the four formless aggregates—which has been established through the appropriate preliminary work—is here termed "the perception of the attainment of cessation."

That which is their non-occurrence in such a manner is described as "ceasing within the cessation. By stating "because of the words 'the mental formation has ceased,'" and so forth, he presents the argument of those who maintain that other [formations] do not cease; therein, by way of demonstrating an over-extension of the principle, he says: ... Thus, having shown the fault in their position through the demonstration of an over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), he concludes: Therefore, because of the words "the mental formation has ceased," it is established that the cessation of the mental formation occurs precisely at the moment of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This is because, if it were otherwise, there would be no distinction between one who has entered the attainment of cessation and one who has not, nor would there be any difference in the duration of the attainment.

Furthermore, since the Blessed One stated, "The mental formation has ceased," this confirms that the cessation of the mental formation is indeed intended here. Thus, the claim that other formations do not cease is refuted. [End of excerpt]

In order to refute that position, he said, “They should be told,” and so forth. “Without making a dogmatic adherence” means without making a dogmatic adherence to the mere literal expression as it has come down.
“Standing on the method of the teachers” means standing on the method of the Dhamma, the guide of the Dhamma, handed down through the succession of teachers.
“While the occurrence consisting of activity is proceeding” refers to the ongoing stream of wholesome and unwholesome states belonging to the limited plane (parittabhūmaka). For in that [stream]:

When [the sense-faculties] are active, there is the occurrence of bodily and verbal activity; the meaning is that this occurs when the grasping of objects takes place by way of seeing, hearing, and so forth.
Therefore he said: "when they strike against the sensitive parts (pasāda) regarding external objects.
They are as if smeared, or as if wiped away, because they are afflicted by the striking. By this, it is shown that this striking belongs to the five-door consciousnesses.
This shows that it is not an object for arising by means of speed. For this very reason he said: "Within the cessation, the five sensitivities shine forth exceedingly.
Following that, having taken what is implied in meaning by the thought "I shall possess consciousness," he says:
"For such a length of time I shall be without consciousness," since the meaning is established by that alone. "That which has been developed in this way..."

In this context, there is no separate cultivation of consciousness; rather, it is accomplished precisely through the preliminary cultivation to be performed for the sake of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), having first determined the duration of time.
This, then, is the discussion on cessation. "By means of two powers" refers to the powers of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). And "three formations" refers to...

349. They do not lead [to the attainment] of the meditative absorptions (jhānas) known as the immeasurable liberation of mind and the liberation of mind through nothingness.

The construction [of the sentence] is to be applied by bringing in the word "also" (*attho pi*) to mean "different. He says "by way of difference in plane," etc., because the jhāna of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), which has received the name "immeasurable liberation of mind" due to its quality of pervasiveness and immeasurability, is different in plane from the others.
He says "by way of difference in plane," etc., regarding the liberation of mind through nothingness, meaning the jhāna of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana).

Vipassanā means the contemplation of impermanence, or indeed all [contemplations]. "That which makes a measure" (pamāṇakaraṇa) is so called because it establishes a measure by way of demonstrating the absence of qualities in that [object] in which it arises.

"By way of pervasion and immeasurability" means by way of pervading and having an immeasurable range. Even Nibbāna is indeed immeasurable, as it is not within the range of those things that have a measure.
This is because even the state of being an object for the defilements does not come into being. *Khala* refers to goods such as sheaves of rice spread out on a threshing floor.
*Kiñcehi* means "by whatever [means]"; thus he said, "the sense of crushing.
That which has no *kiñcana*—meaning no object or nothing that acts as an impediment—is *akiñcana*; the state of being *akiñcana* is *ākiñcañña*.

“Of the sign of form” means of the sign of the kasiṇa-form. “Not grasped” means not grasped as to its specific appearance (sarūpa), but it is indeed grasped as to its meaning. Therefore he said: “Because of the statement ‘It is empty of lust,’ etc., it has entered into all [states]. “Various” is by way of the word;
“of one meaning” is by way of the object—that is, they are of a single nature in their state of being objects. Therefore he said: “The immeasurable... of one meaning.
“By way of the object” means by way of the objective support. For there are four paths and four fruits.
Because they have entered into Nibbāna by way of its object, they are identical in meaning and identical in object.
However, the phrase "in another place" is stated taking each [term] separately; it refers to synonyms such as "immeasurable" and so forth, because they proceed by taking Nibbāna as their object.
Therefore, the word "another" is said with reference to the fact that these terms appear here and there under various such synonyms.
The commentary on the Godattasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputtasutta: 350.

“One who has mastered the tradition” (āgatāgama) refers to one who has mastered the Dhamma as it has been recited. “One who has understood the teaching” (viññātasāsana) refers to one who has penetrated the Teacher’s dispensation.

Therefore he said, "Anāgāmī," and so forth. "Naggabhogga" means: *nagga* because of the state of being homeless; *bhogga* because of having a crooked disposition; and for that very reason, *nissirika*.
For by his nakedness he was destitute of beauty in form, and by his bent state he was destitute of beauty in mind.
"By faith in the Blessed One" (*bhagavato saddhāya*) means: by faith toward the Blessed One. That which is believing in him, that which is conviction in him—this may also be called "his faith."
He obtains it. "I go" means "I come," and "I awaken" is the meaning. This is what was asked by the Nigaṇṭha.
"Having raised up the body" means having lifted the body upward. "Having drawn out the belly" means having pulled the belly forward by inclining the back.
Having extended the neck by stretching it out, he gazes in every direction.
All of this was said by Nigaṇṭha for the purpose of showing his joyful appearance, thinking, "Now it is possible to launch a challenge against the ascetic Gotama.
Therefore he said, "He might [carry off] the wind," and so forth. "With reason" means accompanied by logical justification.
"The path of questioning" (*pañhamagga*): "questioning" (*pañha*) is investigation; thus, the mental investigation as to "it must be so" is the question. "A single summary" (*eko uddeso*).
A single *uddisana* is a concise statement of the meaning. A *veyyākaraṇa* is an exposition, which is speaking after having investigated the meaning.
"In this way" means by this method. "In all cases" means that the meaning is to be understood in detail regarding all the questions, statements, and expositions.
The commentary on the Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputtasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Acelakassapasutta 351.

One who is "adequate" (alaṃ) or capable for the state of a Noble One (ariya-bhāva) is an "Adequate Noble One" (alamariya). Knowledge itself is directly perceived in the sense of knowing what is to be known.
In the sense of seeing, it is "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*); that same thing, in the sense of excellence, is the "distinction of knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanavisesa*).

"Pāvaḷā" refers to the region of the buttocks; it is called "the rubbing of the buttocks" (*pāvaḷanipphoṭanā*) because by means of it the buttocks are rubbed for the purpose of removing dust—it is a practice involving a peacock-feather whisk.
The commentary on the *Acelakassapa Sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Gilānadassanasutta 352.
There was a certain earth-deity named Mattarāja, a lord of spirits who dwelt in the Surāpotala tree. Therefore it is said, “during the time of King Mattarāja.
Having mentioned “herbs, grasses, and forest trees,” he shows them in their respective order: “harītakas... [etc.]”
"And among trees," he said. "Fix your mind by means of aspiration. "It will succeed" means it will succeed according to your intention.
"Therefore" means: because even the gods consider one who has reached such a state to be near death, therefore that [aspiration] will indeed be excellent;
the intention is that it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
The commentary on the Gilānadassana Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Citta Saṃyutta is finished.
8. The Gāmaṇi Saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Caṇḍasutta 353.

“By which [quality] a certain person here is reckoned as ‘fierce,’ indeed as ‘fierce’”—it is by such a question posed by the Dhammasaṅgāhaka Theras that he is given the name “Caṇḍa. He displays his own fierce nature by saying, “I make it manifest.
The commentary on the Caṇḍasutta is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Tālapuṭa Sutta 354.

"Vāla" is said to mean *tāla* (palm); its [fruit] is called *tālapuṭa*. It is similar in size to an *āmalakī* fruit, but it is given the name *tālapuṭa* because its surface color resembles that of a palm fruit.
Therefore he said, "It is said of him... and so forth. One who is endowed with the resolve (*abhinīhāra*).
He has accumulated the requisites for the enlightenment of a disciple over many eons; thus, he was born among the eighty great disciples.
"They give a thousand" means they desire to see a dance. "Samajjavesa" means a festive costume.
"Having performed a play" means having performed a dance-play; the sense is "having danced."
By means of truth (*sacca*) when showing accounts that occurred in the past in such a manner, and by means of falsehood (*alika*) in the opposite case.

"Conditioned by lust" (*rāgapaccayā*) means being the cause for the arising of lust. "From the mouth... seeing, etc."—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes such things as seeing flames of fire issuing from the mouth.

"And others... acting out" (*abhinaya*) refers to those connected with the gratification of sensual desire (*kāmassāda*), as well as those possessing the sentiments of the heroic (*siṅgāra*) and the marvelous (*abbhuta*).
“And others” refers to the dramatic performances that display the sentiments (*rasa*) of wonder and the horrific (*bībhatsa*). “Caused by hatred” means they are the causes for the arising of hatred.

The dramatic performances that display the sentiments of the terrible (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the fearsome (*bhayānaka*), which are included by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “cutting off hands, feet, and so forth,” are “caused by delusion” (*moha*), meaning they are the causes for the arising of delusion. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “such as these,”...
The dramatic performances (*abhinaya*) are those that display the sentiments (*rasa*) of compassion, tranquility, and terror.

For it is with reference to these sentiments that it is stated in the Canon: "Those states that are provocative of lust, those states that are provocative of hatred, and those states that are provocative of delusion.

They manifest only after having assumed the costume of an actor, by way of the ripening of kamma corresponding to the action. "With reference to that" means with reference to what has been stated above.
This refers to being cooked in hell. Thus it is said: "There is a hell named Pahāsa; there one is reborn.

Just as in the world certain verbs, though transitive, become intransitive according to a specific sense—as in "the man is released"—so too here, due to a specific sense, that which is intransitive has been stated as transitive: "I do not..."

“Venerable sir, this is why I weep. But what is that specific meaning? It is non-endurance, non-acceptance; therefore, the meaning is: “I do not weep because I endure, I do not weep because I accept. For one who does not endure the cause for weeping, being overcome by it, weeps.
That specific meaning which serves as the cause for its having an object is expressed by the phrase: “not merely by the shedding of tears.”
It has been said: "Or they weep for one who is dead, mother. Here too, they weep for the dead;
they cannot endure his death, they do not accept it—this meaning is evident.
The commentary on the Tālapuṭa Sutta is finished.
3–5. Commentary on the *Yodhājīva-sutta*, etc. (355–357). Fighting is *yodha*;
one whose livelihood (*ājīva*) is that [fighting] is a *yodhājīva*. Therefore it is said: "one who makes a living by means of war.
Or, "he exerts effort" means he exerts effort by way of engaging in battle. "They cause to perish" means...
They bring about a calamity that ends in death. Therefore he said, "they cause one to undergo death.
"Ill-placed" means that the practice has not reached a state of bringing benefit to oneself or others because it was undertaken in a corrupt manner.
The hell named *Parajita* is so called because those conquered and slain by enemies in battle are born there. The five weapons are the sword, the spear, the club, the iron hook, and the discus.

"Referring to him" means referring to that person who is a professional soldier (*yodhājīva*). This refers to what was stated beginning with "He who... and so forth. "In the fourth and fifth" refers to the discourses on elephant-riders and horse-riders.
"The same method applies" means that this very method stated in the third discourse applies here as well, because there is no difference in meaning.
The commentary on the *Yodhājīva-sutta* and others is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Asibandhakaputta Sutta 358.
“Inhabitants of the western lands” (*pacchābhūmivāsino*) means those who dwell in foreign regions.

“For the purpose of knowing his own state of purification by water” means both for the sake of knowing his own state of purification by water and for the sake of [knowing] this matter: that for the world, purification occurs through water.
And for the purpose of making known. "Causing them to go upward" means causing them to go to the higher Brahma-world. "Making them know correctly" means making them go straight to the heavenly world.
Therefore he said: "They cause them to descend into what is called heaven";
the meaning is that they cause them to enter, they cause them to plunge down. "He should go around" means he should go all around.
The commentary on the Āsibandhakaputtasutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Khettūpamasutta (The Simile of the Field) 359.
*Thaddha* means hard and coarse. *Ūsara* means saline soil. Because it cannot be overcome by any of the four floods (*ogha*), [it is so called].
"I am the island. Because of being invincible by all perils, "I am the shelter.
Because of protection from all suffering and fear, in the sense of being a refuge, "I am the refuge. Because of being free from all terror and harm, "I am the resort"—thus it should be construed.
"A water-jar" (*udakamaṇika*) means a large vessel for water. It is called "non-leaking" (*ahārī*) because it does not let water flow out.

It does not leak away on all sides; thus, it is "non-leaking. The Buddhas teach with full attention because they possess reverence for the True Dhamma and great compassion toward all beings, owing to their state of equal flavor (*samānarasa*).

Furthermore, the four assemblies listen with faith and conviction out of reverence for the Teacher and because they themselves are endowed with faith; therefore, they are joined with the fruit of the teaching.
Because the Teacher’s teaching was successful in that instance, it became known as "the thorough teaching.
The commentary on the Khettūpama Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Saṅkhadhamasutta.

360. Having stated, "Any man whatsoever who takes life or speaks falsehood is one destined for the states of deprivation," and then further stating, "To whatever extent one repeatedly performs [such acts], by that much one goes to an unhappy destination," he contradicts his own position by his own words.

This being the case, if one becomes destined for the states of deprivation through evil karma performed repeatedly, then the statement beginning with "anyone whatsoever who takes the life of a living being" [would be rendered false].
"Wrongly": the four points are the four sections of meaning stated in the manner beginning with, "Whoever takes life," and so forth.
They are the conditions for views for one who emerges unreasonably [thinking], "Indeed, there exists... and so forth. "Endowed with strength" means capable.
"A conch-blower" means one skilled in the function of blowing a conch. "Without suffering" means with ease. "Even the vicinity" (upacāra).
Absorption (appanā) is also appropriate, because both terms share the common quality of being immeasurable (appamāṇa).

Indeed, the state of having been made immeasurable is certainly attained. For it is called "lofty" (mahaggata) because of its capacity to suppress the defilements, its long duration in the continuum, and its abundant fruit.
It does not lag behind (na ohīyati) in that continuum wherein sense-sphere karma and lofty karma have been performed and accumulated, at the time of yielding their result.

Having obtained the opportunity and remaining [in the process of rebirth], sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma is unable to give its own result after having pushed aside the other [exalted karma] and itself remaining behind;
however, exalted (*mahaggata*) karma alone is able to give its own result by warding off the other, due to its weightiness.
Therefore he said, "That sense-sphere karma," and so forth. "By way of defilements" (*kilesavasena*):
By way of the defilements that constitute the root of evil karma. For killing living beings and so forth originate from defilements rooted in hatred, delusion, greed, and the like.
Alternatively, "by way of defilement" means by way of the defilement of karma. For this has been said: "Householder’s son, killing living beings is indeed a defilement of karma," and so on.
"It proceeds according to the connection" means it concludes by way of the connection known as *yathānusandhi*.
It has been concluded because it was brought to completion by means of the qualities of purification arising from the presence of defilement.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhadhamasutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Kulasutta*.

361. *Evaṃ pavattaīhitikā*: thus, there are two kinds of livelihoods (*īhitikā*) that proceed in this way. These two livelihoods are modes of existence that involve difficult means of making a living.
It is called *salākā* because a mere tally-stick (*salāka*) is mentioned here; the latter member of the compound has been elided in the first word. *Ubhatokoṭikaṃ*:
if he says, "I do not praise the non-arising of families," then you should level the charge against him, saying, "O ascetic, you are cruel beings."
Now, [the King] said, "He always says, 'I praise the decline of families.
This being so, why, at a time of such famine, do you, surrounded by a great assembly, wander through the countryside on tour and proceed to bring about the ruin of families?
Thus he dispatched the village headman to raise this dilemma.
"The two extremes" refers to both limits. "To draw out externally" means that by releasing the two extremes—namely, "I do not praise" and "I do praise"—one draws out the matter under discussion;
this is what is meant by "drawing it out. In that context, one who reproaches by pointing out faults makes the matter unasked, as if swallowing it and pushing it back inside.

The passage beginning with "Hence, village headman" is undertaken for the purpose of showing that by giving alms to his own bhikkhus and to other bhikkhus who desire his welfare, he has avoided meeting with what is undesirable.
"Produced by giving" means they have properly attained growth (*bhūti*) through the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya*).
"Truly produced" (*saccasambhūta*) means they have properly arisen through truth, which is the noble mode of speech (*ariyavohāra*); thus he said this.
“Truth” means being a speaker of truth. “The remaining virtue” refers to virtue other than the eightfold noble speech.
“Laid up” means it was deposited as a store by previous ancestors of that family. “Ill-employed” means occupations such as farming, trade, and so forth, which have been poorly managed.
“Fail” means they perish. “A disgrace to the family” means one who is like charcoal to the family.
The person who causes destruction. "Impermanence" means death; it is the total destruction of the wealth of the leading men of that family.
Therefore he said, "having been, there is non-existence," and so forth.
The commentary on the Kula-sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Maṇicūḷaka Sutta 362.
"That assembly" refers to that royal assembly seated in the royal palace. "Grasping the method" means standing by one's own judgment alone, without having heard it from anyone else.
It is proper to have [the dwelling] repaired if there is the possibility of restoration; the destruction of the lodging should not be overlooked.

This is the intended meaning. Here, at the conclusion of his own duties, he said "having made it into a household article" (gihivikataṃ katvā) with reference to that which belongs specifically to householders and is for temporary use.
I do not say this because it is suitable for those who have gone forth.
The commentary on the Maṇicūḷaka Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Bhadraka Sutta 363.
"In the country named thus": there were royal princes from the Mallian clan who were inhabitants of a region;

because they were so numerous that the name "Mallas" was applied to them as a collective designation, it refers to that country named thus. There is no interval of time designated for this attainment.
"Time" means non-time; that itself is "timeless. Therefore he said: "having attained it without transgressing time.
Furthermore, as it was stated—“Whatever suffering arises, all that has its root in desire”—this refers to the fact that suffering has desire as its root.
Because suffering is thus described as having desire as its root, it is said: "In this sutta, the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) is discussed."
The commentary on the Bhadraka Sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Rāsiya Sutta: 364.
Having grouped [the questions] according to Māra’s snares, and having further divided them there by way of internal distinctions, the questions to be asked are as follows:
Having made them into a single heap. *Tapas* is the practice of self-mortification; one who possesses this is a *tapassin*, and thus [the text says] "that ascetic.
Furthermore, because he stands depending upon that austerity, it is said "one who relies on austerity" (*tapanissitaka*).

Moreover, because his mode of living is coarse and harsh through various distinctions, he is called "one who lives coarsely" (*lūkhajīvī*); therefore, it says "one of coarse livelihood" (*lūkhajīvika*). Of the middle...
They are called *anta* (ends) because they are off the path of practice; for that very reason, they are *anta* because of their inferiority.
Even what is inferior is called "end" (*anta*), as in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, this is one end among ways of livelihood.

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, taking them to have a mutual relationship of support, they are described as "parts" (*koṭṭhāsa*). The Pāli reads "a low village" (*hīno gāmo*). The word "village" (*gāma*)—
The term "village-dweller" (*gāmī*) is stated with the intended meaning of "inferior method. It is called "village-dweller" because it exists in the village (*gāme bhavo*).

Here, the word "village" refers to the inhabitants of the village, as in expressions such as "a villager has arrived. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "the Dhamma of those who dwell in the village," the meaning of which is "their conduct.
The word "self" (*atta*) here is a synonym for the body, as in "one who torments himself" (*attantapo*); thus he says, "the meaning is 'causing bodily suffering.'"
Regarding the phrase "in this": why are the two extremes and the middle way mentioned in this context of the basis for austerity and censure?
The intention is that first, the devotion to self-mortification is indeed included because it exists here.

Since the explanation of the intended meaning becomes possible through the demonstration of the objects of austerity and censure associated with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, the intended meaning is stated after showing those [objects].

"Showing that meaning": he reveals the meaning stated as follows: "One who censures only those things worthy of censure among those who indulge in sensual pleasures and rely on self-mortification, and praises only those things worthy of praise. "By reckless action" means by improper action.
"Both by what is lawful and what is unlawful" means by both righteous and unrighteous means. "External [action] proceeding from lack of reflection."

Addressing this, the prompter said, “How? and so forth. The other, showing that this was not intended as such self-mortification, but rather as practice conducted with wise attention (yoniso) according to the Teaching itself, said, “And by way of fourfold energy.
In that context, [the passage] beginning with “Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain,” refers to insight (vipassanā) practiced without regard for the body.
The development of energy that proceeds by way of exertion is called "by way of the four factors of energy.

Likewise, the development of energy that proceeds by way of living in the open air, sitting, or using a particular seat, and which is capable of crushing the defilements, is called "by way of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).

Wearing away (nijjarā) is the abandoning of all defilements without remainder by means of the Noble Path. And that is visible here and now (sanditthika) because it is personally realized through the abandoning of the three root defilements.
And it is said, “three. Therefore he says, “even one,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Rāsiya Sutta is finished.
13. Commentary on the Pāṭaliya Sutta.

365. Regarding the statement, “And I understand illusion (māyā),” while it is certainly intended to show their deceptive nature, for the Blessed One, at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, there was the destruction of the bridge to all evil states such as illusion and guile;
therefore, having entirely abandoned illusion, through his omniscience he understands illusion and all other knowable things in their entirety. Thus it is said: “And I, māyañcāhaṃ...”
“O village headman, I understand,” and so forth. “And I understand illusion” means:
not only do I know illusion, but I also know this and that other thing as well.
“By women and by other desires” means: by women and by desires other than those. “In one place” means: in one location. For each individual...
To a visitor, whether a householder or one who has gone forth. "In accordance with one's strength" means in accordance with the strength of one's wealth.

"In accordance with one's power" means in accordance with the power of one's retinue; or, "in accordance with one's strength" means in accordance with the strength of one’s faith, and "in accordance with one's power" means in accordance with the power of one’s wealth.
Concentration regarding the phenomena (*dhammesu samādhi*) is the settling of the mind upon the ten wholesome phenomena. It is the state of the mind not being seized [by unwholesome states].
[This refers to] being overwhelmed by obsessions. By this, mundane purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) and purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) are stated.
Thus it is said: “What is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight.
To show what must be done next for one established therein, it is said: “Established in the concentration of the Dhamma,” and so forth. This is the practice (*paṭipadā*). Of that—

The word of the Teacher who proclaims the fruit of karma, and this practice of mine—consisting of the restraint of virtue, the divine abodes, and meditative development—leads precisely to the state of being faultless.
Regarding "the victory": in either case, there is no defeat for me whatsoever.
The five factors are called "concentration on the Dhamma," or they are simply the phenomena of insight, the path, and the fruit. In the third alternative:

The sublime abodes (brahmavihāra), together with the purification of virtue and so forth, are called "concentration on the Dhamma" precisely because they bring about the three aforementioned types of states.

The one-pointedness of mind that arises in one who fulfills these is what was referred to as "momentary one-pointedness of mind. That too is called "concentration of mind" because it steadies the mind; it occurs by way of suppressing and completely cutting off its opposites.
The very concentration described above is specifically termed "concentration of mind" (cittasamādhi).
The commentary on the Pāṭaliya Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Gāmaṇi Saṃyutta is finished.
9. Saṃyutta on the Unconditioned (Asaṅkhata-Saṃyutta) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhama-Vagga) 1–11.
Commentary on the Discourses on Mindfulness Directed to the Body and Others (Kāyagatāsati-Suttādi-Vaṇṇanā)
366–376. "Unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) means not conditioned by causes and conditions. Therefore he said, "unmade" (*akata*).
"Seeking the beneficial" means practicing loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Compassionate" means practicing compassion (*karuṇā*). "Having taken up" means having adopted;
this is the meaning, as he said, "having embraced with the mind. "Teaching of the Dhamma without perversion" means the teaching of the Dhamma that is free from error, [as well as] the practice.
The Blessed One is as heavy as his disciples; he bestows the inheritance he has determined for them.
This occurs at the time when the seven favorable conditions—such as the attainment of alms-food—are met.
However, in times of misfortune, the meaning should be understood by reversing what has been stated here. "Heavy" means terrible due to the abundance of suffering.
"It should be obtained from us. "Your instruction" means the instruction that should be given to you.
The commentary on the *Kāyagatāsati-sutta* and others is finished.
2. Second Chapter.
23–33. Commentary on the *Asaṅkhata-sutta* and others (377–409).
In this context, it is called *anata* because there is no bending (*nata*)—that is, craving—in it; or, because when it is attained, there is no further state of being a person (*puggalabhāva*).
The term *anāsava* follows the same method here as well. It is *sacca* by virtue of its true nature (*saccadhammatā*). From the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*),...

It is called "the further shore" (*pāra*) because one goes to the further shore. "In the sense of subtlety" means it is refined in the sense of being subtle; for that very reason, it is difficult to see. It is "undecaying" (*ajajjara*) because its intrinsic nature is eternal.
Or, it is "incomparable" (*anidassana*) because there is nothing to compare it with. When this is attained, there is no [more] cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Or, it is "without proliferation" (*nippapañca*) because it does not proliferate.

When this is attained, there is no death for the person; thus it is "the Deathless" (*amata*). Or, in the sense of not being satiated with, it is "sublime" (*paṇīta*). Or, because it is the cause of happiness, it is "auspicious" (*siva*). It is the "destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaya*) because craving is exhausted therein.
Because nothing else like it exists, it is "unprecedented" (*abhūta*) due to its marvelous nature. Being unproduced from any condition whatsoever, it is "become" (*bhūta*), meaning it is existent.
Therefore he said: "Having been unborn, it exists. There is no suffering here; thus it is "free from suffering" (*niddukkha*).

Its state is the absence of suffering (*niddukkhatta*). Therefore, it is *anītika*, meaning free from calamity (*īti*). "Weaving" (*vāna*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*); by the absence of that, it is *nibbāna*.

"Affliction" (*byābajjha*) is said to be suffering; by the absence of that, it is *abyābajjha*. It exists as the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), as reality (*sacca*), and as the state of purity (*suddhibhāva*).

Sensual pleasures (*kāma*) themselves are "attachments" (*ālaya*) because they are clung to by worldlings (*puthujjana*). This same method applies to the others as well. "In the sense of a foundation" (*patiṭṭhaṭṭhena*).
It is like a lamp for those desiring liberation from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) by virtue of its state as a firm foundation, because it cannot be overwhelmed by the floods (ogha).
"In the sense of being fit to cling to" means because it is worthy of being clung to. "In the sense of protection" means in the sense of protecting oneself and others.
"In the sense of a refuge from fear" means in the sense of destroying fear. "Supreme" (seṭṭha) means most excellent (uttama). "Gati" means the abode of the gandhabbas.
The commentary on the *Asaṅkhata-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta* is finished.
10. The *Abyākata-saṃyutta*.
1. Commentary on the Khemā Sutta 410.
"A female lay follower of Bimbisāra" means a female lay follower who was formerly among the harem attendants of King Bimbisāra. "Wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*) is due to her state of having been trained;

"proficiency" (*veyyattiya*) is due to her state of being confident (*visāradabhāva*). One who is "confident" possesses natural wisdom (*sābhāvikapaññā*) established by a rebirth with three roots (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*); she is endowed with that.

"Skilled in gapless counting" means skilled in counting by nines. "Skilled in counting with finger-joints" means skilled in counting by means of the finger-joints alone, just like a *pādasika* (a type of calculator).
"By counting in groups" refers to counting by way of aggregates for those who are proficient in mental synthesis (*saṅkalanapaṭuppanna*).
"The Tathāgata" refers to one whose taints are destroyed; he asks with reference to such a Tathāgata, thus [the text says] "one whose taints are destroyed."
This designation exists based upon the aggregates (khandhas) developed through mastery over the fruit of Arhatship.
While those aggregates exist, it is possible to designate them by conventional usage as "beings whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava); when they are no longer present, it is not possible.
Therefore, because it was stated [in the Sutta] that "after death," and since those [aggregates] are absent, it was said: "This has not been declared. If...
Thus, because of their non-existence, one might have had to admit "yes" when asked, "Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
However, it should be understood that this was not admitted because the question concerned what is designated as a "being.
The phrase "that form by which... and so forth was stated in order to exclude the form described for the seven [types of] Tathāgatas from the omniscient Tathāgata.
"Depending on what" means depending on that pentad of aggregates. "By the absence of that" means by the absence of that pentad of aggregates.
"The designation of that" refers to the non-existence of the designation of a "being. It does not point to anything ceased.
Because the first sutta spoken by the Elder Nun Khemā illuminates the Blessed One’s supreme meaning, it is said to "belong to the sphere of the highest state," as it were.
The commentary on the Khemā Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Anurādha Sutta: 411.
Here, in this Saḷāyatana Vagga, it was spoken by the compilers of the collection through the process of communal recitation.
3–8. Commentary on the First Sāriputta-Koṭṭhika Sutta, etc., §§412–417.

"Merely form" (*rūpamatta*): here, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding a qualification. What, then, is that qualification? It is the self (*attā*) which is conceptually imagined as being external and is referred to here as the "Tathāgata. "Of an unapprehendable nature" (*anupalabbhiya-sabhāva*): because it is unapprehendable.
The commentary on the First Sāriputta-Koṭṭhika Sutta, etc., is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Kutūhalasālā Sutta 418.
"Of various kinds" (*nānāvidha*) means other miscellaneous talk concerning various sectarian doctrines (*diṭṭhivāda*) or other such idle chatter (*tiracchānakathā*).
The construction is: "the source from which curiosity arises for many. "It goes as far as the Ābhassara Brahma-world" refers to [the range] by fire.
This is said with reference to [the body] going at the time of the world’s emergence (*kappavuṭṭhāna*). "And this body" means this material body (*rūpakāya*).
"He lays it down by means of the death-consciousness" means he lays it down while the death-consciousness is breaking up.
For, prior to the death-consciousness, during the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness, the kamma-born matter that has arisen ceases together with the death-consciousness; after that—

However, kamma-born matter does not arise. If it were to arise, death would not occur; the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) would not fail to produce matter, and nutriment-born matter would simply be impossible.

But temperature-born matter continues to proceed. Because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), a being is said to "arise" for another existence, whereas at the moment of death, the rebirth-linking consciousness has not yet been obtained for another existence.
Therefore it was said: “At the moment of death... [etc] ...it exists.
The commentary on the Kutūhalasālā Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta.
419. "With their tenet" means that this statement, "there is a self," would have been identical with the tenet of those eternalists.
For that very reason, it would not have been in conformity with knowledge; the intention is that it is therefore essence-less. "Would it be in conformity for me with this? means:
would it be in conformity with my insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that there is no-self? The sense is that it would indeed be contrary to it.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Sabhiya-Kaccāna Sutta. 420.
Regarding the reading *yassapassā*, this is the summarized meaning of the passage beginning with "Friend" (*āvuso*). Therein, the connection is as follows: "Friend... [and so forth].

Even for a person who has practiced for three years, if after such a time they were to give only this much explanation—that "when a cause exists, there is the designation 'possessing form' and so forth, and when it does not exist, there is none"—that would already be quite a lot for that person;
what need then to speak of what has gone beyond? Regarding the method of teaching the Dhamma that transcends this, there is simply nothing more to be said.
Having heard the elder’s answer to his question, the wanderer expressed his joy and gladness.
The commentary on the Sabhiya-Kaccāna Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Abyākata Saṃyutta is finished.
